Moreover, the oil and gas sector’s capex response to energy price spikes has softened in recent years, suggesting a smaller boost to GDP from higher oil prices than in prior episodes. The March Labour Force Survey reinforced this message. The economy added just 14.1k jobs last month, which did lit- tle to offset the 109k positions lost over the prior two months. Gains were concentrated in natural resources, the sector poised to benefit the most from higher global oil prices. How- ever, this industry accounts for just 1% of total employment in Canada. Manufacturing, wholesale and retail trade, and transportation meanwhile together employ nearly 30% of the workforce and will face higher input costs on top of tariff- driven demand weakness. Employment in these sectors had already been hit hard by the trade war before shedding an additional 2.6k jobs last month. A US-Iran ceasefire was announced earlier this week, but it remains unclear how long it will take to reach an agreement to end the conflict entirely. Even if a deal is struck, oil prices would not immediately return to pre-conflict levels as supply backlogs, damage to facilities in the region, and lingering uncertainty over the status of the Strait of Hormuz will keep energy costs elevated for some time. Our base case remains a prolonged BoE hold. In this note, we take stock of how financial conditions have evolved in recent weeks, summarise what we know about how the BoE models energy shocks, and try to draw out the likely debates on the MPC at the April meeting. Our base case for April, for now, is an 8-1 vote for a hold, with Chief Economist Pill voting for a hike. Forecasts | How big of an undershoot? Historical sensitivities suggest the Staff could easily model a growth hit in excess of 1pp, given the scale of tightening in financial conditions and the increase in commodity prices. We would expect - even in the central projections - a lesser modelled impact (~50bp cumulatively), as the Staff incorporates some degree of real income resistance, and potentially a lower savings rate. This suggests less of an inflation undershoot over the medium-term than could be inferred from past BoE analyses of energy shocks (i.e. 2022/23). Although the fiscal space built since April 2025 is sufficient to accommodate the fuel tax buffer mechanism and subsidies on natural gas and electricity, the recent surge in energy prices driven by the Middle East conflict is expected to weigh on the budget balance. Our estimates suggest that the tax buffer mechanism has reduced motor fuel taxes by 75% to absorb the impact of rising prices, resulting in $1.2bn (0.1%-pt of GDP) in forgone tax revenues to date. Should motor fuel prices remain at current levels, this cost is expect- ed to persist at $1.2bn per month. Additionally, natural gas and electricity subsidies are expected to exert further pressure on the budget. records.text: ting EU trade and investment restrictions Despite the European Commission’s counter-veiling tariffs (up to 35.3%) on Chinese-built battery electric vehicles (BEVs) effective from 30 October 2024, China’s auto exports to the region have remained resilient. The combined tariff burden—reaching up to 45.3% including the standard 10% import duty—initially weighed on exports, but shipments rebounded thereafter. In 2025, China’s auto exports to the EU rose by around 30%, exceeded 1 million units for the first time, and made the EU the largest destination across EV segments (BEV, PHEV and HEV). From a policy perspective, easing geopolitical risks should reinforce the Bank of Canada’s confidence that downside risks to labor markets, consumption, and growth are not intensifying. At the same time, the risk of second-round inflation effects appears contained. Taken together, this backdrop supports the BoC’s assessment that policy is appropriately calibrated. We continue to expect the Bank to remain on hold through 2026, before beginning a cautious hiking cycle in 1Q27 toward the midpoint of the neutral range. At this stage, we see risks to the policy path as broadly balanced, with the upcoming USMCA review representing the key macro risk in the months ahead. The March employment report points to a stabilization in labor market conditions following two consecutive weak prints, with total employment rising 14.1k after cumulative losses of over 100k in January and February. While the rebound suggests some near-term stabilization, the pace of job growth remains soft, and short-term trends continue to run below longer-term averages. As in prior months, we interpret recent volatility in the LFS as a normalization following the outsized gains in late 2025—which were not reflected in SEPH—rather than a signal of new trends in the labor market. Despite an announced cease-fire, the conflict is not resolved and oil prices could spike from already elevated levels if fears of an extended disruption emerge. An extended disruption in the Strait of Hormuz would also generate physical supply constraints, depressing industrial activity, with Asia most exposed to a loss of Middle East energy imports. Our baseline assumes that the cease-fire is a signal for a grad- ual reopening of the Strait. But the material rundown in buffer stocks has implications for the price path ahead. As we wrote in our Data Center Securitization: An Introduction publication, the terminal value/refinancing risk is the primary risk for bondholders. We have approached the sector with a healthy skepticism. CMBS analysts know well what it is like to buy bonds backed by property types that have a good story but face refinancing issues down the line (office, for example). Even when we wrote this primer late last summer, our personal use of AI was akin to a glorified Google search via chatbots. This lived experience gave us a cautious view of the data center securitization market. But as we venture into the proliferation of agentic AI (AI that can now do things!) and growing enterprise adoption, we are somewhat less concerned. Our working thesis for hyperscale data center securitizations ran something like this: data center shells have very long useful lives (30-40yrs), but GPU cycles are short (2-3yrs and now more like 12 months). Data center operators do not own the GPUs (the tenants do), but they own and operate the physical infrastructure that ultimately allows these GPUs to run efficiently, including power systems, cooling infrastructure, and networking hardware. If GPU useful lives are short (let’s say 2-3 years according to the bears), tenant upgrades of the GPU fleets would cause operators to upgrade the infrastructure to facilitate the GPU

Our baseline view is that for risk management reasons the ECB will hike by 50bp to 2.50%. 2.50% is the upper end of the range of neutral. Hikes to this level signal the ECB's commitment to price stability while not overly burdening growth. The uncertainties are high and there are risks on both sides. At the same time, the longer the normalisation of Middle East energy supply is delayed, the greater the risk that 50bp of hikes might not be sufficient. However, this does not mean the relationship between energy prices and the scale of hikes will be linear. If growth estimates are too optimistic, there might be a limit to how far the ECB can hike. A demand shock that boosts oil prices would also boost corporate profits, whereas an increase in prices that stems from a negative supply shock should have a negative impact on purchasing power and in turn corporate profits. Indeed, with de-escalation under way, coupled with the decline in volatility (see below for details), the swap spread curve has begun to normalize and TFP now sits just one standard deviation above our estimate of fair value (Figure 4). This suggests that there could be further steepening of the swap spread curve in the near-term. In our mid-week publication (see Figure 5 in Dark side of the moon), we examined how far spread curves had retraced back to their pre-conflict levels. In summary, most of the room for further steepening appears to be in curves anchored in the front-end of the curve, with the widening exposure anchored in the 5-7 year sector. In addition, we noted that the 10-year sector appeared most attractive for anchoring narrowers, and we maintained our 7s/10s flattening exposure. Next week also marks the start of bank earnings, which should be interesting on multi- ple fronts. First, with the Middle East conflict pushing yields higher in March, 1Q26 is the first quarter since 2025 in which yields increased over the quarter (Figure 5), suggesting banks are likely to post AOCI losses. We project that the top four banks by size and the next ten will likely, in aggregate, post approximately $2bn of AOCI losses in 1Q26 (Fig- ure 6), which could be a modest headwind for UST demand. Second, we may get commen- tary on the impact of the Middle East conflict, as well as Basel III Endgame and GSIB regu- latory updates

records.text: meeting just around the corner and the outcome dependent on developments in the Middle East, the OIS market was pricing a 56% probability of an April rate hike as of the 9th, implying that both a hold and a hike appear plausible. Attention turns to Governor Ueda’s remarks at the trust association conference on the 13th, which will be the last scheduled BoJ board member communication ahead of the April meeting. That said, it is also worth noting that last year’s remarks at the same conference were brief and did not offer major hints regarding the future course of monetary policy. In addition, because no other BoJ board members are scheduled to communicate before the April meeting, the possibility of the BoJ communicating through the media cannot be ruled out, meaning headline risk may also be present. In the superlong sector, while conditions continue to depend on how developments in the Middle East unfold, the term premium remains above a fair level when viewed over a longer horizon. For it to move from current levels toward fair value, buying would likely need to return on improved sentiment, making the first round of talks between the US and Iran scheduled for the 11th (Reuters, 9 April) one focal point. As seen in this week's 30y auction, even amid opaque conditions, investors are willing to step in when valuations become cheap versus the supply- demand backdrop. In that context, next week’s 20y auction will serve as a test of investors’ stance toward the superlong sector.

At mid-year, the FWC is due to decide this year’s increase in the broader minimum wage. Here we outline expected impacts on the overall wage price index (WPI), in the context of organic wage dynamics coming from the broader economy. Wage growth has already slowed to inflation target-consistent levels in the low 3s, and in our view the above legislated changes won’t disturb that range. Rather, they should prevent a further slowing in the WPI driven by institutional factors and the normalization from a previously tighter labor market. Now you’re all grown-up Retail, fast food and pharmacy businesses disproportionately employ young people, at wages largely determined by the industrial relations framework. The modern Award stipulates minimum wage rates for those under 21, tiered as a propor- tion of “adult” rates reflecting relative “maturity, life experi- ence, and opportunity to have obtained work experience”. For example, those under 16 currently earn 45% of a 21 year old in the same role, under the general retail workers Award. We forecast inflation to rise meaningfully above previous assumptions, with IPCA ending 2026 at 5.0% (from 4.0%), easing to 4.0% in 2027 (from 3.5%), as first round energy effects combine with broader second round pressures, particularly through food prices. This configuration would lead to a qualitative change in the monetary policy reaction function. While we previously assumed 50bp rate cuts per meeting, the higher and more uncertain inflation would likely prompt the BCB to slow the pace of easing to 25bp steps, reflecting increased uncertainty around inflation persistence and expectations. The data underscores a fragile growth outlook where even a minor shock could tip a quarter into negative territory, and highlights that the risks of a recession are rising amid increasing uncertainty and tightening financial conditions. The final Services PMI edged up to 50.2 (flash 50.1), but the key story was the starkly different performance in the periphery. Spain’s services sector significantly beat expectations, while Italy’s performed much worse than anticipated. The strength in Spain may prove temporary, as it was driven by existing orders while future expectations were reportedly more subdued. Conversely, Italy's sharp decline may be a one-off, partly attributed to a post-Winter Olympics slowdown in activity. The latest average reading across the estimates for Q4 2025 is 1.6% . Unsurprisingly, the range of estimates is wide, from 0.9% on the low end, represented by HLW, to 2.8% on the high end, represented by 5y5y TIPS adjusted for a typical spread between CPI and PCE. Based on this dashboard, the current nominal fed funds rate of 3.6% would be exactly in line with the average neutral estimate if inflation were at 2% -- i.e. average r-star of 1.6% plus 2% inflation is equivalent to the current nominal fed funds rate of 3.6% . However, with inflation still well above 2% and projected to remain above target for some time, the current fed funds rate is likely below the neutral setting implied by the average r -star estimate in our dashboard. In this sense, while it may be reasonable to describe policy as in the vicinity of neutral, it may be more accurate to classify policy as somewhat accommodative rather than modestly or moderately restrictive . This alternative assessment of the policy stance would be consistent with the desire of “some” Fed officials to adopt a more two-sided description of the policy outlook, one that included the potential to raise rates if inflation stayed elevated for longer. records.text: 10 April 2026 Focus Europe Page 2 Deutsche Bank AG Starting the year on a softer note: a smaller growth buffer to absorb an energy shock The Iran shock is poised to significantly impact the European economy. We recently downgraded our macro forecast for the euro area, lower annual growth for 2026 to 0.5% from 1.1%. While this week's ceasefire announcement is positive news, there remains a lot of uncertainty, about the durability of a ceasefire, the timing of a full reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and the extent of lasting damage that might already have been done to Middle East energy supply. The number of vessels passing through the Strait of Hormuz remains low despite the ceasefire. The spot price of oil is roughly halfway between the ECB's baseline and 'adverse' scenarios, and the forward price of oil is above the 'adverse' scenario (see here). In short, despite the ceasefire, there will still be a cost to growth. The question is, how much? The Bloomberg consensus forecast for 2026 euro area GDP growth is 1.1%. The ECB's new baseline scenario puts growth at 0.9%. Both look too optimistic, in our view. Before we question some of the ECB's assumed growth dynamics in the second half of this note, in the first half we focus on the signals of a weaker start to growth in 2026 even before the conflict in the Middle East began. Euro Area: Rates Strategy Uneasy The ceasefire has brought some relief to EUR rates but the set-up feels uneasy. A sustained decline in oil price is a necessary condition for further removal of rate hike pricing but some residual hike premium is likely to remain. We also explore why Bund ASWs have stalled after the great fall. An uneasy, unclear truce. After fears of a significant escalation in the Middle East conflict saw oil and front-end yields surge to local highs on Tuesday, the news of the two-week ceasefire allowed the markets to heave a sigh of relief. Developments over this week were once again right out of President Trump's 'escalate to de-escalate' playbook and even as there is a sense of fragility to the truce, there is some comfort to be drawn from the fact that active talks have begun even if the demands from all parties involved appear maximalist at this point in time. One was to adjust Fedwire operations to help banks net outgoing and incoming payments more efficiently, which could reduce the need to maintain large reserve buffers at the start of the day. Another was to encourage greater use of digital payments as a way to temper demand for physical currency, easing one structural source of Fed liabilities. Taken together, it’s clear that the path to a smaller Fed balance sheet is far from straightfor- ward: there are many levers available, and each comes with meaningful tradeoffs. Impor- tantly, a significant decline in the Fed’s balance sheet, particularly one that pushes reserve balances toward scarcity, risks triggering dislocations in funding markets. The events of 2019 are a clear reminder of how quickly conditions can tighten when reserves become constrained. For now, the Fed is therefore likely to proceed cautiously and incrementally, prioritizing market functioning over speed to avoid a repeat of those disruptions. As such, meaningful balance sheet reforms and their practical market implications are unlikely to arrive in the near-term—and the odds of remaining in an ample-reserves regime still look materially higher than a return to a scarce reserves regime.

The 15th Five-Year-Plan suggests energy transition continuity The recently published 15th Five-Year Plan (FYP) suggests that China's long-standing energy transition will continue during 2026-2030, promoting green energy to a more active role while reaching peak fossil fuel consumption. There is a also a clear focus on power transition investment and integration of various power supply and innovations, and the continuing industry reform will mean reduced government intervention in market pricing, which is favorable to renewables. Key highlights of the plan: • Higher new energy share: the technology list covers most green energy types, including wind, solar, hydro, nuclear, distributed energy (solar and wind), biomass, geothermal, marine, full hydrogen chain. The strategy will also expand to the “desert to gobi” hubs. • Cap fossil fuels: reach peak consumption of coal and oil; cut coal use while ensuring supply; upgrade coal power for efficiency/flexibility/heating; reposition coal as grid-balancing; expand exploration of oil and natural gas and integrate them with new energy. • A new type of power system: support the energy strategy with coordinated development of "generation - grid - load - storage"; expand smart grids, micro-grids and digital dispatch; grow demand-side flexibility and virtual power plants; accelerate pumped hydro and new storage; harden grid security. 8 April 2026 12 Barclays | Economics / Sustainable Investing

records.text: 6 Thirsty truth: Semiconductor manufacturing relies heavily on ultrapure water (UPW), which can be either procured externally from specialized service providers or produced on-site through advanced water treatment plants designed to meet the purity requirements of each fabrication facility. The scale of usage is enormous: a large semiconductor fab can use up to 38 million liters per day, equivalent to roughly 500 swimming pools (Interface, 20 June 2024). The rapid expansion of AI infrastructure is driving up chip demand, which in turn is increasing water demand. At the same time, as chip designs evolve, each new generation of semiconductor manufacturing introduces additional etching and cleaning steps per wafer, raising the water intensity of production. North Asia’s water challenge: North Asia remains the global hub for semiconductor manufacturing, but the rising frequency of extreme weather events is testing the sector’s resilience. During the 2021 drought in Taiwan, TSMC had to truck water to its fabrication facilities, incurring USD28.6mn in costs and pushing water expenses to about 2% of its quarterly revenue (Taiwan News, 21 May 2021). Water stress tests US semi ambitions: As part of broader semiconductor reshoring efforts, a wave of new fabs is under construction across the US. For January, a comparison of wage levels between the old and new samples was published; this year, total cash earnings in the new sample are 0.5% lower than in the old sample. However, water availability remains an important constraint on nuclear power deployment. Conventional nuclear reactors rely heavily on freshwater cooling systems, particularly for inland plants, which can create operational challenges in water-stressed regions. Advanced reactor technologies might alleviate some of these constraints. Many next-generation reactor designs use alternative cooling systems that rely on non- water coolants, including gas, molten salt, and liquid metals such as sodium or lead, potentially reducing dependence on freshwater resources (see Nuclear power: A core solution for a carbon-free future, dated 7 August 2025). Improving water efficiency in thermal power generation: Despite the rapid growth of clean energy, much of the near-term electricity demand from AI data centers is likely to continue relying on thermal generation. We expect natural gas to supply a significant share of incremental power demand in the US by 2035. We expect similar dynamics in Europe, while coal is likely to remain an important contributor in parts of APAC in the near term due to existing power system structures and energy security considerations. Under those conditions, which are not very far from the “de-escalation” scenario we discussed last week (here), we would think the ECB could look through what would be ultimately a relatively mild inflation shock and would stay on hold in 2026. But we do not expect that goods prices as soon as March would reflect these new upside risks and pencil in a moderate 0.3% increase in March PPI core goods. The more important components of March PPI will be those that matter for PCE inflation, particularly airfares. In March 2022, airfares in PPI rose in the same month as the large jump in jet fuel prices. This could reflect technical issues of higher ticket prices boosting net revenues (how PPI prices are measured) before airlines actually incur the cost of higher jet fuel. This technical issue keeps us cautious on upside risks for PPI airfares in March. But after March, we would expect softer PPI airfares compared to CPI. PPI airfares have stayed stronger since 2022 compared to CPI airfares, possibly reflecting some buffer that could limit the upside to further net revenue increases with higher input costs again. Other details like medical services prices and financial services will be important for PCE inflation. We expect a modest decline in portfolio management fees in March given falling asset prices, with an even larger drop in April that will help limit some upside to PCE inflation. The current market situation, characterized by the Middle East situation and a dollar rally across the board, has led us to favor isolating the beta to the dollar while maintaining a bullish view on the ARS. To express this view, we have chosen to use the CLP as the funding currency, as we believe ARS is likely to outperform CLP in the current environment. There are three key factors supporting our decision: carry differential and trade profiles. Carry differential: The ARS offers a decent carry of xx% per month in the NDF curve, whereas the CLP has one of the lowest carry in Latam due to the BCCh’s aggressive easing cycle. This carry differential could lead to an outperformance of ARS relative to CLP if market sentiment shifts towards a more risk-on approach and markets reload FX carry positions. Sensitivity to risk sentiment: ARS’s strong carry profil and its FX band mechinsim might have contributed to a more isolated price action than its peers. In fact, during the recent dollar rally, ARS has tended to exhibit the lowest beta and outperform its peers. If external risk sentiment worsens, CLP may be more sensitive to changes in risk sentiment and underperform ARS. Accordingly, we continue to forecast headline inflation declining to 4.1% by YE26 (2027: 3.8%) and core inflation easing to 4.0% (2027: 3.6%). Against this backdrop, this week Banxico released the meeting minutes from its March 26 interest rate decision when amid a split vote. Three board members voted to cut the reference rate by 25bp to 6.50% against two members voting to remain on hold. In our view, the document was very similar to the post-meeting communiqué as it reinforces the division in the board but with the majority assessing space for one additional cut, albeit its timing would be conditioned to the evolution of the geopolitical conflict and its effect on energy prices and pass- through to domestic prices. Deputy Governors Borja and Heath, who voted to stand pat, reiterated the need to be cautious amid current higher uncertainty that makes the inflation outlook more complex. However, for now, Banxico's majority seems to feel comfortable with a moderate oil price shock, given Mexican authorities ability to smooth price adjustments through tax changes. Thus, we maintain our expectation that Banxico will deliver one final cut of 25bp, on May 7 or June 25. records.text: Iran conflict has exposed Asia’s heavy reliance on the Middle East (ME). With about half of the region's crude and over a third of its gas imports transiting through this region, the closure of the Strait of Hormuz had become a critical chokepoint for the region over the last month. We had, therefore, become progressively worried about the lack of energy availability in some Asian economies and the non-linear impact that could have on growth. Earlier this week, the US and Iran announced a two-week ceasefire with the opening of the Strait as part of the temporary deal, coming as a huge relief to Asia. But it’s not clear whether the ceasefire will hold and whether the Strait of Hormuz will close again if no deal is reached. This note, therefore, lays out the relative vulnerability in the region. Which economies are the most vulnerable if the Strait closes again? We had discussed relative vulnerability within Asia in the early weeks of the conflict. However, that analy- sis did not presume that energy availability would become a binding constraint. Instead, it presumed that the shock would transmit through more conventional channels (adverse terms of trade, remittances). As volumes have become a constraint, however, we re-assess vulnerability, explicitly taking into account who is most at risk of an energy shortage if the Strait closes again. During that period, the pullback and foreign and domestic demand was mostly balanced. Yesterday afternoon, the Treasury released a detailed breakdown of the March auction statistics, which provides some perspective on demand across investor categories. Investment funds and foreign and international investors make up the bulk of final demand at auctions. Per the Treasury 2 , investment funds include mutual funds, money market funds, hedge funds, money managers, and investment advisors. Foreign and international investors include private foreign entities, non-private foreign entities, and foreign officials. Overall, foreign participation declined across tenors and has retraced to trend levels following a period of rising demand ( Figure 1). The pullback likely reflects some caution amid heightened uncertainty as rate vol surged in March, rather than a shift in the underlying demand backdrop. Domestic investors also retreated from front-end auctions but stepped up buying at longer tenors, offsetting reduced foreign participation. As rate volatility subsided in April, this month's auctions fared better. The 3y auction earlier this week stopped through with a strong showing from indirect bidders having taken down 75% of the supply, one of the highest in history. First, the size of these packages remains several orders of magnitude smaller than those implemented over 2021–23, when we estimate that the cumulative fiscal response reached close to 3% of euro area GDP . Second, cross-country heterogeneity in policy approaches remains pronounced, with southern European economies taking a more proactive stance in rolling out mitigating schemes than Germany and France. Looking ahead, should energy prices remain elevated for a prolonged period, we would expect governments to deploy additional policy support. Rolled over the remainder of 2026, we estimate that such measures could amount to between 0.2pp and 0.5pp of GDP at the euro area level, depending on the trajectory of energy prices. The fiscal cost of these interventions could be partly offset if governments introduce windfall profit taxes, as floated by several capitals, including Italy, Germany and Spain. Beyond direct support measures, we see the evolution of fiscal metrics this year as hinging on a combination of factors: while higher energy prices may temporarily boost energy-related indirect tax receipts, this effect is likely to be more than offset by higher interest expenditures

This highlights Indo- nesia’s relative insulation from the energy driven chaos of Mar, with USD length focused on energy deficit FX like THB, KRW and PHP (Figure 7 F X p e r f o r m a n c e b r e a k d o w n o v e r M a r ). As we have argued, the rupi- ah may even be considered a safe haven at some point, if the coal rally can continue to offset the hit from oil prices. This safe haven status has yet to be truly tested, however, with JCI dividends payments, a $2bn+ reduction in GBI-EM alloca- tions, and ongoing concerns about fiscal sustainability, credit ratings and MSCI related outflows still looming over markets. This suggests a highly path-dependent outlook for IDR, which remains negative in the near term but could turn more positive if the energy rally broadens out. The challenge for the rupiah, is net FX reserves have now fallen below the $90bn line in the sand, which may have motivated the BI to let $IDR break 17K this week. Identifying rating action drivers To calibrate our scoring weights, we analyzed 63 water and sewer issuers that were either upgraded (47) or downgraded (16) by Moody’s or S&P over 2024 through 1Q26 and for which complete data was available in Moody’s MFRA database, benchmarking their fiscal 2024 metrics against medians for Moody’s entire rated universe 4. Given the small sample size, we supplemented our quantitative work by parsing the individual rating action descriptions across S&P’s four quarterly water and sewer reports for full-year 2025, which encompassed 78 downgrades and 29 upgrades. For each negative action, we identified the credit factors S&P cited as drivers of the rating change. These two analyses produced consistent results: • Debt service coverage appears to be the strongest differentiator . The downgraded cohort posted a median debt service coverage (DSC) of 1.3x, roughly half the upgrad- ed cohort’s 2.7x and well below the all-issuer median of 2.5x. Fifteen of 16 downgrad- ed issuers (94%) had coverage below the all-issuer median, making this the single most predictive metric in the dataset. In the S&P analysis, weak or declining DSC was explicitly cited in 35 of 78 downgrades (45%). • Liquidity is a close second. Since we’ve already discussed agricultural prices above, we want to isolate the portion of energy costs in the 88% of food spending that goes to non-farm sources like retail overhead. The USDA Food Dollar tells us that 3% of total costs are energy-related (less than half as much as the household CPI share), and for simplicity we assume the same for just the non-farm portion, since it is difficult to strip out farm energy used solely for domestic food. Of that energy expense, petroleum-linked costs like diesel transportation are most relevant. However, past studies don’t find much pass-through from energy prices to food prices, at least outside of agricultural goods. Baumeister and Kilian (2014) remark that there is no evidence of oil price shocks leading to more than a negligible increase in retail food pric- es. Likewise, Diab and Karak (2023) note that while higher gasoline prices raise food costs, they do not find an effect on non-farm food costs. With 97% of final food costs coming from non-energy sources, labor costs are more important, especially in food away from home, and wage inflation is much lower now than during the commodity price surge in 2022. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 15 Key Recommendations We like owning the basis here with a focus on owning assets slightly less exposed to vol - 15yr mortgages, agency CMBS, and floaters on a first order, and then production specs, belly coupon Ginnie and Fannies, and maybe even deep discounts on a second order. We prefer to own vs swaps given that the largest buyers (GSEs and banks specifically) hedge with swaps and deregulation should be supportive. The risk is geopolitical concerns increasing and vol picking up. We also like owning mortgages vs. credit for indexed investors as we think the regulatory backdrop bringing bank demand and GSE support are positive for mortgages, while the supply headwinds and concerns around BDC/Private Credit will weigh on corporate credit. The risks are that the outlook for the US economy and growth are still fine, causing IG to outperform, and the entry point on valuations is not compelling. From a relative value perspective, we like owning FNCL 4.5s vs. 3.5s and 5.5s. The trade looks oversold, is correlated with adding basis exposure near local wides, and should benefit from positive MBS technicals. records.text: M Update 2 There are many ways to create a “Financial Conditions Index (FCI)”. The specific value of the recent ECB work lies in integrating financial variables (the calculated FCI is a weighted combination of interest rates, credit spreads, equity prices and exchange rates) and macroeconomic outcomes within a single model1 . This allows for a fully consistent framework to measure financial conditions, identify “structural” financial shocks and ultimately assess their impact on the growth and inflation outlook. We think this is how ECB Governors are likely to think about that topic (at least we would not be surprised if that sort of analysis would be rather influential in the Council). According to our replication of this paper, financial conditions tightened significantly in March, because of both lower equity prices and higher bonds yields. Last week, this metric stood at its highest (i.e. tightest) level since early 2025. The structural analysis shows however that only one-third of the observed deterioration of financial conditions in March stemmed from a “pure financial shock”. The rest was driven by structural “demand” and “supply” shocks affecting primarily (and more directly) activity and inflation. Through the same model, we estimate the pure “financial shock” observed in March to reduce EA GDP by -15bp within 2 to 3 months and reduce EA headline inflation by around -15bp 12 months from now. Inflation expectations the key to the current strategy The RBA’s strategy of engineering disinflation to target without a negative output gap crucially relies on inflation expectations remaining anchored. If expectations stay anchored, inflation can fall through easing demand pressures, slower margin expansion, and a gradual cooling in demand without requiring a negative output gap or sharp rise in unemployment. Because expectations feed directly into realised inflation, a loss of anchoring typically results in higher inflation volatility. The inversion of the inflation curve indicates that markets currently interpret the conflict as generating predominantly near‑term inflationary pressures rather than a shift in the long‑run inflation regime. This stability suggests continued confidence in the RBA’s framework and a clear distinction between transitory, cyclical inflation shocks and structurally persistent inflation dynamics. A key limitation of simple policy rules is that they do not distinguish between demand- and supply-driven inflation shocks, despite central banks typically responding very differently to each. In practice, central banks tend to place greater weight on the expected persistence of inflation, second round effects, and implications for inflation expectations, rather than responding symmetrically to all deviations from target. records.text: he growing interaction between AI infrastructure, water constraints and energy demand. The region has positioned itself as a digital gateway connecting Europe, Asia, and Africa, attracting significant investment in data center capacity. However, the Middle East conflict, with strikes on data centers in the UAE and Bahrain, has put a brake on the region’s AI momentum. Compounding this geopolitical uncertainty, water scarcity remains a structural constraint. The UAE, Saudi Arabia and Qatar are among the most water-stressed countries on earth (World Resources Institute, 2023). To meet cooling needs, many facilities in the region rely on desalinated water, as the corrosive properties and mineral content of raw seawater could damage electrical equipment. However, desalination itself carries a significant energy footprint. Thermal desalination technologies still dominate in the Gulf, and these systems primarily rely on natural gas. This highlights the importance of scaling cleaner desalination solutions, particularly less energy-intensive reverse osmosis, to support both data center cooling needs and municipal drinking water demand. ARS’ FX band mechanism (free floating within inflation linked FX band) might have contributed to a more isolated price action than its peers. In fact, during the recent dollar rally amid worsening risk sentiment, ARS has tended to exhibit the lowest beta and outperform its peers. KEY MESSAGES We are taking a short USDARS NDF position, believing the peso will stay supported by the government’s reserve-building, a stable political backdrop, and the upcoming April-June harvest. While medium-term USD-flow pressures remain, the initial reserve accumulation should ease near-term amortisation concerns and keep sentiment upbeat for the next few months. The harvest is set to boost agricultural exports, bringing larger USD inflows that will be converted into ARS, further buttressing the peso and reducing the risk of a sharp, sustained depreciation. records.text: power system China's energy mix reached a structural inflection point in 2024, as non-fossil-fuel sources overtook crude oil in primary energy consumption for the first time. The share of renewables plus nuclear rose to ~20% in 2024 from 9% in 2010, while coal’s share fell to about 53.2%1 , extending its multi-year decline (Figure 1). We note that oil's 18% share in China's energy consumption is well below the global average of 30%, according to IEA data2 . We estimate China's energy exposure to the Middle East via oil (~5.5%) and natural gas (~1%) accounted for a manageable 6.5% of its total energy consumption, and assessed channels energy shocks could hit the economy in China Outlook: Less vulnerable, 13 March 2026. China's power generation mix tells a similar story. While coal-fired power still accounted for about 54% of total electricity generation in 2025, renewables have grown rapidly: the shares of both solar and wind power rose to 11% each in 2025, up from 2% and 7%, respectively, in 2020, according to the NBS. Oil and gas account for ~4% of China's electricity generation, among the lowest compared with other Asian countries, and also significantly lower than 20-40% shares in the US (43%), Japan (37%) and Germany (20%; Figure 2). According to energy think tank Ember, ~84% of China’s incremental electricity demand in 2024 was met by clean generation, mainly solar and wind. records.text: Global Synthesis Truce and dare The US-Iran ceasefire announcement triggered a drop in oil and a rally in risk assets. However, so far, the Strait of Hormuz remains de facto closed and much will depend on the upcoming negotiations. In the meantime, the risk of economic disruptions has risen and central banks will remain vigilant. Truce and dare in geopolitics Stepping back from the brink... This sixth week of the war started with a series of threats by Trump to escalate the war to new extremes (including the warnings that 'all hell' would be unleashed and Iran's 'whole civilisation will die') ahead of a deadline he had set Iran to re-open the Strait of Hormuz. On Tuesday, just hours before the deadline, Trump then declared a two-week 'double-sided CEASEFIRE' (emphasis by Trump), brokered by Pakistan. The details of the ceasefire remain nebulous, as it was based on a series of social media statements and the re-posting of others without any written document. Apparently, two different frameworks exist – a 10-point plan by Iran and a 15-point proposal by the US –but only partial and at times conflicting summaries of these have become public. The one central and explicit demand by Trump was that any ceasefire would be 'subject to the Islamic Republic of Iran agreeing to the COMPLETE, IMMEDIATE, and SAFE OPENING of the Strait of Hormuz' (emphasis by Trump). records.text: simultaneous occurrence of energy and logistics shocks, which present a more complex challenge for policymakers. While Korea’s inventory buffers provide some resilience, these shocks are raising both downside risks to growth and upside risks to inflation. Although we have revised up our growth outlook on the back of record-high export growth driven by the tech cycle, there is heightened uncertainty about the outlook for sectors more exposed to supply disruptions, such as petrochemicals. As the situation evolves, the Bank of Korea will need to remain vigilant to these potential head- winds, balancing the need to support growth with the impera- tive to contain inflationary pressures arising from ongoing supply-side shocks. Coordination with other policy tools Given this backdrop, the current response to cost-push infla- tion is to address shocks through micro-level fiscal measures rather than tightening macro/monetary policy. The supple- mentary budget submitted to the National Assembly includes subsidies equivalent to about 0.4% of GDP and wholesale price caps to smooth price shocks through burden-sharing among the government, consumers, and businesses. To coun- ter downside risks to growth, programs to support low-in- come consumer purchasing power and stabilize affected industries and supply chains are proposed at about 0.5% of GDP. At present, the shock is more sector-specific than a broad- based macroeconomic price shock, so micro-level fiscal responses are prioritized. I

As the conflict evolves, we are turning cautiously optimistic while remaining highly selective in implementation. EMFX performance since the outbreak of the war has largely tracked the magnitude and direction of terms-of-trade shocks: countries benefiting from higher energy prices have outperformed those burdened by them (Figure 2). In this context, Brazil and Turkey stand out. Both have seen a clear improvement in their terms of trade, yet experienced spot currency depreciation amid a strong dollar and broad risk-off conditions, creating attractive entry points. We therefore continue to favour BRL and TRY as the tentative recovery in risk appetite takes shape. Energy dynamics support TRY and BRL. Turkey’s case runs counter to the initial assumption that rising oil prices are unambiguously negative for a net energy importer. Although gas prices remain contained and roughly in line with the baseline scenario, spot oil prices are roughly halfway between the baseline and 'adverse' scenarios. records.text: Obviously, the recent rise in equity volatility owes largely to increased uncertainty about the Iran War and its macro implications. We “beta-adjust” longer-dated equity volatility by stripping out the portion (the beta) of the change in equity volatility that is attributable to its historical relationship with changes in the equity index, leaving only the change that has been “in excess” of index moves. Exhibit 7 shows that most, but not all, of the rise in longer-dated volatility since the start of the year has been in line with declines in the index (dark blue line slightly higher YTD). That is especially true since the start of the Iran War, as the market has put more weight on the possibility of more challenging macro outcomes. If our nonrecessionary baseline plays out and the market can reduce the weight on downside tail scenarios, as it is already doing, implied volatility is likely to drop across the volatility curve as the most recent risk-premium-driven increases reverse. But we still think the underlying structural path is more likely to be higher. Exhibit 7 shows that there has been a rise in this “beta-adjusted” measure of longer-dated equity volatility over the last several months, particularly in late 2025. Our model-predicted measures of 12-month implied volatility average to around 19 (20 when including market concentration and 17 without it), which is now above current levels and clearly higher than levels before the Iran War. Global supply (inverted) Brent While previous geopolitical shocks produced an immediate scramble for oil that intensified price pressures, substantial current supply buffers and widespread optimism that this dis- ruption will be transitory have limited price increases to date. Despite an announced cease-fire, the conflict is not resolved and oil prices could spike from already elevated levels if fears of an extended disruption emerge. An extended disruption in the Strait of Hormuz would also generate physical supply constraints, depressing industrial activity, with Asia most exposed to a loss of Middle East energy imports. Our baseline assumes that the cease-fire is a signal for a grad- ual reopening of the Strait. But the material rundown in buffer stocks has implications for the price path ahead. Combined with a likely sustained geopolitical risk premium, only a par- tial normalization in energy prices is anticipated during 2H26. Relative to our pre-crisis forecast for Brent crude to average $60bbl, we anticipate crude oil prices to settle closer to $85/ bbl.

Fortunately, prices away from energy were better behaved last month, and core CPI increased a trend-like 0.2%. Higher energy prices are also starting to affect consumer psychology, as the University of Michigan consumer sentiment gauge fell to a record low of 47.6, and expectations for inflation in the year ahead jumped a full percentage point to 4.8%. While the conflict is leaving a mark on price-related data, it has yet to have a noticeable impact on economic activity data. According to ADP, private employment increased at a 26,000 average weekly pace in the four weeks ending March 21. Through the cycle a lower level of unemployment tends to raise the ratio of vacancies to the unemployed (V/U) and so the relative bar- gaining power of labor. This works through both centralized wage determination, and by increasing the likelihood of job- switching, which in less centralized contracts can generate extra wage growth. We have already shown that an unem- ployment rate in the low 4s appears consistent with aggregate wage growth in the low 3s, which is inflation-target-consis- tent. The argument could be challenged if V/U were in fact higher than it used to be at given levels of unemployment, which would confer an extra wage impulse. That is, the Bev- eridge Curve might have shifted out. records.text: dated implied volatility in recent months already, in excess of its usual relationship to the equity index. We see more than one route to higher equity volatility. The obvious one is a n deterioration in the macro cycle, but we also think there is an underlying supportive force for longer-dated equity volatility. So we continue to see merit in pairing upside in longer-dated equity volatility with long risk exposures, especially on any relaxation in the near term, as we have seen recently. The Case for Structurally Higher US Equity Volatility Equity implied volatility has risen more sharply in recent weeks across tenors, extending its move higher since the mid-2025 lows (Exhibit 1). The bulk of that recent shift is because equity volatility tends to rise when equities come under pressure, as they have since the start of the Iran War. But we have argued that there are good reasons to expect that equity volatility could move structurally higher over time, even with a benign macro backdrop and even if equity prices continue to rise, as some of the forces that pushed equity volatility higher in the late 1990s as the tech investment boom matured come increasingly into play (Exhibit 2). records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 51 investors who hedge with treasuries (money managers, overseas) probably see less value in MBS but are unlikely in our view to want to allocate towards credit given the upcoming supply and AI-related disruption concerns. In effect, we think that despite the tightening, MBS is best positioned to outperform, in particular vs swaps. What's the best method for playing this? We like owning bonds that are easy to hedge with less exposure to higher vol, giving up some yield for better convexity. Agency CMBS, 15yr mortgages, CMO floaters that don't have much cap risk (though we're willing to sell some cap risk) and production specs are all straightforward examples of assets that fare a bit better through potential volatility. For investors comfortable with the exposure, belly coupons don't look nearly as attractive on a treasury basis but still look fine on a SOFR basis. Belly Ginnies as a proxy for Treasury also look attractive despite the outperformance – they continue to face high net issuance and fast prepay concerns. Finally, we would also consider deep discount bonds on swap. This March prepay report likely still reflects pre- conflict rates, but nonetheless was constructive for investors, with speeds increasing less than expected, particularly for higher-coupon Ginnies. records.text: Megan Green noted, "Inflation has been above target for the best part of five years, and households and businesses are likely to be more sensitive to upside surprises in inflation given successive negative supply shocks. " A "wait and see" view might feel the right thing to do, but runs the risk that it leaves ambiguity in the MPC's response to a rise in inflation. As noted in the latest Thinking Macro with regard to the central bank reaction functions, "The pivot is sticky, even if the rationale softens. " That being the case, it would suggest that on a relative basis, the market might well be underestimating the risk that — be it either by accident or design — the MPC might deliver more than is priced given its historically difficult relationship with spot inflation and heightened concerns over spillover effects. April pricing in 4bp of tightening might seem too complacent — could the MPC really wait until the point at which the market is pricing a cumulative 25bp of tightening? A worsening of the external situation will put more pressure on expectations for April and June, where 4bp and 11bp is priced respectively. records.text: China Outlook Uneven inflation imprint March data show higher oil prices drove a sharp rise in PPI, while the pass-through to CPI remained limited. In contrast to the surge in input prices, downstream pricing power stayed weak, keeping consumer goods PPI and CPI subdued and leaving room for modest policy easing despite the oil shock. PPI ended its deflation, while (core) CPI softened The March price indicators suggest the increase in oil prices significantly pushed up PPI inflation, while the impact on CPI inflation would be manageable. PPI turned positive for the first time since late 2022, registering 0.5% y/y in March from -0.9% in February, while PPI also rose 1.0%m/m in March from 0.4% in February. The breakdown data showed such rebound was mainly led by raw materials and mining. We think the recovery in PPI will support industrial profits, particularly for the upstream sectors. First, higher oil prices were quickly transmitted to PPI in oil and gas components (~4% of PPI basket) given China’s ~70% oil import dependence. Real consumer spending in 2026 got off to a slow start with January and February real personal consumption expenditures rising just 0.7% at an annual rate. While March auto and light truck sales perked up, likely helped by the bumper tax refunds, the weak January and February consumer spending followed soggy November and December, and comes ahead of the leg up in headline inflation. Headline CPI surged 0.9% today, on the back of energy goods (i.e. gasoline) posting the largest 1-month increase in their nearly 70 year history. Core CPI rose 0.20% seasonally- adjusted in March, leaving core CPI inflation at 2.60%, up from 2.46% in February. As expected, core PCE prices rose a strong 0.37% in February, and core PCE inflation moved down from 3.05% to 2.97%. This year, constricted oil supply following the outbreak of war in the Middle East has sharply boosted global energy prices. Despite its status as a net energy exporter, the Canadian economy overall is unlikely to benefit from this second shock. The boost from higher oil prices will be narrowly concentrated in the energy sector, while the damage will be more broadly distributed across the rest of the economy. Energy is a key input cost for manufac- turing and other industries already under pressure from tariffs. We see little scope for this combination of shocks to have a net positive impact on growth. Little trade substitution, spreading damage Since the first round of US tariffs in March 2025, nominal exports to the US have fallen C$10.9bn, or 19.6% (Figure 1). Exports to the rest of the world have surged 49.5% over the same period, but these gains—which amount to C$6.8bn— have not come close to closing the shortfall. records.text: 4 We have previously written about why "No, 1y breakevens are not over 5%" , flagging that Bloomberg's generic "USGGBE01" index was still tracking the TIIOct26s (Three thoughts to start the week, March 30, 2026). However, in mid April, after the new 5y TIPS auction, we expect Bloomberg to roll that ticker to track the TIIApr27s. So for practical purposes, we can use the TIIApr27s as "1y breakevens" both now and through July. FIGURE 2. 5y TIPS real yield carry history by month Source: Barclays Research Intuitively, why will carry be so high in May and June? We frequently are asked how to think about carry as intuitively as possible, so wanted to use this as an opportunity to throw out a framework that helps us when thinking through the key moving pieces. At a high level, we can simplify the invoice/dirty price in nominal terms (abstracting away from coupon complications) of a TIPS to be: Dirty TIPS price ≈ Clean TIPS price × Inflation uplift If we think instead in change terms, and assume that expected TIPS returns should approximately equal the nominal risk free rate (which we proxy with term SOFR), and then: SOFR ≈ Nominal TIPS return ≈ Clean TIPS price change + Inflation accrual For a given nominal return, higher inflation accrual means that the clean price must go down to offset, all else equal, and a lower clean price implies a higher real yield, and, in turn, for a given nominal comparator yield, higher real yields mechanically compress the breakeven spread. ⇒ ↑ Inflatio

We are especially keen to understand if rising inflation expectations are solely responsible for rates underperformance, or if changing real yields are also having an influence on investor preferences. This is especially important given the varying degrees of oil dependence across the developed markets. Therefore, while short end dynamics have been broadly consistent across the largest developed markets, the long end has shown different influences, with inflation expectations having a much bigger influence on rising Bunds yields, while TIPs yields have been the predominant influence on Treasury yields. records.text: Japan Outlook Strong wage picture, cautious stance Wages rose clearly in February and negotiated hikes remained robust in the third tally, including among SMEs, but after a flurry of hawkish signals, the BoJ emphasized economic risk at Monday's branch managers meeting amid geopolitical uncertainty. Wages show strength sharply beating expectations in February In February's Maikin Monthly Labour Survey, total cash earnings rose 3.3% y/y (January revised: +2.5%) and scheduled cash earnings increased 3.3% y/y (+3.0%), both up sharply from the previous month. The 3.3% growth in scheduled earnings was the strongest since June 1992. On a same-sample basis as well, total cash earnings and scheduled earnings both grew at a faster pace of 3.1% y/y (versus +2.3% and +2.7%, respectively, in January). Real wages (total cash earnings minus CPI excluding imputed rent) surged 1.9% y/y (+0.7%) with support from slower inflation, staying positive for a second consecutive month. Factoring in the negative impact of annual changes to the survey sample (see below), the latest figures mark a strong result overall. In the February preliminary and January revised releases, published at the same time, one-third of the overall sample was replaced, as usual at this time of the year. records.text: US Rates Weekly 10 April 2026 Citi Research 8 Short-end: Tax receipts and SOFR/FF into Tax Day As we had been expecting, funding markets did not show major signs of stress at quarter-end last week. As we show in Figure 14, the 1-day change in SOFR/IORB on the last day of the quarter was in line with the recent trend we have observed on coupon paydown days since reserves have moved above $3tn. Since then, SOFR and TGCR have gapped lower and RRP usage even picked up on Tuesday, albeit temporarily. In our view, this signals that we have returned to a lightly abundant reserves regime. Or, in other words, the ongoing Fed’s RMPs and Treasury’s declining T-bill auction sizes, combined with the lower TGA balance pushing cash into the financial system, have all driven the sharp move lower in SOFR and TGCR over the past few days. Indeed, as Figure 15 shows, TGCR and SOFR are back levels similar to those from the summer in 2025. Back in February, we got long April SOFR/FF basis as a “cheap” option to play for a possible return to this lightly abundant reserves regime (see US Rates Weekly - Renewed appeal as risk-off hedge). The March VaR shock pushed forwards against us, but we reiterated our view and added onto the position (see Figure 16, Short- End Notes - Still like April SOFR/FF). Winter heating remains a critical pressure point, driving a sharp seasonal spike in natural gas demand. Many Northern provinces (including Beijing) have shifted district heating from coal to gas, while southern regions rely on household gas furnaces for supplemental heat. During the recent four-month heating season (mid-November 2025 to mid-March 2026), China consumed an estimated 180 bcm of natural gas, equivalent to 42% of 2025 demand. Despite a steady rise in domestic output over the past decade, local production covered only ~60% of last year’s consumption (Figure 26). This leaves Beijing with limited buffer and elevates the urgency to secure incremental supplies ahead of next winter, particularly in the event of supply disruptions from the Middle East. records.text: 14 Global Economic Weekly | 10 April 2026 A weak labour market, potential demand weakness from higher energy prices and mildly restrictive rates would likely limit strong second-round effects as long as the energy price shock is short-lived. But the longer the shock is, the more BoE would likely worry about second round effects and inflation expectations moving higher, especially given above-target inflation in the past few years and already elevated inflation/wage expectations. The March Decision Maker Panel showed that firms’ year ahead own price growth expectations rose from 3.4% to 3.7% and one year ahead inflation expectations jumped from 3.0% to 3.5% the biggest monthly jump since September 2022. Given our expectation of high energy prices persisting through 2026, we expect two hikes in June and July 2026 (with risks of one and done) to 4.25% as an insurance to guard against second round effects (vs our previous call of two cuts in 2026). We then expect three quarterly cuts from Q2 2027 (once inflation peak is behind us) in April, July and November 2027 to 3.5%, with risks of 3.25% and earlier cuts. Hikes are likely to be followed by cuts in 2027 once inflation peaks and the BoE contends with the medium term growth and labour market implications of this real income shock. But it’s a close call- the situation is fluid and stagflation poses a difficult trade-off for the BoE. The two-week ceasefire – signaling a possible de-escalation – is likely to shave some of the EM premium that has built up over the past week. Even if the market does not fully price a diplomatic settlement, the truce lowers the negative tail risk of further escalation in the conflict, at least for now. We favor January 28 receiver for three key reasons. First, the DI curve was the most affected Latam curve during the sell-off (Figure 1). Before the Middle East flare-up, the market was already long the receiver side, anticipating Banco Central do Brasil’s easing cycle. Moreover, the DI curve tends to keep a high beta to global fixed-income, especially in stressful periods. Second, the strong sell-off has created a wider gap between the policy path embedded in the curve and the path the BCB is likely to follow, given Brazil’s macro fundamentals. This tends to consistently drag WPI growth toward a mid-business cycle position. The last few years were a case in point, as even the tightest labor market on record and multi-decade highs in inflation only dragged the WPI up to a peak of 4.3%oya, with the WPI slowing since despite an only-gradual rise in unemployment. In the absence of a very low unemployment rate (or sharp falls in unemployment), wage growth tends to be quite stable at around target-consis- tent levels. GBP: Switching to Cable. For much of the past year we had been arguing for n regional Sterling underperformance on a host of mostly UK-specific factors: labour market vulnerabilities, lingering political and fiscal risk premium, slowing data and room for BoE easing. We had seen regional Sterling crosses (particularly EUR/GBP) as offering the best expressions to narrow in on those UK themes. But as these domestic considerations have been sidelined with the global energy shock taking centre stage, EUR/GBP price action has instead been dictated by risk and terms of trade impulses.

At the same time, uncertainty surrounding the speed of normalisation of transit through the Strait of Hormuz remains very elevated. As highlighted by our oil analyst, current forward curves appear to be priced for a relatively rapid normalisation of flows through the strait. As a result, any delay in reopening the Strait or a renewed escalation would pose upside risks to oil prices from current levels. A scenario analysis exemplifies this: in the hypothetical case where normalisation is delayed until end-April, Brent prices could already average around $100/bbl in 2026, which would de facto place the energy price path much closer to the ECB's adverse scenario. Second, with the distribution of medium-term inflation risks still skewed to the upside, and given that the baseline scenario – calibrated on the assumption of a rapid normalisation in energy supply – only sees inflation return to target in 2027, conditional on a yield curve pricing slightly below two 25bp policy rate increases, a robust policy response would argue for recalibrating policy in a tighter direction and acting sooner rather than later. records.text: TRADE IDEA TRADE IDEA 08/04/2026 1 FX: Reload short USDARS position We are initiating a short USDARS trade idea to express our bullish stance on the ARS. Elevated energy prices and expected USD inflows from agricultural exports during the April–June harvest season underpin this view. The central bank’s reserve-building program and a stable political climate add further support. High energy prices and harvest season support the ARS through the trade channel: High energy prices improve Argentina’s trade balance even as the Middle East conflict creates global uncertainty. We estimate a 10% rise in crude oil price would boost exports by about 0.1% of GDP (more than USD0.6bn). During the April– June harvest, agricultural shipments are likely to generate additional USD inflows, which exporters will convert into ARS. We have modelled several Brent-oil scenarios in light of the ongoing conflict (see Europe: Energy shock prompts market paradigm shift, dated 20 March). records.text: US Economics Weekly10 April 2026 ab 15 Core CPI rises 0.20%, 12-month core inflation rises to 2.60% Core CPI prices rose 0.20% seasonally-adjusted in March, below both our projection and the Bloomberg consensus average .12-month core CPI inflation increased from 2.46% in last month’s report from February to 2.60% in today’s March release. We expect that the 2.46% in last month's report was the low point for the year. The headline CPI increased 0.87% (seasonally-adjusted) in March — only 0.01pp below our expectations and 0.09pp below the Bloomberg consensus average. On a 12-month change basis, headline CPI inflation jumped strongly from 2.41% in February to 3.26% in March. However, 12-month inflation remains downward biased by around 0.09pp due to the inability of the BLS to collect rents during the government shutdown in October. This final remaining bias from the government shutdown should reverse in next month's release of the April CPI (scheduled for release on Tuesday, May 12) when the April/October housing panel is re-sampled. CLOs: Remaining defensive, but we see opportunities for senior risk on the horizon Developments in the broadly syndicated leveraged loan market—and, by extension, the CLO universe—remain a focus for many market participants. On a year-to-date basis, CLO spreads have moved wider alongside other segments of the credit market. AAA spreads in BSL CLOs have widened by over 20bp from January tights, underperforming USD IG, which is not surprising given the rise in dispersion and the heavier left tail in loan prices. So far the market's attention has predominantly focused on the risk of persistent inflation stemming from the energy shock rather than on the potential for growth to be hit harder than assumed. This week's ceasefire announcement is positive news. But uncertainties persist, oil prices remain elevated and in this note we focus on the downside risks to growth. In the first half of this note we look at growth conditions in the euro area in early 2026 prior to the start of the conflict in the Middle East. There is a growing risk that economic growth was softer at the start of this year than the consensus and ECB projections. In other words, there may have been less of a growth buffer to absorb an energy shock. With oil prices remaining elevated despite the ceasefire announcement – 2027 oil forwards are above the ECB's 'adverse' scenario – in the second half of this note we explore the ECB's growth assumptions under the alternative scenarios. Some of the assumptions are optimistic, in our view. A more persistent energy shock could potentially hit growth harder than the ECB thinks. records.text: Euro Area—Will Wages Wiggle? Wages are a key “second-round” channel that could turn a temporary energy shock into a more persistent inflation problem. After the 2022 energy crisis, for instance, workers recouped their purchasing power by bargaining for higher pay, which led firms in wage-sensitive sectors to raise prices in response (a process that ECB President Lagarde later described as “tit-for-tat” inflation). What are the risks of a similar response of wages today? One worry is that, before the start of the conflict in the Middle East, wage growth was still uncomfortably high. Our wage tracker—which averages across our three preferred measures of year-over-year pay growth—stood at 3.3% at the end of last year, above the 2.5-3% range that we estimate to be consistent with the ECB’s inflation target (Exhibit 1). But we see two reasons to look for a more limited response of wages to the current increase in energy prices than in 2022, in addition to the size and breadth of the commodity shock. First, workers entered the conflict with a purchasing power “cushion”. More precisely, real wages were running slightly ahead of labour productivity — a gap that should narrow over time (Exhibit 2, left). This means that, as energy prices erode purchasing power, firms have room to resist nominal wage increases without pushing real wages below productivity. records.text: Late last year, we conducted a deep-dive analysis on the ‘state of play’ in the collateralized loan obligation (CLO) market, which has grown to a sizable global market and has become a core part of many investors’ fixed income allocations. At the time, we saw scope for valuations of senior risk to move tighter—especially considering that today’s CLO 2.0 structures are more robust vs. the CLO 1.0 cohort. That said, we also highlighted that tight valuations across the capital structure underscored the importance for junior investors to prioritize cleaner collateral and higher-quality managers. Now, as we begin 2Q2026, the macro backdrop—albeit incredibly volatile in recent days—has shifted to reflect a more challenging growth, inflation, and policy mix. As a result, we refresh our relative value views on the CLO market and highlight the following takeaways. While fundamentals for CLOs are not showing signs of deterioration, we believe the n balance of risks has shifted more negative. Furthermore, market pricing of CLO debt and loans has shifted alongside. We reiterate our defensive call: favoring higher-quality managers, cleaner collateral, n and newly issued deals. We favor CLO mezzanine tranches relative to owning broadly syndicated leveraged n loans on an outright basis, given the better structural protections and attractive valuations in the CLO structures. records.text: Introduction to DEVal (Debt-to-Equity Relative Valuation Gap) - Barclays QPS Research Jingling Guan(v) BCI, US | Arik Ben Dor(v) BCI, US Bonds and equity of an issuer are linked as their performance is driven by the same fundamentals, such as the firm's management team, business models, and products, etc. However, their valuations could also be driven by different non-fundamental components that affect each market separately. For example, the sentiment of credit investors could cause a bond's price to deviate from its fundamental value, while its equity price may not be affected in the same way due to a different investor base. Given the fundamental link between bonds and equities, we can assess the relative cheapness/expensiveness of a bond using its equity. To achieve this, the QPS team developed a metric called DEVal (debt-to-equity relative valuation gap) through the use of a structural model (Credit Grades model). This approach starts with an issuer’s equity market value and volatility, and uses a structural model to estimate the issuer's bonds' default probabilities and the respective bond spread based on them. The gap between the market-based bond spread (OAS) versus the equity-implied bond spread, denoted as DEVal, captures the difference in valuation of default risk from the perspective of bond vs. equity market investors. records.text: 4 Massive water demand from hyperscalers: As computing intensity increases, the risk of overheating rises, and cooling systems become critical to maintaining operations. Cooling demand is also highly seasonal, often peaking during summer months when water resources tend to be constrained. Water consumption among hyperscalers has increased sharply in recent years as AI workloads expand. For example, Google’s water consumption rose by about 28% y/y in 2024. Most of this usage is associated with its data center operations (Figure 2). The scale of the water consumption in data center cooling is already significant. In 2023, US data centers directly consumed about 66 billion liters of water for cooling, similar to the annual water consumption of San Francisco (see Shehabi et al., 2024). Often water-stressed locations: A significant share of existing data centers already operate in regions experiencing significant water stress, and a large proportion of the capacity currently under development is in similarly constrained areas (Figure 3). We think this reflects the historical treatment of water availability as secondary to other planning considerations, such as land availability, power access, fiber connectivity, and regulatory incentives. In addition, while the Supreme Court striking down the IEEPA tariffs near the end of February may have been taken positively in the first instance, policy uncertainty could flare back up as the administration seeks to enact a "Plan B." Combined with the conflict in the Middle East, resumed tariff uncertainty may have pushed the small business uncertainty index higher in March. The uncertainty index peaked at 110 in October 2024, and generally trended down since the beginning of 2025. records.text: Marvin Loh Cayla Seder April 10, 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General Fund connect quarterly: MM investors see through the fog of war Change is the only constant, and the markets are once again faced with once in a lifetime uncertainty. Military conflict is not new to the lexicon of investors, although the gravity of closing the strait was immediately reflected in the largest surge in weekly oil prices ever witnessed. The duration of the conflict has also caught investors off guard, although if the ceasefire holds it does cut off the left tail for risk assets. Investors are now faced with weighing the energy shock through a transitory, inflationary, or growth lens, with the truth likely lying within these intersections. For the moment, inflation is occupying a larger share of rates investors mindshare, with global yields higher and policy expectations moving to a tightening bias. From the Fed’s perspective, the market has now delayed rate cuts into late 2027, essentially marking the end of the cutting cycle. For our part, we will retain our call for 1 -cut, although our view that the normalization cycle is effectively done remains. records.text: Higher Natural Gas Prices, Slightly Larger Economic Headwinds Energy prices have risen sharply due to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, which our commodity strategists assume will remain closed until mid-April. Under this baseline assumption, we expect that Brent will average $90/bbl in Q2 before gradually declining to $80/bbl in Q4. Our commodity strategists similarly expect that the disruption to Qatar’s LNG exports (19% of global supply) will lift European natural gas (TTF) and global LNG (JKM) prices, which we expect will respectively average $16.90/mmBtu and $18.15/mmBtu in Q2 before declining to $13.65 and $14.65 by Q4. Risks are skewed toward worse outcomes and higher prices. When analyzing the economic impact of higher energy prices, we have leaned on our standard oil rules of thumb which imply that each 10% increase in oil prices lowers global growth by a bit more than 0.1pp and raise headline inflation by a bit more than 0.2pp. Under our baseline oil forecasts, these rules imply that the energy price shock will add 0.7pp to global headline inflation (with a smaller 0.2pp impact on core inflation) and lower GDP growth by 0.4pp over the next year (excluding the larger impact on GDP growth in the Middle East itself). Our oil-price rules of thumb will also capture the effects of broader energy price increases if non-oil energy prices shift in a manner consistent with historical patterns, as oil serves as a proxy for overall energy. Price stability, full employment and the economic prosperity and welfare of the people of Australia have been joint objectives since the 1959 legislation that established the RBA. The RBA adopted flexible inflation targeting in the 1990s based on these three objectives. Equal consideration does not mean equal weight There is a crucial distinction between consideration and weight on the RBA’s inflation and full employment objectives. In setting policy, the Board must consider both inflation and full employment, but that does not imply that they always assign equal importance to each objective. records.text: Other Considerations A limitation to our accounting-based approach is that we do not account for discretionary policy changes that might limit the economic impacts of higher natural gas prices. To the extent that governments decide to offset higher natural gas prices, the impacts could arrive as a deterioration in fiscal balances rather than the near-term economic impacts highlighted above. Likewise, our analysis focuses on the impacts of higher prices rather than the outright shortages that could emerge if global LNG supply is restricted for much longer than we expect. We also do not consider the FX implications of an outsized natural gas price shock, which could lead to differential effects on terms of trade and inflation. To highlight these other considerations, Exhibit 14 compares the changes in our country-team’s headline inflation and GDP forecasts (which do factor in these considerations) with our top-down estimates. There is a strong positive correlation between our top-down and bottom-up estimates and the implied overall global impacts similar. But there are a few differences. On inflation, our actual forecast upgrades have been somewhat smaller than our top-down estimates would suggest in Central Europe and Asia, largely reflecting an expectation that policy interventions will limit consumer price increases. Australia and New Zealand RBNZ hike premium partly justified, but still excessive. RBNZ held rates this week, n noting that weak demand and excess productive capacity should to some extent contain second-round effects of the oil price shock on inflation. While the assessment of the monetary stance, including a discussion about preemptive hikes, was incrementally more hawkish than it has been previously, the RBNZ is still on the dovish side among G10 central banks, and our economists continue to expect it to keep rates on hold until December. However, in contrast to the RBA, where a relatively front-footed approach has stabilized the forwards, markets now price the most hikes for RBNZ through 2027 among the G10. While we have sympathy with some hike premium in light of upside risks around the commodities outlook, we view current pricing of six hikes by the second half of 2027 (about 80bp above the RBNZ’s estimated neutral rate) as excessive. Rather than outright longs, we think steepeners (e.g. 2s5s or 5s10s) may be more insulated (and still positive carry) expressions for a more gradual approach to rate hikes.
