March CPI takeaways March CPI inflation was slightly lower than market expectations. Both headline and core MoM inflation for March at 0.87% and 0.2%, respectively, were slightly lower than market expectations. While energy inflation was close to market expectations, we did not see any impact of higher energy prices on food inflation in March. We expect that to change, and we will likely see some pass-through of higher energy costs into food inflation in the coming months. Moving on to core inflation components, after a couple of months of 0.2% shelter inflation, we saw an increase to 0.27% in March. This was mainly driven by 0.28% MoM increase in the owner’s equivalent rent (OER) component of shelter. It follows that a potential delay or a further escalation poses upside risks to our price forecast of a $85 average for Brent in 2026 (our current baseline, adjusted in mid-March). Against an average of $68 in 2025, this implies a 20-30% higher oil price at the minimum. The interest rate environment will also likely remain higher than where it would have been (ie, in our original pre-war baseline). Much has changed since the Q1 edition of our Fund Connect Quarterly, when markets were focused on when to return policy rates to neutral in the US, if they weren’t there already. Today, attention has shifted to the evolving conflict in Iran, leaving cash managers to navigate a rapidly changing rate environment alongside heightened FX volatility. Below, we assess the outlook for US rates, the path of the USD, and share insights into how real money investors are managing their cash allocations. Conflict Policy Transmission Prior to the conflict, markets did not fully price a rate cut until July 2026, ultimately expecting the Fed to lower rates to a 3.00–2.75% range by year end. That first cut has since been pushed out by roughly a year, which when put into context of stability in the near term, helps explain why volatility in cash markets has been more muted at the 3‑month tenor compared with 6‑month and 1‑year maturities. This contrasts with prior episodes of elevated volatility —most notably in 2024 —when the scope of volatil ity was greater and more uniform across the very front end of the curve given rates were further from neutral. records.text: M Idea 16 March CMO Update: $49.1bn of Issuance Issuance in CMO (collateralized mortgage obligations) rose 45% MoM to total $49.1bn in March, the highest level of issuance we have on record since our data begin in 2011. Ex-Re-REMIC, CMO issuance increased $15.6bn, while Re-REMIC CMO issuance declined $0.4bn. Ginnie issuance maintained a similar pace of issuance as last month (albeit reaching a slightly new high) with $23.8bn – the difference is that we saw a significant conventional demand surge in March, more than doubling conventional issuance to its own historical high of $26.0bn. Into recent basis widening, floaters roughly maintained a 54% share in March after the initial 21pp jump over February. We continue to like CMO floaters as an expression of basis for investors who may be more wary of convexity risks. More broadly, across both fixed and floating CMOs, PAC structures declined to 18% of issuance share. Sequential structure share was flat at 15% and supports came in at 3%. The most popular collateral combination was generic 5.5s, which took a total of 40% combined issuance share. Semi-seasoned 5s and 5.5s followed with combined 21% share. records.text: We build on our existing macro models of equity volatility to examine the recent increase and to consider where volatility might be heading. We expand our work to model longer-dated volatility for the first time and update our existing model of shorter-dated volatility. We model and focus on implied volatility here, but we have found in the past that these drivers apply to realized volatility as well. While short-term movements in asset market volatility can be hard to predict, we have long argued that the underlying trends in volatility can be linked to the economic cycle. We consider four main buckets of drivers in our updated macro models. The macro cycle: levels and changes in the US unemployment rate. Higher levels of n unemployment vs. the non-accelerating inflation rate of unemployment (NAIRU) and increasing unemployment are both associated with higher volatility. The intuition here is that these measures are indicators of the stage of the economic cycle. Macro volatility: the volatility of the unemployment rate. Higher volatility in n month-to-month changes in the unemployment rate is associated with higher volatility. We find a statistically significant relationship between volatility in labor market data and equity volatility—the channel here is likely through uncertainty about future outcomes (where higher data volatility is associated with increased uncertainty about the macro outlook). Since February, energy price expectations have risen and we have nudged down real GDP growth, taken up inflation, and nudged up but pushed out projected increases in the unemployment rate. So far the economy's anecdotes, surveys, and highest frequency data have looked fairly resilient. However, the combination of features suggests we should push back our expectations for Federal Reserve rate cuts. Headed into the oil price shock we projected two rate cuts this year with risk of one. We now expect only one, a 25 bp rate cut at the December FOMC meeting. We think the risks skew toward earlier rather than later for that next rate cut, based on our current assessment of the distribution of risks. We expect two 25 bp rate cuts in 2027. Since oil prices moved higher, the domestic economy has displayed barely a shimmer. The highest frequency data looks little changed overall, except for maybe mortgage applications for a home purchase pulling back a bit alongside the backup in mortgage rates. In addition to mortgage rates, equity markets are a little lower, and gasoline prices are higher. Ceasefire does not take 2026 ECB hikes off the table The US-Iran ceasefire announcement has the potential to reduce the near-term risk of a broad- based escalation of the Middle East conflict. Nevertheless, with inflationary pressures already in the pipeline, we continue to think the ECB will need to recalibrate monetary policy in a tighter direction this year. At this stage, we maintain our call for the ECB to raise key policy rates by 25bp at both the April and June meetings, but acknowledge that, at face value, easing geopolitical tensions could argue for a more patient Governing Council. Our assessment rests on two main considerations. First, even after the ceasefire announcement, the energy price path implied by the market remains somewhat higher than that embedded in the ECB's baseline. Forward prices for 2026 still imply oil and gas prices averaging around $85.3/bbl for Brent crude and €45.3/MWh for TTF gas, compared with the ECB’s March baseline assumptions of oil prices averaging $81/bbl and gas prices averaging €46/MWh in 2026. As a result of these changes, we expect a modestly positive effect on funding and repo, though the impact is likely to be marginal rather than meaningful. Since the GSIB capital surcharge is the additional capital that GSIBs must hold based on a score range calculated at year-end, this has often prompted GSIBs to scale back their balance sheets in the days and weeks leading up to year-end to minimize their GSIB surcharge given the cliff effects when they cross a surcharge bucket. records.text: ets look severely impacted. Repair timelines vary widely: Qatar’s Ras Laffan complex may take years to restore 17% of damaged capacity, and Bahrain’s Sitra refinery has been hit twice. Refining has been a key target for both sides, with an estimat- ed 2.4 mbd shut in across 20 plants—many already restarted or were precautionary outages. Of the remaining losses, ~900 kbd could return within weeks, ~800 kbd in about a month, while ~700 kbd (notably Sitra and Iran’s Tehran refinery) may take much longer. Saudi’s update quantifies impacts, including a 700 kbd East-West pipeline throughput loss (Oil Flash Note, Apr 9th). Europe’s low post-winter gas inventories mean higher prices are likely needed to refill storage ahead of next win- ter, leading us to revise our forecasts to 55/60/65 EUR/ MWh for Q2/Q3/Q4 2026, with risks from Qatar timing and EU policy incentives. NWE ended winter at 17.6% stor- age (second-lowest in 15 years) versus 27.7% for the broader EU. To reach 80% by winter (consistent with the EU’s “90% minus 10%” flexibility), NWE/EU must inject ~31/56 Bcm from April–October—about 5 Bcm more than last year (+4.8% YoY). The supply mix is expected to include gas-to- coal switching (2 Bcm), higher Norwegian pipeline flows (1 Bcm), and stronger LNG imports (2 Bcm). Globally, extra non–Middle East LNG could replace up to half of lost Qatari/ UAE volumes; the rest likely comes via demand cuts, espe- cially in Asia (European Natural Gas, Apr 8th). The reform shifts that authority to the provinces, giving them the mandate to conduct technical assessments of these zones’ hydrological role. Where certain areas are found not to function as water reserves, the reform would allow for mining projects that were previously prohibited. This more federal approach gives mining provinces greater room to define more precise criteria for identifying and protecting glacier and periglacial areas, bringing clearer guardrails—and greater certainty—to inves- tors and to the sector’s project pipeline. The mining industry expects the revised regulatory frame- work to help unlock roughly US$30bn in investments in the near term, supported by the broader transformation driven by RIGI, with several lithium projects advancing and multiple copper developments moving through earlier-stage pipelines. The key risk remains execution, given Argentina’s record of abrupt policy shifts, episodes of FX and macro fragility, and recurring political turbulence; however, RIGI and the Glaciers Law aim to provide the credibility needed to offset that lega- cy and help translate the sector’s potential into sustained pro- ductive activity, as highlighted in our recent note. Yes, both economic and financial conditions are behaving like monetary policy is not noticeably restrictive. At present, core PCE inflation is 1 percentage point above target, and has demonstrated no evidence of moving closer to target over the past 18 months. Clearly some of this is due to one-time price increases from tariffs, but inflation is likely running above target even excluding these effects (e.g., Powell attributes 0.5-75pp of the current overshoot to tariffs). On the other side of the dual mandate, the unemployment rate is currently very close to the Fed’s assessment of NAIRU (4.3% versus 4.2%) and has been mostly stable since last summer. Given the inherent uncertainty in estimating NAIRU, it is reasonable to describe the labor market as close to target. records.text: F O C U S FOCUS 109/04/2026 Energy: Potential for de-escalation but upside risks remain Current state of play – Hormuz constrained and temporary ceasefire : The current situation for energy has remained in our ‘Hormuz constrained’ scenario (see Global macro: Crude reality (4), dated 4 March), where reduced flows through the Strait of Hormuz elevate energy prices as buffers run out. This has seen TTF and Brent crude prices rise by about 55% and 53%, respectively, since the start of the Middle East conflict. The situation in oil products is worse, with price rises of about 185% and 260% for gasoil and jet fuel, respectively. A 2-week ceasefire, announced on 7 April, has taken some of the price pressure off, as the market prices in a higher probability of de-escalation and resumption of Hormuz flows. However, we note the situation remains delicate. News flow suggests attacks are ongoing, with energy infrastructure an increasingly common target. We therefore see tail risks of escalatory attacks on critical energy infrastructure in the Middle East, which would pose significant upside price risks. Normalisation of flows likely to take months, even with imminent de- escalation: The speed of the resumption in flows through the Strait of Hormuz will be determined by the extent of damage inflicted on harbours and energy assets, as well as the ability to ramp up oil and gas production . records.text: Even as the path forward remains uncertain, the potential for a negotiated conclusion to the conflict in Iran offers a compression of right tail outcomes that justifies a reduction in volatility and a tentative return towards selective carry. Assuming it continues, that consolidation points to a rebuild in conviction that the asymmetry is towards rate cuts in the US. While recent signs of labor market stability can contain the market’s tail to deeper cuts for now, we think medium-term risks continue to skew towards lower terminal rate pricing. In Europe, we continue to think short expiry, short maturity volatility will fall further as outcomes narrow, even as front-end pricing has limited room to fall further. With the distribution of front-end EUR rates narrower and fiscal expansion likely to limit declines in core yields, we think that sovereign credit offers the best risk reward for further de-escalation—go long 3y France, Italy and Spain vs OIS. The Gilt curve should benefit from passing the peak in oil prices—contingent on relief continuing—but we prefer longs in the front-end given the potential for any over-eager BoE dovishness to boost Gilt risk premium. This dynamic has been evident in Japan, where higher inflation and global yield pressure has shown up in long-end yields rather than front-end pricing. Addressing democratic legitimacy Once an institution’s inability to resist political meddling is demonstrated, trust in the system is damaged, and that erosion takes a long time to rebuild. This is perhaps the most conse- quential insight for Colombia’s current situation. The tension between central bank independence and democratic account- ability is not unique to Colombia. It is a structural feature of the delegation model: an unelected body makes decisions with profound distributional consequences. The academic and institutional response to this tension has evolved consider- ably, and several mechanisms have emerged as best practices. Modern inflation-targeting central banks have invested heavi- ly in communication as a tool for building public understand- ing and legitimacy. BanRep already publishes Monetary Poli- cy Reports, minutes, and regular press conferences. However, the Bernanke Review of the Bank of England (2024) high- lighted that even sophisticated central banks can fall short in communicating uncertainty, the rationale for policy decisions, and the conditionality of the outlook. March trade deficit expected to widen We expect the trade deficit to widen in March to $34bn nsa, reflecting trade disruptions and higher oil prices linked to the Middle East conflict. As there are a number of moving parts, the degree of confidence in the forecast is low. While the oil import bill is likely to rise, the near-term impact should be partly moderated because import costs typically adjust with some lag. In addition, reduced oil and gas import volumes – given the effective shutdown of the Strait of Hormuz – could partially offset the price effect. More immediate pressure is likely to come from higher freight costs and softer exports to the Middle East, with 14% of our exports going to the region. Exports could see some tailwinds in March (fiscal year end). While gold prices have eased, this may be offset by a season- al pick-up in precious metal imports at the fiscal year-end. To separate the portion of the PeruGB-UST spread that stems from the oil shock and from any election-related premium, we compare the current oil shock episode spread with those observed during past, comparable oil-shock episodes. From the perspective of investors, a right-leaning government would probably adopt more market-friendly policies—pro-mining measures, privatizing Petroperú, etc.—and therefore it would benefit local assets. The risk, however, comes from a left-leaning win; higher fiscal spending or a repeat of the 2021 Castillo precedent could precipitate a rising pressure on local assets. Historical pattern shows that short-term pressure intensifies during the runoff: Peru’s local assets— Peruvian sol (PEN) and sovereign bonds (PeruGB)— have traditionally increased volatility after the initial round of elections. In the past election cycles, the 3-month rolling USDPEN realized volatility typically starts to rise about one month before the election and peaks significantly after the elections (see Figure 3). From a relative-performance standpoint, there is no consistent trend of the PEN either underperforming or outperforming across past elections. However, the Figure 4 shows that elections results can impact the PEN’s relative performance against Latam FX quite significantly in either direction once the elections are behind. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 49 Weekly Summary for Overseas Investors Market Recap Earlier this week we moved from a neutral position to a long position in the basis. Mortgage valuations still look compelling vs. swaps and align with the perspectives of GSEs, banks, and REITs, who we expect to be the largest buyers this year. Valuations vs treasuries are less compelling, but the alternative for treasury-based investors (money managers, overseas) is corporate credit. Credit faces huge supply and uncertain demand base. MBS has minimal supply and clear demand base, so the asset allocation support could continue. Technicals are also great – supply is running at the lowest level since 2015, and a material pickup in seasonal activity at these rate levels seems unlikely. Of course, the uncertainty in the outlook for how sustained the ceasefire will be could cause vol to stay elevated, which is a concern for our basis outlook. At this point, we still prefer to own basis via assets slightly less exposed to vol, such as 15y, agency CMBS, and floaters; then production specs and belly coupons, maybe even deep discounts on a second order. We note premium coupons look wide, and are supported by benign prepays and high CMO demand, but we're less certain of technicals and prefer 4.5s vs wings. Many focused on easing regulatory constraints and further reducing the stigma of the Fed's facilities as options to shrink the balance sheet, suggesting liquidity reform is rising on the deregulatory agenda. We think the Fed is likely to proceed cautiously and incrementally, prioritizing market functioning over speed to avoid disruptions in funding markets. As such, meaningful balance sheet reforms are unlikely to arrive in the near term, and the odds of remaining in an ample-reserves regime still look materially higher than a return to a scarce- reserves regime (see Short-term fixed income). However, other pieces of the deregulatory agenda are already underway. Last month, US banking regulators released the long-awaited Basel III endgame and GSIB surcharge proposals. As we have discussed previously, the new Basel III proposal will have a great impact on securitized products (see US Fixed Income Overview, 3/20/26); however in rates, the more relevant development is in the GSIB surcharge proposal. Changes include moving from single measurement dates to daily/monthly average values for a number of indicators that feed into a firm’s GSIB, establishing narrower surcharge bands, and redesigning the methodology for the Short-Term Wholesale Funding input. Scenarios in which Canadian energy producers benefit more from higher oil prices are also scenarios in which the broader economy suffers proportionately more. Implications for the Bank of Canada The combination of a persistent trade shock and a supply- driven energy price spike presents the Bank of Canada with a policy dilemma. Core inflation was decelerating before the oil shock hit, but headline CPI is now being pushed sharply high- er by energy prices. The labor market is weakening, the trade deficit is widening, and business investment outside of energy remains subdued—and an energy shock should exacerbate these negative activity trends. Markets are currently pricing between one and two rate hikes by year-end. As a small open economy with an explicit infla- tion target, it is plausible that the BoC has a lower threshold to tighten policy than some other DM central banks, and the Governing Council has appeared more proactive in shifting its policy stance in recent years. records.text: Estimating the pass-through from higher natural gas prices to headline inflation varies widely based on domestic price-setting conventions. Using the change in natural gas prices in 2022-23 (vs. 2020-21 average) relative to the relevant pricing benchmark as a proxy (Exhibit 5), we find that pass-through rates ranged from 40-70% for economies where wholesale and retail gas prices are mostly determined by market forces (e.g., Western Europe, North America, and Australia/New Zealand), by 20-40% in economies where prices are more heavily regulated (e.g., many economies in LatAm, Central Europe, and East Asia), and by less than 20% in economies where prices are more rigidly controlled by the government (e.g., Mainland China, Taiwan). While the 2022-2023 experience was unusual given the sudden loss of supply, based on these patterns we assume a 70% pass-through rate in economies where prices are mostly determined by market forces but smaller passthrough rate (30%) in economies where prices are more heavily regulated or government controlled (10%). records.text: 10 April 2026 Focus Europe Deutsche Bank AG Page 7 For euro area growth to be this low in 2026 would require GDP to contract by about 0.3% qoq in both Q2 and Q3. In short, it would indicate a recession. Takeaways: Growth and the ECB response to inflation There is a focus at the moment on the extent to which the Iran shock will increase inflation and pressure the ECB into hiking policy rates. The ceasefire announcement is potentially good news but there are uncertainties and oil prices remain elevated. Spot oil prices are about halfway between the ECB's baseline and 'adverse' scenarios. Forward oil prices are above the 'adverse' scenario. Relative to the ECB's baseline, there is still upside risk for inflation. There is also downside risk to growth. Growth was arguably more resilient than expected in the last energy shock in 2022. Will it be resilient again in 2026? There were some exceptional circumstances like the post-pandemic economic momentum and labour hoarding that don't apply in 2026. The fiscal easing isn't as significant in 2026 either. The market should keep its mind open to the prospect of weaker growth. In this note we highlight that economic growth looks to have been softer than expected in early 2026 even before the Middle East conflict began (we recently showed that recession risks are rising). In this note we also show that some of the assumptions the ECB made in its scenario analysis were optimistic. In other words, a more persistent energy shock could potent

aise inflation to 3.3% this year and 2.1% next, with core at 2.3% and 2.2%, respectively. Oil will drive up inflation swiftly and our assumption that elevated gas prices will be lasting delivers extra persistence. We expect indirect effects but think proper second round effects are likely to be small. Inflation undershoot gets delayed until 2H27E for headline, end-27E for core, but remains a key feature of our outlook. records.text: been moving higher over the last few years. That supports the view we have had that this is a less friendly environment for vol than it has been. The driving forces behind the rise in predicted equity volatility in our models over the last three years comes primarily from rising equity market concentration and an unemployment rate that has drifted higher. The unemployment rate has risen slowly from the 2023 cycle lows, and so it is the rising level and not the change in the unemployment rate that has contributed to higher predicted volatility, but the fact the unemployment rate has not been a vol-dampening factor in our models highlights that, even though the macro outlook is benign without clear imbalances, it is a “late-cycle” macro environment without obvious large macro tailwinds. AI optimism has been behind much of the US equity gains of the last few years, and the market has built significant value into AI-related companies. We think the concentration of value in AI-related areas of the market adds to the risk of higher volatility over time as focus increases on whether the benefits from AI justify that value as the AI cycle matures. Equity market concentration and valuation—the “non-macro” market factors in our model—are not direct measures of those AI-related risks, but they are in our view proxies for the impact that AI has had on equity markets in recent years. records.text: meeting just around the corner and the outcome dependent on developments in the Middle East, the OIS market was pricing a 56% probability of an April rate hike as of the 9th, implying that both a hold and a hike appear plausible. Attention turns to Governor Ueda’s remarks at the trust association conference on the 13th, which will be the last scheduled BoJ board member communication ahead of the April meeting. That said, it is also worth noting that last year’s remarks at the same conference were brief and did not offer major hints regarding the future course of monetary policy. In addition, because no other BoJ board members are scheduled to communicate before the April meeting, the possibility of the BoJ communicating through the media cannot be ruled out, meaning headline risk may also be present. In the superlong sector, while conditions continue to depend on how developments in the Middle East unfold, the term premium remains above a fair level when viewed over a longer horizon. For it to move from current levels toward fair value, buying would likely need to return on improved sentiment, making the first round of talks between the US and Iran scheduled for the 11th (Reuters, 9 April) one focal point. As seen in this week's 30y auction, even amid opaque conditions, investors are willing to step in when valuations become cheap versus the supply- demand backdrop. In that context, next week’s 20y auction will serve as a test of investors’ stance toward the superlong sector.

Whether the likely hawkish tone is acted upon will ultimately depend on forward-looking survey data and evidence of pass-through of the energy shock into core inflation - beyond the obvious and relatively direct effects, such as likely firmer air fares due to higher jet fuel prices. Our base case is that we see limited evidence of any immediate pass-through to underlying services inflation, and continued well-behaved pay settlements, on aggregate. We do worry more about wage growth in the public sector and lower paid private sectors, given the aforementioned evidence on the behavior of these firms as implicit wage bargainers. That said, we think any upwards inflection in aggregate wage growth will be capped by relatively soft earnings growth in the white-collar services sectors, and any pass-through to core inflation tempered by margin compression. The degree of that advantage may narrow over time, but we expect it to be strong enough to at least maintain the speed differential in the near term. With respect to buyouts, the reintroduction of trial mods at FHA means that more discount borrowers will eventually roll to foreclosure instead of curing repeatedly with partial claims/payment supplements. Moreover, the reinstatement of the limit on the frequency with which workout options can be used will also lead to more dispositions. The resulting uptick in speeds probably won’t be felt for at least a year, which won’t do much for rolls but gives us some confidence in a medium term pickup in the G2/FN speed advantage. Similar- ly, the reintroduction of a V A partial claim is much less attractive to the G2 discount buyer than the V ASP program was, but it also requires a trial and thus won’t be a panacea. A decent share of those borrowers will likely eventually be removed from the pools due to their inabil- ity to reinstate. Assuming that buyouts return to contributing at least an additional half CPR in favor of Ginnies, we think model projections (and market-implied speed differences) look reasonable. Morgan; Robust regression (1Q04-3Q25) Tracking the impact of oil prices on activity is complicated by the difficulty in differentiating demand versus supply impacts. A demand shock that boosts oil prices would also boost corporate profits, whereas an increase in prices that stems from a negative supply shock should have a negative impact on purchasing power and in turn corporate profits. To isolate these effects, we rely on data that isolates demand from supply shocks in the oil market.2We remove the estimat- ed oil price impact owing to demand shocks from total oil price changes to produce a proxy for supply shock-induced price changes. Regressing this proxy on corporate profit growth provides a gauge for how global profits are impacted by changes in oil prices that are unrelated to the underlying demand cycle. Unsurprisingly, a 10% oil supply shock is a drag on profits across the board, with the exception of the energy sector (Fig- ure 14). Looking ahead, we would frame risks as: (i) ECB repricing reasserting itself in Schatz (potentially slowing near-term narrowing if concerns around Middle-East conflict remains/ accelerates), (ii) any shift in funding/repo stability that challenges the current range logic, and (iii) the path of 10s/30s swaps as the primary determinant of whether Buxl widening per- sists. The ECB made the following assumptions: n Labour Market: The ECB assumes a resilient labor market, stating, "[t]he labour market is projected to remain resilient overall, as firms are expected to hoard labour in reaction to a temporary dip in economic activity owing to the war in the Middle East." Under the severe scenario, the ECB sees the unemployment rate increasing by only 0.1 percentage point (pp) against its baseline. Keeping the labour force unchanged, this would be consistent with a mere 0.1 pp deterioration in employment growth relative to the ECB's baseline. The ECB's argument largely relies on labour hoarding, making the labour market less sensitive to the business cycle. However, labour hoarding is weakening (for more see our latest labour chart book here), and employment has probably become more sensitive to the business cycle, potentially resembling the 1995-2015 period more than 2021-2025 (Figure 8). Using this former elasticity, employment could decline by a larger amount, potentially closer to 0.3 pp against the baseline in 2026. Labor market: stabilizing around full employment • The labor market has been buffeted by shocks to supply (immigration restrictions) and demand (tariff uncertainty, AI, DOGE). In our view, the supply shock is likely to be the bigger driver of soft job growth this year, especially as labor demand starts to recover on the back of fading tariff uncertainty, a positive fiscal policy impulse and consumer resilience. Hence, we have payrolls averaging 30k in 2026. Immigration tightening likely lowers breakeven job growth to about 20k, keeping payrolls close to full employment. Our revisions to the GDP trajectory should imply slower job growth. But with GDP still close to trend, we wouldn't expect the labor market to roll over. The main risk to our view is that the MAS raises the slope of the SGD NEER policy band slightly by 50bp, to an estimated 1.0%. Since the Middle East conflict began, we shifted from policy easing to tightening in the Philippines. With the ceasefire likely to raise hopes of a more enduring de-escalation at Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) — which recently held an off-cycle meeting where policymakers seem to have not been able to agree on a rate hike — focus would likely shift towards the potential damage inflicted by the conflict on the domestic economy. The Philippines – which shifted to a four-day work-week for the civil service to conserve fuel – would likely be a jurisdiction where policymakers would be concerned over a deepening of the economic challenges already present before the Middle East conflict broke out. We thus no longer expect a 25bp rate hike in April. While we retain our base case of a 25bp rate hike in June (followed by two 25bp rate cuts in February and April 2027, versus three previously in February, April and June), the risk is that a lasting de-escalation would quickly shift the central bank back to easing mode. However, hawkish sentiment already appears to be fading. While a similar dynamic is evident for the RBNZ, the adjustment has been more pronounced for the BoE. records.text: FX Strategy: JPY appreciation remains limited despite decline in crude oil prices Shinichiro Kadota BSJL, Japan | Lhamsuren Sharavdemberel BSJL, Japan JPY strength was limited and short-lived this week despite the drop in crude oil prices. At the start of the week, financial markets were subdued due to Easter Monday, but as US President Trump stepped up pressure on Iran, crude oil prices stayed elevated and USD strength was maintained, with USDJPY rising from the upper-159s to around 160 at one point. Subsequently, Pakistan, acting as an intermediary, requested the US extend the negotiation deadline by two weeks, and President Trump agreed. This pushed WTI crude down briefly from the 110s to 91, and USDJPY also saw USD selling and JPY buying, falling from around the mid-159s to around 158. However, with uncertainty still surrounding this weekend’s talks, the pair was bought back to around 159, and the JPY appreciation proved short-lived. In the week ahead, the biggest focus will be this weekend’s US-Iran talks on the 11th, and markets early in the week will likely be heavily influenced by the outcome. On the domestic front, BoJ Governor Ueda is scheduled to deliver remarks at a trust association conference on the 13th. But gains may also be capped because the broader uncertainty surrounding Middle East tensions and elevated oil prices may prevent Peruvian assets from delivering robust outperformance. From the perspective of investors, a right-leaning government would probably adopt more market-friendly policies—pro-mining measures, privatizing Petroperú, etc.—and therefore it would benefit local assets. The Monetary Policy Report also notes "The balanced-approach rule was analyzed in John B. Taylor (1999), “A Historical Analysis of Monetary Policy Rules,” in John B. Perhaps it is not an accident that in 2024, after maintaining the same stance of policy, the FOMC then caught down to the rule. The same happened again in 2025. Figure 1 Varied Volatility at the front end of the curve Source: State Street Markets, Bloomberg The Fed has been unique in that markets are not pricing additional rate hikes at this stage—unlike peers such as the BOE and ECB. In the UK, expectations have swung sharply from two cuts to two hikes, while in the euro area policy expectations have shifted toward a renewed hiking cycle, with two hikes now priced by December. Inflation is clearly being affected by the war. Nearly every developed‑market economy in our PriceStats daily inflation dataset is experiencing above‑average —or seasonally record‑high—price increases. For central banks, the key question is whether this rapid acceleration feeds through into longer‑run inflation expectations, particularly given that many have yet to sustainably achieve 2% inflation since the pandemic. In the US, longer‑term inflation expectations have reverted to roughly February levels while consumer inflation expectations remain low , reinforcing the Fed’s view that expectations remain anchored, (Figure 2). Figure 2 Expectations still anchored Source: State Street Markets, Bloomberg The next question is whether—and when—higher prices will begin to generate demand destruction. records.text: 2 Insights SPOTLIGHT VIEWS: LONG RUN INFLATION VS SHORT TERM PRICING Long run expectations. Inflation is clearly being impacted by the war. Nearly every developed‑market economy in our PriceStats dataset is experiencing above‑average—or seasonally record‑high—price increases. For central banks, the key question is whether this rapid price acceleration feeds through into long‑run inflation expectations, particularly given that many have yet to sustain 2% inflation since the pandemic. So far, the signal is mixed and, in aggregate, does not suggest an urgent need to hike. Since the start of the conflict, 5y5y inflation swaps indicate that long‑run inflation expectations have risen on net in both the UK and the Eurozone (Figure 3). However, these levels remain well below those seen in 2022–23. As such, while the direction of travel bears monitoring, it does not necessarily imply that the ECB or the BoE will rush to tighten—especially against the backdrop of moderating growth expectations (see page 3). Meanwhile, the long‑term inflation outlook in the US has reverted to around February levels, reinforcing the Fed’s view that inflation expectations remain anchored. While this outlook could change depending on the extent of damage to energy infrastructure and the duration of any Strait closure, current market pricing of long‑run inflation gives central banks scope to be patient before tightening prematurely—particularly those that had not already begun hiking prior to the conflict S

ies and supply chains are proposed at about 0.5% of GDP. At present, the shock is more sector-specific than a broad- based macroeconomic price shock, so micro-level fiscal responses are prioritized. If the situation evolves to require nominal anchoring and inflation stability—even at the cost of some consumption and growth drags—monetary policy action may follow. However, given current economic and labor market conditions, there are no strong early signs of broad-based price instability beyond oil-related prices, so a wait-and-see approach is preferred. Of course, other factors such as KRW depreciation—possibly driven by geopolitical developments and tightening stances from major central banks—could prompt the Bank of Korea to raise rates in consideration of KRW depreciation’s spill- over effect to inflation. However, the contribution of rate hikes to FX stability may be limited, so costs and benefits must be carefully calibrated. The authorities will continue to monitor macroprudential policy to prevent one-sided FX mar- ket expectations from becoming self-fulfilling. Exchange rate movements, within the bounds of balance sheet stability for economic agents, should be seen as a shock absorber for external conditions. More important, the EU-wide deadline to draw RRF funds is 31 August 2026, leaving limited time for any new government to secure the full amount. In addition, €6.4bn of cohesion funds remains blocked until 2030, implying roughly €1.3bn per year once compliance issues are resolved. Any new government would also face a challenging inflation and fiscal backdrop. Four inflation risks stand out: 1) the end of price controls: profit-margin caps continue to distort measured CPI; adjusting for an estimated 1.5pp understatement, true headline inflation could be closer to 3.3% y/y in March 2026 rather than the reported 1.4%; 2) ongoing fiscal easing adds further upward pressure; 3) FX volatility could increase due to the election outcome; and 4) higher global energy prices could add at least another 1.1pp to CPI if Brent stabilises at about $100 through YE26. The NBH has reactivated its FX-liquidity facility for energy importers; when used for 3-4 months in 2022, it cost about €1.5bn in reserves. records.text: more valuable. But what about layer 4? It stands to reason that layer 4 is more valuable today as inference demand growth accelerates. Meanwhile, data center construction delays due to supply chain bottlenecks seem to be a more palpable risk today, according to JLL’s 2026 Global Data Center Outlook. At the hardware layer, GPU shortages aren’t the only constraint. Memory is facing a structural shortage, as our semiconductor equity analysts (Harlan Sur and team) note in their Micron earnings recap. Further exacerbating the hardware shortage is a helium shortage due to the Middle East conflict, according to the New York Times. These bottle- necks appear to be significant buffers against compute cost deterioration. It's also worth noting that just because more capable frontier models are released does not mean older models are rendered useless. In fact, with rising inference token demand, users will have to optimize for token cost structures that are variable. Older models are cheaper and cutting edge models are more expensive. records.text: US Economics Weekly10 April 2026 ab 18 UMich 5-10 year inflation expectations rise to 3.4% in April Median 5-to-10 year ahead inflation expectations rose 0.2 pp to 3.4% in the preliminary April data from the University of Michigan Survey Research Center, a move higher but a full percentage point lower than last April, following liberation day tariff announcements. Median one-year ahead inflation expectations rose 1.0 pp to 4.8%, matching the August 2025 level and undoing the gradual progress seen since then. Since the Middle East conflict began, the average price of retails gas prices have risen over one dollar per gallon, and we expected a sizable jump in near-term expectations in response to this. However, the preliminary estimate has had the tendency to revise down in the past several months, saving March and December. Both January and February also saw 5-10 year preliminary expectations rose to 3.4% before revising to 3.3%. But that was before the oil price shock, and that tendency may end. Consumer sentiment fell 5.7 points to 47.6, continuing its downward trend to an all time low. The deterioration was broad-based, as the current conditions subcomponent fell 5.7 points to 50.1, and the expectations subcomponent fell 5.6 points to 46.1. records.text: 2 US Watch | 10 April 2026 Rates and FX: Financial initial market reaction Rates: Print that endorses core views Weaker-than-anticipated core CPI inflation allowed the US rates curve to modestly bull steepen. Fed pricing was little changed on net, however, with market reflecting about 10bps of cuts this year and roughly 30bps in total through the end of next year. We continue to see room for front-end and belly rates to compress more in line with our economists’ call for two 25bps Fed cuts this year. Readthrough to benign core PCE supports this view as well. We favor real yield longs in the belly of the curve on stagflation risks. We also see 5y5y inflation as underpriced and think that for the Fed to meaningfully consider hikes, longer-term inflation expectations need to reflect risk of unanchoring. FX: USD slightly lower on a slight miss The USD depreciated broadly on back of the slightly softer-than-expected CPI report, though the moves were relatively modest on net. The slight miss on the core reading (and more favorable passthrough to PCE) is likely a welcomed development for the Fed, though it still feels early to see this moving the needle in terms of materially bringing forward cut expectations. That said, a potentially higher print could have reignited concerns over the need for hikes, so the avoidance of that (for now) has kept the USD on the back foot. records.text: US Economics Weekly10 April 2026 ab 29 US Economics Weekly UBS Research Week Ahead: PCE tracking and the Beige Book The March PPI and import price data will refine our estimate of the March core PCE price increase, currently 0.31%, and could shift that notably. If not, that would push core PCE inflation from 2.97% in February to 3.19% in March. We are tracking a punchier 0.68% increase in headline PCE prices in March, owing to the run-up in energy prices. Next week, we expect headline industrial production was flat in March, held back by motor vehicle and parts production. The first regional manufacturing surveys for April likely remained subdued due to uncertainty and higher energy prices. Small business optimism likely fell in March due to cost and logistical headwinds. Existing home sales likely edged down in March and the housing market index was likely unchanged at a low level, adding to an overall weak picture of housing activity. The Beige Book's anecdata should add color on how the Fed's firm contacts are digesting the Middle East conflict and the IEEPA tariff decision. Talks between the US and Iran concerning the ceasefire could take place on Saturday in Islamabad with a US delegation expected to include Vice President JD Vance, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner (link here). Next week will be the last opportunity for FOMC participants to hit the tapes before the pre-meeting quiet period begins. Governor Miran will speak at the Washington Economic Festival on Thursday.

Solar and wind to reduce water footprint: The transition toward renewable power sources can significantly reduce upstream water use (Figure 9). Solar PV and wind power require minimal operational water compared with thermal generation technologies, which rely on steam cycles and cooling systems. Energy security concerns triggered by the Middle East conflict might accelerate the deployment of domestic renewables capacity, reinforced by hyperscalers’ commitments to clean electricity procurement and increasing regulatory scrutiny on emissions (see US data center power demand: Supply, infrastructure to hamper growth, dated 28 January). As renewable penetration increases, the water intensity of electricity generation should decline, helping to moderate the upstream water footprint of data centers. records.text: month. Food prices remained unchanged, but we see upside risk if fuel and fertilizer shortages persist. Meanwhile, the core index increased a soft 0.2% in March (consensus: 0.3%), the smallest increase since last May. Weakness was most apparent in the core services ex- shelter component, which increased just 0.18% last month, largely as medical care service prices remained broadly unchanged. Shelter prices rebounded from a soft February, as owner's equivalent and tenant’s rent increased 0.28% and 0.19%, respectively. Core goods prices rose 0.11%, similar to last month, in part as apparel prices increased a firm 1.0% in March. Computer software prices, which have a greater weight in PCE, again showed sizeable gains, rising 4.0% last month. Based on this report, we expect core PCE inflation rose 0.257% in March, pushing the year-ago measure to 3.1%, which should keep the Fed comfortable continuing to keep rates on hold for a time (see US: March CPI inflation was moderate outside energy, Abiel Reinhart, 4/10/26).

In our view, the RBI likely sought to discourage these trades given their potential to distort the DF and NDF forward curves and, at the margin, add to upward pressure on the spot USD/INR. These regulation changes force a broad unwind as the tighter NOP constraint limits dealers’ capacity to run the position themselves, while the NDF restriction restricts their ability to quote NDFs to any party running the carry trade. As a consequence of these announcements, spot USD/INR and both DF and NDF outright curves shifted lower as dealers unwound the carry trades. Meanwhile, the NDF-DF spread widened further. In our view, the RBI may not be particularly concerned by higher NDF points, as they push NDF-implied yields to elevated levels (around 12%-16% in the 1M-3M tenors) (Exhibit 6). This makes it increasingly expensive to express a bearish INR view via NDFs, in line with the objective of reducing speculative activity. A lower DF (outright) curve also reduces hedging costs for corporates with future USD payables and genuine Dollar demand. In reality, moves in LFPR swamp the moves in population growth in pushing around the unemployment rate. records.text: Oil prices have risen sharply due to the war in Iran, but liquified natural gas (LNG) n prices have risen even more sharply (and remain elevated under our commodity forecasts) due to the disruption of Qatar’s supply and damage to its infrastructure. For countries that rely on LNG, this outsized price response suggests rising energy prices will have a larger impact on inflation and activity than oil prices alone would suggest. The rise in gas prices will impact inflation through three distinct channels. First, n higher gas prices will directly increase costs for natural gas consumed by households, with impacts depending on energy composition and domestic utility passthrough rates. Second, higher gas prices will raise household electricity prices, with statistical estimates pointing to a 25% passthrough rate on the share of electricity produced with gas. Third, higher gas prices will raise producer costs, thereby leading to downstream boosts to core inflation. Combining our estimates from each of these channels, we estimate that a 10% n increase in natural gas prices (separate from other energy price increases) raises global headline inflation by 8bp. After merging these estimates with our standing oil-price impulses, we estimate that the war in Iran will raise global inflation by 0.8% (vs. 0.7% based on oil price increases alone). The country heads to general elections this Sunday, April 12 and polls paint a very uncertain landscape (See Peru: Political blind date). We see an asymmetrically negative balance of risks considering that even if a pro-market candidate is elected, there could be a weak mandate, making instability likely to persist amid the risk of populist options emerging. A highly fragmented electorate does not provide clarity. There are more than 35 candidates running, none of them havemore than 15% support, and more than a quarter of the electorate is still undecided, which leaves significant room for surprises. In Argentina, we expect the March CPI to be 3.3%, affected by a 20% increase in gasoline prices. This would leave annual inflation virtually unchanged at 33%, in a streak of ten consecutive months where monthly inflation either rose or stayed unchanged. This upward trend mostly reflects the pass-through from the 20% real devaluation Argentina experienced between April and October 2025, in our view. But the FX has been very stable since the mid-term elections, so we expect this to induce a slow disinflation starting in April, conditional on a wind-down of the current Middle East conflict. Our 2026 inflation forecast is 31%. Why a slow disinflation? Because we don't see any strong convincing anchors. The ceiling of the band crawls at past inflation, the FX has been contained but there's no guarantee this will remain the case, and regulated prices are still rising in relative terms.

records.text: Emerging Asia Outlook Treading with caution Despite the ceasefire, Emerging Asia is unlikely to escape at least some lasting economic drags from persistent supply constraints. Both RBI and BoK kept policy rates on hold this week. We no longer expect an April hike from the BSP . MAS is likely to keep FX policy settings unchanged next week. While it remains too early to draw definitive conclusions, the announcement of a ceasefire between US-Iran provides some cause for optimism that a resolution of the conflict is in sight. Our baseline has been for the normalisation of the Strait of Hormuz by early April (The day after (the Middle East conflict ends), 26 March 2026). It remains to be seen if a more enduring de-escalation will be achieved. While the ceasefire could help to relieve some of the bottlenecks for oil & gas supply, flows through the Strait of Hormuz have remained muted despite the ceasefire announcement. Our commodities analyst sees an upside risk to the Brent forecast of USD85/barrel for 2026 from a potential delay in the normalisation of the Strait or further escalation. Brent crude oil prices fell to $94/bbl on 8 April from above $110/bbl before the announcement, and rose again above $97/b at the time of writing. records.text: Core CPI 12-month % change Source: BLS, Haver, UBS. October 2026 changes estimated based on surrounding months and CPI imputation guidance. Based on today’s CPI we project core PCE prices rose 0.31% in March with headline PCE prices increasing 0.68%. Today’s estimate would see 12-month core PCE price inflation at 3.19% through March and headline PCE price inflation at 3.49%. Both headline and core PCE remain above their CPI counterparts, but by our estimate the gap between the inflation measures should close a bit with this month's data. However, we would discount today’s projection for PCE prices as we do not yet have either PPI or import prices for March and incorporating those prices could alter the PCE price translation notably. Additionally in the next couple of days we will improve our estimates for some series used in PCE prices that were not published in today's CPI. The March PPI is scheduled for release on Tuesday next week (April 14), import prices on Wednesday (April 15). PCE prices for March are currently scheduled to be publish in three weeks (Thursday, April 30). This downward bias from the government shutdown should reverse in next month's release of April CPI. We project that inflation rates will peak in the next couple of months with headline CPI inflation around 3.8% in April and core CPI inflation around 2.9% in May. records.text: ide a catalyst HG cash has lagged the broader rally in risk-assets post cease-fire and this is somewhat unsurprising given how much it had outperformed in the first 5 weeks of the conflict. JULI is 3.5bp tighter since the cease-fire but only 2.5bp tighter WTD to 93bp or 6bp tighter since the conflict began. What is somewhat more surprising is that, as of this writing, the UST 10yr is only 3bp lower WTD versus the S&P500 up >3.5%. This is a positive for spreads in that we thought yields might rally more on a cease-fire announcement and thus temper the bid for credit. The bid for credit has been mixed lately, with notably dealers net buying $8bn of bonds this week and thus inventories rising to 88% of their 3m range, though still deeply net short in the belly and long-end of the curve. This lines up with a demand backdrop of mixed flows and a pending ramp up in supply with bank earnings kicking off next week followed by the usual ramp up in Financials issuance. On the fund flow side, while we did see a resumption in overall inflows (+$597mn) after last week’s outflows (-$1bn), we wouldn’t characterize these inflows as particularly convincing just yet given how concentrated they were into just a handful of funds, in line with the daily trend which has remained choppy over the past week. We turned less bearish but stopped short of turning outright bullish on CAD through the conflict, because we never felt that the oil shock alone would sufficiently make up for Canada’s domestic shortcomings. That remains the case, as the structural decoupling from the US still overwhelms the national income increase from oil revenues and as carry will be prohibitive in a renewed pro-cy- clical push if the ceasefire holds. In North Asia, both the majors JPY and CNY emerge from the episode with their medium-term narratives arguably more entrenched than before, as corroborated by this week’s price action: USD/CNY has swiftly fallen to reclaim pre-war lows, while USD/JPY is little changed just below the 160 interven- tion line. For JPY, ROW central banks have repriced hikes materially higher in the wake of the conflict, throwing into sharper relief the BoJ's glacial tightening cadence (one hike per six months), which looks increasingly insufficient to arrest yen weakness on a cross-rate basis. The energy shock compounds this through two channels simultaneously — first, by reigniting fiscal concerns and thereby re-tightening the negative correlation between super-long JGB yields and JPY that had briefly loosened; and second, by reviving trade bal- ance deterioration concerns given Japan's structural energy import dependency. This is a cumulative growth loss of 90bp vs prior forecasts. We assume the Euro area avoids a technical recession. In 2Q26, we assume consumers buffer the initial impact with a reduction in the savings rate. In 2H26, the mechanical impact of German fiscal stimulus should help (although Germany is probably still the country where recessionary risks are highest). But consumer confidence responded strongly in March already; business sentiment is likely to follow, we think. The sequential growth recovery from 4Q26 is likely to be shallow, pushing GDP levels below pre-shock trajectories persistently. Fiscal policy is unlikely to come to a substantial rescue this time around. We would expect small, targeted packages to come through to help avoid non-linear effects on highly energy-exposed sectors and/or low-income groups.

Consequently, futures prices for this year’s harvest, while not completely insensitive to fertilizers, don’t represent what would happen were fertilizer prices to remain elevated for an entire season. Farmers in the US often lock in prices for the upcoming sea- son during the summer, with additional purchases in the fall and winter, so prices later this year will be important to watch. To get additional insight on the connection between fertilizer prices and agriculture prices, we look at the share of farm expenses devoted to fertilizer and the historical correlation between fertilizer and crop prices. For farm expenses, fertiliz- ers, lime, and soil conditioners of all types accounted for 7% of costs in 2024. Given the Food Dollar data showing that 12% of final food costs go to farms, dollar-for-dollar pass- through would imply a 10% increase in all fertilizer costs would translate into a 70bp increase in farm prices and 8bp increase in CPI food. This note examines the academic foundations of central bank independence (CBI) and reviews the empirical evidence on its macroeconomic benefits. We survey international precedents for addressing political critiques of monetary policy through institutional mechanisms such as external reviews, and assess the economic consequences should BanRep’s de facto inde- pendence be compromised. We argue that while political crit- icism of monetary policy is legitimate in a democratic society, undermining central bank independence carries well-docu- mented and severe economic costs. Proactive institutional responses—including an external review of its monetary poli- cy framework—could help to strengthen both its analytical underpinnings and its democratic legitimacy. The Petro-BanRep confrontation The confrontation between the Petro administration and Ban- Rep is not new. But it has escalated sharply in the first quarter of 2026 amid a deteriorating inflation outlook driven by the unprecedented minimum wage administrative decision, pro- cyclical fiscal policy, and the Iran-related oil shock. By majority vote BanRep had already raised rates by 100bp in January 2026, followed by another 100bp hike in March (to 11.25%). President Petro’s critique can be organized along several axes. The PPI y/y print turned positive for the first time since late 2022, led by raw materials and mining, and was consistent with the surge in the official manufacturing PMI input prices. In contrast, March headline CPI inflation edged lower, to 1.0% y/y in March, reflecting that authorities allowed only a limited pass through fromglobal crude oil prices into gasoline prices (we estimate less than 50%) and suggesting still-soft domestic demand. Deteriorating consumer confidence and softer real spending While last week, we were still pointing to the apparent relative resilience in some of the incoming consumer survey data in the US and Europe, that changed this week. The University of Michigan survey showed a jump in short-term inflation expectations (while longer-term expectations remained anchored) and a sharp drop in consumer expectations. Open-ended comments show that many consumers blame the Iran conflict for unfavorable changes to the economy. Also this week, the hard data on real consumer spending in February, ie, before the war, were somewhat weaker than expected. This reflected slower services spending, a decline in nominal personal income driven by weaker non-wage components, and elevated inflation weighing on real gains. Last week's March payroll report also showed income fundamentals becoming less supportive independent of the war. 10 April 2026 6 Barclays | Global Economics Weekly: Truce and dare

Morgan; *Includes 2025 preliminary, 2026 investment intentions Oil and gas share of capital expenditures* Brent crude oil price Part of the explanation comes from the fact that Canadian heavy crude is more energy-intensive to extract and refine than other major sources of global oil supply. With long development timelines and high upfront costs, oil sands oper- ators need prices to remain durably high before committing to new investment. The current uncertainty makes a repeat of the 2010-14 capex boom look unlikely. In addition, Canada’s oil and gas sector has undergone significant consolidation in recent years. Just five companies now account for 85% of Alberta’s oil sands production, and these firms have increas- ingly prioritized shareholder returns, debt reduction, and buy- backs over production growth. Moreover, the oil and gas sector accounts for just 1% of total employment. While oil and gas employment does tend to move in tandem with crude prices (Figure 6), even a robust hiring response by the energy sector would be unlikely to pro- vide a meaningful boost to a labor market already under sig- nificant pressure. We remain bearish on the PHP , THB and INR, given their exposure to energy imports and relatively weak BoP/growth outlooks. India has tightened FX regulations meaningfully over the past fortnight, by n capping authorized dealers’ end-of-day net open position at US$100mn, a sharp reduction from the prior limit of around 20%-25% of Tier I and II capital (in some cases US$1bn+ for foreign banks in India), and restricted authorized dealers from offering INR non-deliverable forwards (NDFs) to residents or non-residents. In our view, these steps are aimed at curbing speculative INR short positioning, n particularly “FX carry trades” that buy USD/INR deliverable forwards (DF) onshore, and simultaneously selling USD/INR NDFs at the same maturity. As a consequence, spot USD/INR and both DF and NDF outright curves shifted lower as dealers unwound the carry trades. Given the 10th April deadline for dealers to adhere to the rules, we think the n position unwind is mostly complete. However, these measures do not resolve the underlying external backdrop. We suspect the labor market may not be as healthy as the current FOMC assumes, and thus still think the labor market evidence could motivate another rate cut after inflation peaks and the monthly run rates fall back. If the monthly run rates of inflation fall back, that would be a signal to FOMC participants that the price level shift from the energy prices is passing through, tariff effects are waning, and the inflation impacts proving temporary. We could imagine a cut at the September meeting, like the last two years. People also seem to underestimate the role of the labor force participation rate. Although we expect core inflation in 2026 to trend somewhat higher than the output gap alone would suggest, it is unlikely to approach the peaks observed in 2023, given the current degree of domestic slack. Second, it is important to consider the sequencing and nature of supply chain and raw material price shocks. In the previous hiking cycle, the negative effects of pandemic-related supply chain disruptions had largely subsided by the time policy tightening began, and the growth outlook was already improving. Although the Russia-Ukraine war in 2022 led to further increases in energy prices, there were no significant supply shortages, so the primary policy focus remained on managing inflation risks rather than addressing growth con- cerns. This environment allowed the Bank of Korea to pro- ceed with rate hikes without the added complication of simul- taneous supply-side constraints weighing on real activity. records.text: Europe EUR rates: tails compress, lower vol, front-end ‘fair’, long sovereign credit. n Although uncertainty remains and commodity market relief is likely to be at best gradual, we think the revealed preference on both sides of a path towards negotiation and conflict cessation will compress the tail of much higher inflation / weaker growth that contributed to a sharp rise in European rate volatility. Hikes remain a likely outcome, with probability mass on 2-3 hikes still high. However, the urgency for the ECB to act in April has diminished — while a hike is possible, there now needs to be some probability on an April hold (with the market currently pricing +8bp), which would in turn likely have dovish implications for Z6 pricing from here. This suggests to us that i) there is further room for short-expiry short maturity vol to fall as the distribution of outcomes for the front-end narrows, ii) Z6 pricing may drift slightly lower in yield, but is unlikely to see significant declines without sharper commodity price relief, and iii) sovereign credit spreads will likely tighten as the combination of lower rate volatility and a floor on growth risks benefits EGBs outside of Germany (where, together with the EU, fiscal needs are only likely to increase from here, see below). Anxiety has spread beyond crude, with renewed questions over the availability of fertilizers, aluminum, and other critical industrial inputs caught up in the disruption. We’ve only modestly trimmed our EM growth forecast on expectations of an early normal- ization of passage through the Hormuz Strait. There is a clear risk that non-linearities caused by fuel and fertilizer shortages could have a stronger inflationary and growth impact than currently envisioned, should the conflict be more prolonged. While a temporary ceasefire has been announced, uncertainty still prevails on whether it will hold and on the extent to which the spillovers from the conflict will impact EM growth and inflation. Following February 28, EM capital flows had shifted from a synchronized upswing to outflows, but with performance increasingly differentiated across countries (Figure 1). EM Asia appears most exposed (after the GCC) to energy-market fallout, and this has played out in local equity markets, as several economies are headed toward a dual shock of higher prices and potential fuel shortages. records.text: Investing: The past and future of energy transition Dave Dai, CFA(i) Barclays Bank, Hong Kong China is comparatively insulated from potential energy supply disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, given its ongoing energy transition and declining reliance on imported fuel. The 15th Five-Year Plan reinforces this trajectory, highlighting a greater role for green energy, restrained coal and oil consumption, and accelerated power grid upgrades. The transition is anchored by China’s ongoing power sector reform, extensive domestic manufacturing base and sustained policy support for sustainable finance. Energy security slowly improving but electricity more resilient China’s energy mix has undergone a decisive shift over the past decade, moving away from coal toward renewables, hydro and nuclear. However, oil’s share held steady at 18% in 2024, while natural gas edged up from 6% to 9% (Figure 21). While overall energy import dependence eased slightly from 17% to 16%, we point out that this was driven by China’s emergence as a net coal exporter while coal and gas depend more on imports (Figure 22). 8 April 2026 10 Barclays | Economics / Sustainable Investing

(2025) , BNP Paribas Mining to power AI boom: The construction of data centers requires significant quantities of metals and minerals across multiple parts of the supply chain. These include materials used in semiconductors and microelectronics (e.g. boron, silicon), data storage components (e.g. gallium), and power generation and storage technologies (e.g. lithium, graphite). Most modern mining processes are highly water- intensive, as water is required for ore processing and mineral separation, cooling machinery, and dust suppression during extraction and transport. Copper as an example: Though copper is not the thirstiest mineral in terms of water use in extraction (Figure 11), it illustrates the growing tension between rising mineral demand and water availability. Copper mines are estimated to have withdrawn 13.6 trillion liters of water in 2015–19, with water use increasing at a rate 50% higher than copper production, suggesting an increase in the water intensity of copper production (see Lutter et al., 2025 and Figure 12). We expect the expansion of AI infrastructure and electrification technologies to drive copper demand in the coming decades, which will also increase water demand. records.text: Latin America Outlook Burning oil The region's CPIs are already reflecting part of the oil shock, especially where containment measures have been more modest. We expect cautious central banks in this context, but aggressive reactions are not our base case. • In Brazil, inflation surprised higher for a second consecutive month, with pressures on fuel prices and also foodstuff. We still expect the BCB to cut the Selic rate 25bp on 29 April, to 14.50%, given its recent communication, but additional deterioration in medium-term expectations may represent upside risks to our forecast of it reaching 13.00% by September. • In Mexico, direct energy-related pressures remained contained as the government smooths gasoline prices through the excise tax (IEPS) mechanism. records.text: 10 April 2026 Focus Europe Page 4 Deutsche Bank AG In addition to a new baseline macro scenario, in March the ECB also presented two alternative or risk scenarios conditioned on higher oil and gas prices. In the new baseline scenario, the ECB expects GDP growth of 0.9% in 2026. This assumes oil peaks around USD90/bbl before easing quickly. In the 'adverse' scenario, with oil spiking to USD 119/bbl in Q2 before easing quickly, the ECB foresees 0.6% GDP growth. In the 'severe' scenario, with oil spiking to USD 145/bbl in Q2 and remaining elevated, the ECB projects 0.4% growth in 2026. Although gas prices remain contained and roughly in line with the baseline scenario, spot oil prices are roughly halfway between the baseline and 'adverse' scenarios. Moreover, forward oil prices for 2026 are currently above the 'adverse' scenario. In other words, at today's energy prices, the 0.9% baseline forecast looks optimistic. If the Strait of Hormuz remains effectively closely despite the ceasefire announcement, it is possible that oil prices rise further. For example, our strategists foresee oil prices reaching USD 130-150/bbl if disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz persist until June (Figure 7). Against this background and despite the ceasefire announcement, in this section we examine the underlying assumptions made by the ECB when deriving its growth estimates. This is because the likely next step, in our view, is that note investors may demand more spread concession, increasing CLO’s cost of debt. Issuance mix: Fewer resets may point to less conviction A notable shift in 2026 has been the mix of gross CLO creation across the three main categories of 1) new issue activity, 2) refinancings (which adjust the interest rate of CLO liability tranches), and 3) resets (which are more comprehensive than refinancings, as they also extend CLO maturity and reinvestment periods). After resets dominated activity in 2024 and 2025, new issues and refinancings have been meaningfully stronger than resets to start 2026. Resets total $31 billion vs. $38 billion of new-issue creation year to date, dropping the share of resets from 42% to 33% of CLO creation year over year (Exhibit 7). This may be indicative of less conviction from CLO managers in the durability of the cycle. It may also reflect the limits of existing collateral pools and, in some cases, the reduced economic appeal of extending reinvestment on older collateral. From a relative-performance standpoint, there is no consistent trend of the PEN either underperforming or outperforming across past elections. A comparable dynamic is evident in the local bond market: volatility increases ahead of the first-round election (Figure 5), and the 2021 underperformance was similarly recovered after the run-off vote (Figure 6). From the perspective of investors, a right-leaning government would probably adopt more market-friendly policies—pro-mining measures, privatizing Petroperú, etc.—and therefore it would benefit local assets. The risk, however, comes from a left-leaning win; higher fiscal spending or a repeat of the 2021 Castillo precedent could precipitate a rising pressure on local assets. Historical pattern shows that short-term pressure intensifies during the runoff: Peru’s local assets— Peruvian sol (PEN) and sovereign bonds (PeruGB)— have traditionally responded to political uncertainty with short-term volatility and underperformance, which tend to show correction after the run-off elections. records.text: Asian FX Outlook Post Ceasefire and Implications of India’s FX Regulations Risk sentiment improved discernibly after the ceasefire announcement, and front-end rates in Asia fell sharply. Asian local rates markets sold off significantly last month, particularly the front end, and most curves bear-flattened (Exhibit 1), as the market flipped from approaching end-of-cycle scenarios to pricing in hikes across several markets. At the peak of the Middle East conflict, towards the end of March, rates curves were pricing in around 4-5 hikes in India, ~5 hikes in South Korea, ~3 hikes in Thailand and ~1 hike in Malaysia. After the ceasefire announcement on 8th April, front-end Asian rates fell sharply (by around 5-30bp across the region, with the largest move noted in India), as markets partially unwound the rate hike expectations amid the sharp drop in oil prices. As we wrote in a previous note, we viewed the hikes priced in several Asian curves as overdone. We outlined that 2026 is different to 2022 for a variety of reasons, and the primary policy response to the oil shock is more likely to be fiscal (if the conflict is short-lived). In our view, monetary policy tightening is likely to happen sooner in economies that have higher FX vulnerabilities (i.e. those with already weak current account balances, high levels of external debt or high exposure to the Middle East). records.text: empirical evidence overwhelmingly shows that central bank independence benefits precisely the constituen- cies the government says it wants to protect: low-income households, workers, and borrowers. Independent central banks deliver lower inflation, more stable currencies, reduced sovereign risk premia, and lower borrowing costs for the gov- ernment itself. At the same time, central banks are not above legitimate democratic scrutiny. The appropriate institutional response is not political subordination but structured account- ability: external reviews, independent evaluation, enhanced communication. The stakes are high. If BanRep’s independence is compro- mised—whether through formal legal changes, de facto polit- ical pressure, or the appointment of acquiescent board mem- bers—the consequences would be predictable, severe, and difficult to reverse. Türkiye and Argentina provide cautionary tales that Colombia cannot, in our view, afford to replicate. records.text: 10 April 2026 Focus Europe Page 2 Deutsche Bank AG Starting the year on a softer note: a smaller growth buffer to absorb an energy shock The Iran shock is poised to significantly impact the European economy. We recently downgraded our macro forecast for the euro area, lower annual growth for 2026 to 0.5% from 1.1%. While this week's ceasefire announcement is positive news, there remains a lot of uncertainty, about the durability of a ceasefire, the timing of a full reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and the extent of lasting damage that might already have been done to Middle East energy supply. The number of vessels passing through the Strait of Hormuz remains low despite the ceasefire. The spot price of oil is roughly halfway between the ECB's baseline and 'adverse' scenarios, and the forward price of oil is above the 'adverse' scenario (see here). In short, despite the ceasefire, there will still be a cost to growth. The question is, how much? The Bloomberg consensus forecast for 2026 euro area GDP growth is 1.1%. The ECB's new baseline scenario puts growth at 0.9%. Both look too optimistic, in our view. Before we question some of the ECB's assumed growth dynamics in the second half of this note, in the first half we focus on the signals of a weaker start to growth in 2026 even before the conflict in the Middle East began. The weakness of industrial production is the best indicator of the early-2026 vulnerability of growth (Figure 1). Output fell across the board in February

They deemed a pre-emptive hike to "guard against the risk of inflation expectations becoming unan- chored" had some merit, but could "cause unnecessary vola- tility… if the conflict was resolved" or if growth turned out weaker near-term. Were core inflation, wage growth or medi- um-/long-term inflation expectations to move higher, "deci- sive and timely increases in the OCR would be required." The contrast with the RBA's March hike is striking. Both cen- tral banks acknowledge inflation risks, but the RBNZ appears less inclined to act pre-emptively despite New Zealand's larg- er cumulative CPI deviation from target since the pandemic arguably presenting a greater risk of expectations de-anchor- ing. This likely reflects differing lessons from 2022–23: the RBA, which hiked less than peers and seems to somewhat regret last year's shallow easing, has adopted a sterner pos- ture. While the RBNZ — having hiked aggressively, endured much weaker growth and was forced to cut deeply — explic- itly cautioned against reapplying the 2022 template to the cur- rent supply shock in a recent speech.
