records.text: Michael Metcalfe, Caroline Coughlin7 April 2026Core question in US inflation fright At the beginning of March, Alberto Cavallo warned here that large energy shocks increasingly travel fast. Twenty-six days later, they have. The State Street PriceStats series for the US rose 1.5% m/m (NSA) in March, the largest monthly rise in the US price level since our data series began in July 2008. And early April is not cooling things down. The US, of course, is not alone in experiencing much higher inflation. Figures 5–10 overleaf detail the nuances of this global inflation shock, which in most countries is bigger than February 2022. But this piece focuses on what the State Street PriceStats readings mean for the US official inflation print for the month, and whether the detail behind the headlines will be as shocking. The headline isn’t the headline. With daily futures prices, one might assume that energy, or indeed food, price shocks should not surprise forecasters, but as Figure 2 shows, estimating pass-through can still lead to sizeable errors. As large as the headline move in the State Street PriceStats series is, our more granular forecasting methodology is consistent with a more modest 1% mom gain (SA) in headline CPI for March. This is in line with the median economist forecast, but there is an unusually large range of estimates: some are as high as the 1.5% raw State Street PriceStats reading, with others as low as 0.6% mom. Additionally, we move CEMBI Middle East real estate to OW considering the attractive valuation versus fundamental factors as well as strong domestic demand. The spread of CEMBI BD IG over US HG rose to 15bp after reaching flat level in mid- March, and the main driver of the widening in the basis is not suprisingly the Middle East. Granted, the current basis is still within the 5-25bp range since the middle of 2024 so does not suggest a significant underperformance. Nevertheless, we have been of the view that the basis can compress further during 2026 given the divergence in supply dynamics whereby US HG is delivering elevated issuance while the primary market in EM corporates is more in line with the recent historical trend. The main variable will be the extent of recov- ery in CEMBI Middle East spread, where the basis over the respective US HG segments has expanded to 20-30bp from 0-10bp prior to the conflict. records.text: Outlook for the economy and prices (last updated 19 March) Real GDP growth in Q4 25 was revised up to 1.3% in the second estimate, reflecting strong capex, among other factors. Looking ahead, a rebound in inventory investment is expected following the large negative contribution seen this time around. Furthermore, housing investment, which fell sharply due to institutional factors in Q3, is likely to recover. Companies are actively investing to address labor shortages and rebuild supply chains in response to tariffs, and we continue to expect consumption to recover gradually on support from large wage increases and easing inflation. That said, the surge in crude oil prices stemming from the Middle East conflict is likely to exert some downside pressure on the economy, particularly on consumption. As the magnitude and duration of higher crude oil prices could cause the adverse impact on the economy to evolve over time, careful monitoring is warranted. On the price front, we expect CPI inflation excluding perishables (core) to ease as a trend, albeit with fluctuations, in the near term due mainly to declines (y/y base effects) in goods, especially food. However, inflation is increasingly sticky, suggesting any deceleration will be more moderate than we previously expected. The +3.3% growth in scheduled earnings marked the strongest since June 1992. On a same-sample basis as well, total cash earnings and scheduled earnings both grew at a faster pace of +3.1% y/y (+2.3% and +2.7%, respectively in January). Real wages (total cash earnings minus CPI excluding imputed rent) surged +1.9% y/y (+0.7%) with support from slower inflation, staying positive for a second consecutive month. records.text: Late last year, we conducted a deep-dive analysis on the ‘state of play’ in the collateralized loan obligation (CLO) market, which has grown to a sizable global market and has become a core part of many investors’ fixed income allocations. At the time, we saw scope for valuations of senior risk to move tighter—especially considering that today’s CLO 2.0 structures are more robust vs. the CLO 1.0 cohort. That said, we also highlighted that tight valuations across the capital structure underscored the importance for junior investors to prioritize cleaner collateral and higher-quality managers. Now, as we begin 2Q2026, the macro backdrop—albeit incredibly volatile in recent days—has shifted to reflect a more challenging growth, inflation, and policy mix. As a result, we refresh our relative value views on the CLO market and highlight the following takeaways. While fundamentals for CLOs are not showing signs of deterioration, we believe the n balance of risks has shifted more negative. Furthermore, market pricing of CLO debt and loans has shifted alongside. We reiterate our defensive call: favoring higher-quality managers, cleaner collateral, n and newly issued deals. We favor CLO mezzanine tranches relative to owning broadly syndicated leveraged n loans on an outright basis, given the better structural protections and attractive valuations in the CLO structures. Such a structural shift away from fossil fuel has been underpinned by the unmatched speed and scale of China's renewables build-out in recent years (Figure 3). In 2024, China accounted for over 80% of installed manufacturing capacity in every part of the solar photovoltaics value chain, and nearly 80% for nacelles and over 70% for blades for wind power components (Figure 4). It's position in battery manufacturing is even stronger, with China representing at least 85% of global production in all parts of the value chain3 . These trends have driven China's power system into a renewable-first model in terms of installed capacity. In early 2025, China's wind and solar capacity overtook its coal power capacity for the first time. By end 2025, non-fossil fuel power accounted for over 60% of China's total installed power generation capacity, including 47% renewables (solar and wind), 12% hydro and 2% nuclear. Newly installed solar and wind capacity exceeded 430 GW in 2025 (+22% y/y), lifting cumulative grid-connected wind and solar capacity to 1840 GW – 47.3% of total installed power capacity, and surpassing thermal power for the first time4 . 8 April 2026 2 Barclays | Economics / Sustainable Investing

Chile’s CBC follows this recommendation. A growing number of central banks have submitted to exter- nal reviews as a mechanism for institutional renewal and democratic legitimacy. These reviews serve a dual purpose: they provide an objective assessment of whether the monetary policy framework is fit for purpose, and they demonstrate an openness to scrutiny that can deflect politically motivated criticism. England, Australia and Sweden are recent exam- ples, together with Chile in the region. The review should be led by an internationally recognized economist with no politi- cal affiliation to the government or opposition. An external review would serve multiple objectives simultaneously. It would demonstrate institutional openness to scrutiny, poten- tially identify genuine improvements to the framework, and establish a precedent for evidence-based institutional adapta- tion rather than politically driven reform. Flawed premises Academic research and international experience indicate that the administration’s critique of BanRep operates on flawed premises. records.text: Cayla Seder 8 April 2026 1 Insights Classification: Complimentary Material Developed Markets Strategy Weekly : Dancing through the lightning strikes KEY THEMES THIS WEEK: Where has pricing gone too far? We penned much of this piece before announcement of a two-week ceasefire in the Middle East, but given our focus was on constructing a portfolio resilient to trends that extend beyond the next 24–36 hours the analysis holds. We assess inflation risk versus growth risk and where the market reaction may already have gone too far (and is now reversing). Within our daily PriceStats data, the month‑over‑month increases in headline inflation are striking, with developed‑market monthly inflation rising by more than 1% and reaching record highs across our 15‑year dataset (read more here). That said, it will take time for these pressures to fully feed through into official—and, more importantly, core—inflation readings, particularly ahead of the US March CPI release (read our preview here). Meanwhile, growth expectations are beginning to erode. Against this backdrop, we see scope to further refine the portfolio to better align risk and reward that balances the geopolitical event uncertainty. Portfolio Updates. This leave the overarching themes of our portfolio remain largely unchanged. Until we see the how the ceasefire will ultimately settle, it would be premature to eliminate our USD overweight completely or move away from a preference for energy exporters, with the exception of JPY.

records.text: US Economics Weekly10 April 2026 ab 35 We've recently pointed out ongoing ups and downs in California, likely related to biweekly certification in the state, which seemingly pushed around the national headline since the end of 2025. After three consecutive weeks of relative calm, California continuing claims fell -8K on a NSA basis in the last week of March, contributing to the decline in the national headline. That said, other states also recorded sizable NSA declines, such as Illinois and Iowa (both -4K), Michigan (-7K), New Jersey (-5K), New York (-5K), Pennsylvania (-6K), and Texas (-10K), so the fall in continuing claims in the most recent data was fairly broadly based. Recent revisions to seasonal factors do not appear to have dampened the residual seasonality visible in the claims data in the past several years. The recent pattern of initial claims troughing in the beginning of the year and rising higher into the summer was left intact. Looking ahead, if the pattern of 2023, 2024 and 2025 reasserts itself, we expect initial claims to trend higher into the coming summer. FRB of New York services index (Mar), 8:30 AM We expect the FRB of New York services index remained soft, up 2.6 points to -20.0 in April. The passthrough of oil prices is fairly quick while gas prices are likely to affect inflation with a lag of three months. Elevated gas and oil prices throughout the year bring persistence in our inflation profile until Q1 2027. If the ceasefire doesn’t hold, we see energy prices trading in line with our ‘Hormuz Constrained’ scenario. Higher-for-longer prices in the medium term: We see a clearer pathway to de- escalation, given the temporary ceasefire, but risks of higher-for-longer energy prices remain, in our view. We assume each of our scenarios result in instability in Iran (and potentially in the Middle East region as a whole), supporting prices given the region’s oil and gas production . According to the Treasury refunds issued year-to-date totalled $247bn, ~$30bn or 13.8% ahead of the same point last year in data to April 8. Refunds paid by electronic transfer year-to-date, at $238bn, are running ~$35bn or 17% ahead of the same point last year in data to April 8. In the latest weekly data from the IRS, see here, the number of tax returns filed as of March 27 was down by 1.3% and the number processed was 1.1% lower than the same point last year. Tax filing and processing could be slower this year with added complexity and a ~25% reduction in IRS staffing last year. The total amount refunded was up 14% according to that data, not far off the 15% increase we're expecting. LLC Global Markets Daily: The Case for Structurally Higher US Equity Volatility 9 April 2026 | 8:42AM EDT We have focused recently on the potential for longer-dated equity volatility to n move higher over time, even if equity prices continue to rise. Our models of the macro and market drivers of equity volatility suggest that n longer-dated implied volatility “should” have been rising in recent years, driven largely by rising equity market concentration and a slowly rising unemployment rate. We think the concentration of value in AI-related areas of the market adds to the n risk of higher volatility over time as focus increases on whether the benefits justify that value. Rising market concentration and high valuations—”non-macro” market forces that factor into our models—are not direct measures of those AI-related risks, but they are symptoms of the AI-driven market, as they were in the late 1990s tech boom, and so they are proxies for the impact that AI has had on equity markets in recent years. The recent rise in equity volatility is due to the Iran War, so we expect volatility to n fall in the short term if the market reduces weight on downside macro outcomes. But there has been a structural rise in longer-dated implied volatility in recent months already, in excess of its usual relationship to the equity index. " Predictability of DEVal To test the predictability of DEVal, we use our constrained optimization framework called EMAP .1 This framework allows us to control for risk properly, which is important because the high and low DEVal names may differ in their risk characteristic. For each asset class, we constructed a pair of long-short portfolios, in which the long portfolio invests in the cheap securities according to DEVal (ie, high DEVal for bonds and low DEVal for equities) and the short takes the expensive securities, while matching sector weights and major risk characteristics between the long and short sides. This way, the long and short portfolios differ in their DEVal, but are the same in other risks. The portfolio returns are reported in Figure 1 and line up nicely with our expectations. We find that in both bonds and equities, after controlling for risk, the cheap securities outperformed the more-expensive securities. For HY bonds, the cheap (high DEVal) bonds outperformed the more- expensive ones (low DEVal) by 6.76% per year with an information ratio of 1.43. The predictive power came from both the long and short portfolios, was present in both bonds and equities, and was consistent over time. records.text: Alexandre Stott +33(1)4212-1108 | alexandre.stott@gs.com Goldman Sachs Bank Europe SE - Paris Branch European Daily: Euro Area—Will Wages Wiggle? 10 April 2026 | 5:04PM CEST Wages are one of the key “second-round” channels that could turn a temporary n energy shock into a more persistent inflation problem. After the 2022 energy crisis, for instance, workers recouped their purchasing power by bargaining for higher pay, which led firms in wage-sensitive sectors to raise prices in response. So what are the risks of a similar response of wages today? We see two reasons to look for a more limited response of wages to the current n increase in energy prices than in 2022, in addition to the size and breadth of the commodity shock. First, real wages were running slightly ahead of labour productivity before the start of the conflict, which means that firms are likely to initially resist granting nominal wage increases. Second, labour markets now look somewhat looser than during the 2022 energy shock, which is likely to reduce workers’ bargaining power. As a result, we continue to expect year-over-year compensation-per-employee n to slow over coming quarters. That said, the net impact on wage growth of the modest increases in inflation and the unemployment rate we now forecast is likely to be a small delay in the return to the 2.5-3% target-consistent range. Core PCE prices increased 0.37%, and headline PCE prices increased 0.38%. Despite the strong monthly increases in March, they were a bit below the increase in March of last year and as a result 12-month inflation fell. Over the next few months we expect that inflation will rise, pushed up by rising gasoline prices, continued gradual pass-through of tariffs, and a April reversal of the downward bias to housing rents from the government shutdown. Excluding the volatile aircraft and defense components, orders of nondefense capital goods ex-aircraft (core orders) rose 0.6% in February. The January data were downwardly revised, leaving the level of core orders 0.5% lower relative to the prior vintage, but the decent increase in February generally maintained the recent hook higher in core orders. records.text: At the higher end of the rating spectrum, CLOs still trade wider than IG bonds in absolute spread terms, but the differential sits at the tighter end of the historical relationship (Exhibit 13). We would use widening in senior CLO spreads as opportunities to add relative exposure. While the underlying leveraged loans in the CLO structures skew towards a less defensive borrower base (relative to IG-rated borrowers), historical data shows the risk of impairment for senior tranches remains low, owing to structural protections which include overcollateralization and interest coverage tests that can redirect cash flows away from junior liabilities. In fact, according to S&P’s most recent CLO Default study (published in July 2025), there have not been any defaults of investment grade CLO tranches (rated BBB- or higher) since 2010. Additionally, no USD or EUR broadly syndicated loan CLO tranche originally rated AAA has ever defaulted. This should help senior tranches remain resilient, absent a broad, systemic impairment of market beta—not our base case. Finally, we also assess CLO relative value with other segments of structured credit. To us, this does seem consistent with a 10% rise in oil and gas prices, although it is possible Taylor is modelling an even broader shock. The impact of such a shock on headline inflation after year 1 is not too dissimilar - we estimate it at ~50-60bp. However, the persistence of the shock in Taylor's simulations seems much stronger than in the modelling from the August MPR. The totality of the impacts - direct and indirect - doesn’t turn negative until well into year 3 following the shock, and the pass-through to services inflation seems rather sizable, and very sticky. In countries where internet retailing is a small share of transactions, retailers tend to tie their online prices to offline prices in order to minimise the costs associated with making pricing decisions. In countries where online transactions have a significant market share, online and offline prices are closely related and online prices may lead offline, as the demographic of computer-literate, middle-class, cash-rich, and time-poor consumers to which online retailers sell are less price-sensitive than the average consumer. As purchasing habits change, these online price series capture prices and changes in product information and can provide real-time information on consumer behaviour. records.text: M Idea 24 March Prepay Speeds Please note that this is a re-print of a prior report, previously published here. Investor prepay concerns have generally eased as the Iran conflict has pushed 30-year mortgage rates up 50bp to near 6.5%. This March prepay report likely still reflects pre-conflict rates, but nonetheless was constructive for investors, with speeds increasing less than expected, particularly for higher-coupon Ginnies. Headline speeds increased 22% MoM for 30-year conventionals, 24% for Ginnies, and 16% for 15-year conventionals – all slower than forecasts of 23%, 29%, and 23%, respectively. Much of the MoM pickup was likely mechanical, as lenders had 3 business days to operate in March versus February. The slower-than-expected speeds may reflect shorter borrower lag times and emerging burnout. Net issuance continued to be negative for the second month in a row, a positive for MBS from the supply side. Investor concerns around prepays have eased somewhat as rates have sold off sharply in the wake of the Iran conflict. 30-year mortgage rates have effectively been on a one-way street higher since the conflict began and are now grazing 6.5%, the highest level since fall 2025 and ~50bp higher since the beginning of March (Exhibit 47 ). That said, the latest March prepay report still likely reflects mortgage rates that were in place before the recent geopolitical tensions. Changes in the gap between 5 yr bond yields and 1 -year swap rates show that high -beta, high-carry currencies , especially those that entered the shock with higher inflation pressure, have experienced the sharpest curve flattening, with front -end rates rising much more than the 5-year during the bond selloff. This reflects a market focus on near -term inflation and policy risk. As geopolitical risks begin to peak, these same economies also have the greatest potential to see rate cuts repriced back into the curve. Below, we summarize the outlook and drivers for each major maturity. Short- and Medium-Term JGBs: Buying Opportunities as Rate Hikes Are Priced In Our economists expect 25bp rate hikes in both April and October, with the policy rate reach- ing 1.25% by year-end. In the BoJ swap market, the probability of a 25bp rate hike in April is about 60%, and a hike to 1.25% by December is almost fully priced in. The 1-year rate starting two years from now exceeds 1.9%, surpassing the center of the BoJ’s newly estimat- ed neutral rate range (real -0.9% to +0.5%, nominal +1.1% to +2.5% assuming 2% infla- tion). While there remains a risk that rate hikes will be priced in at a faster pace if the yen depreci- ates further, at present, concerns about supply constraints across supply chains due to heightened tensions in the Middle East have made it necessary to consider scenarios where the pace of rate hikes slows. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 5 persistence of the energy shock - as was the case in 2022/23 and 2025 - will set the tone of the April meeting. As a number of MPC speakers have suggested in recent weeks - Governor Bailey amongst them - it is not possible for monetary policy to prevent the near- term rise in headline inflation. It is also unlikely it can impact short-term inflation expectations, which the BoE analyses largely link to spot fuel and food inflation. Short-term inflation expectations tend to seep into wage growth, particularly amongst what the February MPR called "bargaining firms", which cover 40% of UK private sector workers and whose wage setting resembles collective bargaining behaviour; another 40% of workers are employed by what the BoE called "cost minimisers", where wages are set in part in response to changes in the NLW, which itself is set in part in response to headline inflation. With pay growth forecasts in April then likely taking into account this type of corporate behaviour - vs. the traditional BoE pay growth models, which Chief Economist Pill said "were estimated on the much more benign period from the late 1990s up until the financial crisis" - it is highly likely that both the growth hit and any medium-term inflation undershoot won't be as severe as one might infer from, for example, historical sensitivities of macro variables to changes in financial conditions. Issuance mix: Fewer resets may point to less conviction A notable shift in 2026 has been the mix of gross CLO creation across the three main categories of 1) new issue activity, 2) refinancings (which adjust the interest rate of CLO liability tranches), and 3) resets (which are more comprehensive than refinancings, as they also extend CLO maturity and reinvestment periods). After resets dominated activity in 2024 and 2025, new issues and refinancings have been meaningfully stronger than resets to start 2026. Resets total $31 billion vs. $38 billion of new-issue creation year to date, dropping the share of resets from 42% to 33% of CLO creation year over year (Exhibit 7). This may be indicative of less conviction from CLO managers in the durability of the cycle. It may also reflect the limits of existing collateral pools and, in some cases, the reduced economic appeal of extending reinvestment on older collateral. A prolonged conflict would likely accelerate the global green transition, benefiting China as the world’s leading green-technology powerhouse and supporting growth through stronger exports. For context, China's green tech sector, covering solar power, wind power, EVs, nuclear power, electricity storage and hydrogen, contributed a record CNY15.4trn to China's economy in 2025 (~18.4% y/y growth in 2025), according to the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA). This translated to 11% of GDP in 2025, up from 9.6% in 2024, and contributed 1.8pp to headline GDP growth of 5% in 2025, by our estimate (Figure 11). The growing importance of green tech sectors gives China a substantial economic stake in the global transition to clean energy technologies. 8 April 2026 5 Barclays | Economics / Sustainable Investing

records.text: US Economics Weekly10 April 2026 ab 32 Wednesday, April 15 Manufacturing Surveys (Apr), 8:30 AM We expect the Empire State index fell 1.8 points to -2.0 in April and the FRB of Philadelphia manufacturing index fell 8.1 points to 10.0. The two manufacturing indexes will be the first indicators of manufacturing activity in April. In March, manufacturing surveys generally showed limited impact from the Middle East conflict and the run-up in fuel prices. Four of the five regional manufacturing indexes improved in March, adjusted to ISM weights, and all five were above 50. The S&P Global manufacturing PMI rose 0.7 points to 52.2. That said, the ISM manufacturing composite had less encouraging details — its 0.3-point edge up to 52.7 owed in large part to lengthening supplier delivery times as supply chains snarled, which was highlighted in comments (link here). Meanwhile, the new orders components softened. Note that according to the ISM methodology (link here), firms can submit responses to the survey throughout the reference month. Thus, ISM respondent firms likely had more time to digest the Middle East conflict and its ramifications for their businesses compared to respondents to surveys with earlier response windows such as the March Empire State index. To get additional insight on the connection between fertilizer prices and agriculture prices, we look at the share of farm expenses devoted to fertilizer and the historical correlation between fertilizer and crop prices. Passenger NEV sales penetration reached 59% by end-2025, up sharply from 22.5% in 2021 (Figure 7). At the same time,China’s high-speed rail (HSR) network has reached a density of ~4.7meters per square kilometres, far exceeding that of US (0.08m per sq km) and slightly higher than Germany (around 4.6m per sq km; Figure 8), and 97% of cities with a population of more than 500,000 are now connected by HSR. This extensive rail coverage has increasingly substituted for short-haul flights and long-distance bus travel, significantly reducing reliance on aviation fuel and diesel. Reflecting the above, China’s electrification rate – defined as electricity’s share of total final energy consumption – reached ~29% in 2023-24, well above levels in the US (~21% in 2023) and Germany (~20%), while broadly in line with Japan6 (~30%; Figure 9). China's electrification rate is expected to continue to rise by ~1pp annually during the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026– 2030), according to the China Electricity Council. At that rate, electrification rate would reach roughly 35% by 20307 , placing China 8–10 percentage points above the OECD average. Commentary balanced the continued improvement in domestic activity with emergent risks from the Middle East, with the latter further nuanced by the ‘con- siderably’ higher inflation vs shortage-driven growth risks. Risks to forecasts skew incrementally stagflationary, pointing to higher inflation and lower growth than previously estimat- ed, with prior assumptions for crude in the mid-60s. In the press conference, Rhee downplayed the need to act in the near term. The focus remained on second order effects, sug- gesting a willingness to look past the shock, at least initially. FX pressures were seen as less of Korea-specific risk, given the slowing of retail outflows of late, with the won largely swinging with broad USD strength, which could reverse on any resolution (Figure 11 R o l l i n g 2 1 d R e t a i l f l o w ). If our forecast is realized, it would result in 4.4% over-year-ago growth for headline PPI prices, the highest reading in the current cycle. Energy prices are a clear source of inflationary pressure, as the conflict-driven surge in global crude prices caught up with retail gasoline, which reached a peak of $3.4 per gallon through the end of the month. Elevated prices were also evident in propane, which could reflect rising LPG producer prices. The other compo- nents of the energy complex are set to decline in March, as natural gas prices normalized after a brief spike in January. February food PPI saw the largest single-month rise since May 2021, with a 2.4% m/m increase, and food-related com- modity prices have been on an upward trajectory through March, which should result in a 1.0% m/m uptick in the com- ing report. Away from food and energy, we expect core PPI prices increased 0.5% m/m, resulting in an over-year-ago pace of 4.2%. The national PMI and ISM manufacturing and services surveys were synonymous in their message of rising prices, with qualitative comments noting shipping challenges and higher supplier prices owing to the war. True, peak inflation may be lower and earlier then. ECB rate cuts could come faster and swifter. An intensification of the conflict could see oil prices move to USD 140 or higher, and a longer TTF shock than in 2022. That would push the Euro area into recession. Since early March, the 10y PeruGB–UST spread has widened by more than that of other Latam countries, with a performance that represents one of the worst seen in a supply-driven oil shock. We see this underperformance as a strong signal that the market is likely pricing in an election-related risk premium on top of the energy-shock premium (see Figure 5). That could be seen as a surprise – the latest polling suggests right-leaning candidates may perform well which is often seen by markets as a positive for local assets. We think, however, that there remains a lingering uncertainty about the outcome in what is a highly fragmented race. The market will recall the example of the 2021 election, in which candidates’ popularity swung dramatically in the week before the run-off vote, underscoring a sizable margin of error in the polls. Downside asymmetry: We think the risks for local assets lie asymmetrically to the downside from the election outcome – particularly if left-leaning candidates gain traction. While tensions were rising, Tuesday’s 30y JGB auction cleared smoothly after the previous day’s bear- steepening made the issue look cheap versus our supply-demand model. On Wednesday, yields fell led by the superlong sector and the curve bull flattened after the US and Iran agreed to a two-week ceasefire (Bloomberg, 7 April). However, later that day Iran claimed the ceasefire agreement had been broken, and as uncertainty about the outlook rose again, yields climbed on Thursday, retracing the previous day’s decline. The 5y JGB auction held the same day also produced a somewhat weak outcome. As a result, while daily moves were sizable, the curve ended broadly unchanged for the week as a whole. records.text: M Update 4 Personal income and spending Real personal spending rose by a tenth (0.1% m/m), in line with our expectations. Within the components, goods spending was up 0.2%, and services at 0.1%. The strength in goods spending was largely due to a reversal of the weakness in real MV spending: after declining 4.2% in January, auto sales were up 4.3% in February, leaving the average for the year so far flat. Barring clothing and footwear, every other goods category was down on the month. Within services, most services were flat or slightly up. However, we did see the first m/m decline in the real spending on recreational services: this was down 0.4% m/m in February. As we wrote here, we will be tracking how this and other discretionary services spending evolves to gauge the spending health of the upper-income consumers. It is important to note that services spending often gets revised considerably in the first and second revisions of GDP when the BEA incorporates data from the Quarterly Services Survey. Right now, some of the services spending, including parts of recreation services, are based off the establishment survey (i.e. payrolls data), which had declined sharply in February. The ceasefire deal this week reduces the risks of a severe stagflation shock and the need for costly fiscal support or aggressive monetary tightening. The deal increases the risk of one hike vs. our base case of two hikes and the risk of earlier/faster cuts in 2027. But uncertainty remains and energy prices are likely to take time to correct lower. Even under the assumption of the geopolitical conflict to de-escalate by late-April, some permanent damage to energy supply will likely prevent a swift correction in global energy prices, according to our commodity analysts. If however by mid-year, the price shock subsides and it looks like energy prices are moving somewhat lower or the labour market worsens materially, then we would expect the BoE to look through the shock and be on hold in 2026, with cuts resuming in 2027. At the same time, if energy prices move to higher levels sustainably, we can see the BoE hike more than twice, even as early as April, if it moves to higher levels by then, though that risk has reduced somewhat after the ceasefire deal. We also expect hikes to be modest, given the economy/ labour market is weak, risks of second round effects are less than before, rates are restrictive, and fiscal response is unlikely to be that forceful. records.text: on the likely debate around a “precautionary hike” to us seems aligned with a median MPC member that wants the front end of the curve to still price some chance of hikes further down the road. All in all, on the current information set, our starting point for April is a hawkish hold, at an 8-1 vote split. We think Chief Economist Pill would vote for a hike. A hawkish hold at current pricing, we think, implies the headline inflation forecast at barely below 2%Y in 2Q28 - marrying the impact of tighter financial conditions and some persistence in the energy shock. The scenario of higher headline inflation would see inflation persistence as more embedded in the projections, akin to what Taylor presented in his illustrative example of an energy shock. Headline inflation would not return to target until early 2029 in this scenario, we think. The scenario of lower inflation would likely see a non-linear hit to growth via the labour market, and thus a faster dissipation of the energy shock (i.e. next to no second round effects, as a margin squeeze counters any inflection higher in pay growth), with tighter financial conditions also pushing headline inflation to well below the 2% target at the policy relevant horizon (2Q28).

records.text: 20 Global Economic Weekly | 10 April 2026 The escalation scenario and the end of the easing cycle Finally, in the escalation scenario the regime would shift materially. Persistent high oil prices would establish a new price level, leading the shock to be perceived as structural rather than transitory. As a result, inflation expectations would become elevated, with stronger and more generalized second round effects via fuel, freight and fertilizer prices. In this context, the BCB might no longer see room for additional rate cuts, effectively interrupting the easing cycle and keeping the Selic at 14.50% throughout 2026 and 2027 to preserve credibility. records.text: See Appendix A-1 for Analyst Certification, Important Disclosures and Research Analyst Affiliations. 10 Apr 2026 18:04:13 ET │ 28 pages US Rates Weekly Short-term uncertainty but long-term value CITI'S TAKE We reiterate our “buy-the-dip” trades we have been adding to our portfolio over the past few weeks. We see significant value in long belly duration positions, outright long 5y spreads, long 20y spreads in various relative value structures, and long 30y TIPS breakevens (which is also our favorite short expression for those who disagree with our core view). Typically, structures like long-end spreads take time to “revert, ” so investors have time to get long still. We continue to like our below 4% call for 10y yields by year-end, which should be anchored by further rate cuts to be priced into 2027 /2028. Short-end — This week’s move lower in TGCR and SOFR relative to IORB is evidence, in our view, that we are temporarily back to a lightly abundant reserves regime. We think funding markets are unlikely to face significant stress on Tax Day next week. While the TGA balance will surge towards $1tn on the 15th, the TGA was close to this level at the end of January and repo remained contained. We discuss what line items we are monitoring on the Daily Treasury Statement as well as our T- bill issuance expectations after Tax Day. The ECB made the following assumptions: n Labour Market: The ECB assumes a resilient labor market, stating, "[t]he labour market is projected to remain resilient overall, as firms are expected to hoard labour in reaction to a temporary dip in economic activity owing to the war in the Middle East." Under the severe scenario, the ECB sees the unemployment rate increasing by only 0.1 percentage point (pp) against its baseline. Keeping the labour force unchanged, this would be consistent with a mere 0.1 pp deterioration in employment growth relative to the ECB's baseline. The ECB's argument largely relies on labour hoarding, making the labour market less sensitive to the business cycle. However, labour hoarding is weakening (for more see our latest labour chart book here), and employment has probably become more sensitive to the business cycle, potentially resembling the 1995-2015 period more than 2021-2025 (Figure 8). Using this former elasticity, employment could decline by a larger amount, potentially closer to 0.3 pp against the baseline in 2026. records.text: mand. Water scarcity already constrains mining region: Many of the world’s most productive mining regions are located in areas already facing water scarcity. At least 16% of global critical mineral mines, deposits, and districts are thought to be located in regions experiencing extremely high water stress (World Resources Institute, 2024). In Chile’s Atacama Desert, one of the world’s most important regions for copper and lithium production, mining operations are estimated to consume more than 65% of local water supplies (Alam and Sepúlveda, 2022). Challenges beyond water extraction: Mining operations must also manage large volumes of tailings water, the liquid waste generated after mineral extraction. Globally, the mining industry produces around 13 billion tonnes of tailings each year (Franks et al., 2021), which may involve long-term risks to human life, ecosystems, and water resources if not managed properly. Solutions: To mitigate these constraints, mining companies are increasingly exploring alternative water solutions, including seawater desalination, wastewater recycling, and dry or filtered tailings technologies. If implemented, these approaches should help reduce freshwater withdrawals while minimizing contamination and disaster risks. Liability spreads have widened, and mezzanine tranches have underperformed the decline in loan prices as investors demand more compensation for subordination and tail risk. Fundamentals do not yet reflect this more challenging backdrop. The share of n CCC loans is below typical limits and has trended lower. Additionally, loan downgrades into CCC territory have declined and upgrade rates out of the CCC bucket have remained stable. The market, however, is pricing for deterioration, reflected in a rising share of collateral trading at distressed levels. On technicals, a lower share of resets could imply less manager conviction over n the durability of the cycle and reduced economic appeal of extending reinvestment on older collateral at current spreads. Remaining defensive and preferring structure We continue to recommend defensive positioning across managers and collateral n pools. Reset and refi deals screen as less clean, with higher distressed exposure and, in some cases, reinvestment funded by selling weaker loans at discounts. For floating-rate investors, we prefer CLO mezzanine tranches vs. leveraged n loans. However, the path to lower implieds can be fraught with temporary spikes in implieds and high delivered volatility. In other words, elevated jump risk makes medium-term short volatility positions less attractive. On the other hand, elevated levels of implieds make outright long volatility positions un-attractive. For investors who want to sell gamma, we prefer selling gamma via OTM receivers to bene- fit from current rich skew. As mentioned, implieds have recently behaved like a duration proxy. This totaled 2,399 contracts on April 3, 1,332 contracts on April 6, and 1,332 contracts on April 7, for a total of 5,063 contracts. What is notable is that the price is ¥0.03 above the closing price. If these are transactions between investors and dealers, it suggests investors are buying futures. The spread is just over 0.3 bp, so it makes sense as a switch trade out of JGBs using closing prices. According to futures trading statistics, trust banks' net longs expanded by almost the same number in the week of April 3. It is natural to expect such transactions are done by pension funds. However, it is a bit strange to see unrounded contract numbers. Of course, this could be the result of precise calculations of interest rate risks, but the notional amount of bonds implied by the futures volume will not provide a round number for on-the-runs. Basis trades cannot explain this either. The JB370, where SLF usage was increasing, could be the reason, but there is still a discrepancy and it is lagging behind the decline in SLF usage. Meanwhile, the MYR did not outperform as much as our expectations (despite Malaysia being a net energy exporter). We think this can be explained by the degree of its outperformance since the start of 2025, which meant that a broad risk reduction led to the MYR paring back some of its previous gains. The reaction in Asian FX markets on the day of the ceasefire announcement was broadly just a reversal of the underperformers, with KRW, PHP and THB outperforming (Exhibit 4). The INR had already rallied significantly following the changes to FX regulations from the RBI (more on this below). Our commodities team have adjusted their Q2-2026 Brent oil forecasts slightly lower to US$90/bbl (from US$99/bbl), to reflect lower risk premium, while keeping their Q3 and Q4 forecast unchanged at US$82/bbl and US$80/bbl respectively. However, our commodities team highlight that the risks to their oil forecasts are to the upside, as the situation remains fluid. Fundamentally, we remain most constructive on the CNY and the MYR. China’s diversified energy sources, export outperformance and still significant undervaluation underpin our bullish CNY view. The MYR is also still undervalued (vs GS DEER), is a net energy exporter, and positioning is likely cleaner than pre-war. We remain bearish on the PHP , THB and INR,

A 25bp cut in Q4 26 would leave the ex-post real policy rate at about 160bp, which we would view as adequate. In a negative scenario of Brent averaging $100/bbl in 2026, the NBH would likely remain on hold for the rest of this year, but the risks of hikes are clearly skewed to upside. The NBH might use a wide interest rate corridor as the main line of defence in the case of elevated HUF volatility. If that proves insufficient, it would likely deliver some rate hikes. The Governor’s comments that markets are getting ahead of themselves by pricing in hikes was a more dovish message relative to the March meeting and makes the bar for an April hike high. But the Governor did keep the door open for precautionary hikes and continued to note that monetary policy will act if it’s appropriate to do so. We think that a protracted shock and rising household/business inflation expectations can shift the majority narrative towards hikes by mid-year, but they are likely to be modest. At the same time cuts in 2027 could come earlier, especially if gas prices do not rise as durably as in our forecasts. Alternative scenarios In a de-escalation scenario (where oil moves lower to close to $80 through this year with lower gas prices), inflation is still likely to be higher in 2026 but with a much lower peak (3.2% in H2) and less persistence. In this scenario, we would expect the BoE to be on hold in 2026 (with risks of a cut in Q4). We would then expect cuts to resume in early 2027 to 3.25%. In an intensification scenario, where oil prices move to ~USD 150 along with a significant gas shock, inflation could peak close to 6% in Q42026. Growth is likely to be halt to zero or lower, with a recession likely due to nonlinear effects and sharper than expected labour market slowdown. records.text: as one might infer from, for example, historical sensitivities of macro variables to changes in financial conditions. We highlight that the Bank's analyses find no change in the share of workers employed by "bargaining firms" over the past 20 years, and instead chalk down the 2024/25 pay growth strength to the "lagged response to labour market conditions" by these firms. Indeed, in 2011, when headline inflation peaked at above 5% (and the jobless rate was ~8%), such firms did not respond by hiking pay growth to match headline inflation. In our view, apart from fiscal and regulatory changes (e.g. minimum pay was hiked by 2.5% in October 2011, vs. a cumulative ~50% increase since 2019) the most plausible explanation for any structural shifts in pay setting stems not from labour but product markets. Near-perfect pricing power in the food retail sector, for example, means any operational cost increase can be passed on to the consumer; it is then easier for corporates in this sector to react to headline inflation when setting wages. In periods of tighter labour market conditions - e.g. 2022/23 - such pay setting can have an indirect effect in sectors where product markets probably haven't seen major shifts, such as discretionary retail or hospitality. When labour markets are looser, such indirect effects are less likely, we think. In our view, these benefits tend to materialize only if the rise in commodity prices is incremental and sustained, rather than abrupt and disruptive, as was the case with oil prices over the past month. There is, therefore, a constructive scenario for Brazil's growth outlook if the conflict stabilizes—as suggest- ed by the recently announced tentative cease-fire in the Mid- dle East conflict—and oil prices settle somewhat above their levels at the beginning of the year. Crucially, higher but non- stressed price levels would only modestly affect CPI and con- sumption, but appreciate the exchange rate due to better terms of trade, which would still allow the BCB to cut rates mean- ingfully this year, thereby easing part of the interest burden while at the same time generating higher profits for the oil and public sectors. Against this backdrop of lingering and contradictory forces, the range of outcomes around our projections remains wider than usual. Since the onset of the conflict, we have revised our CPI projection upward from 3.6% to 4.3%, narrowed our current account deficit estimate from 2.6% to 2.3% of GDP, and reduced our primary fiscal deficit forecast from -0.8% to -0.5% of GDP—all to accommodate the assumption that oil will average roughly US$25 higher this year. US Economics Research March CPI inflation hottest since mid-2022 Headline CPI inflation surged to 0.9% m/m SA (3.3% y/y), fueled by higher gas prices. Core CPI, however, slowed to 0.20% m/m (2.6% y/y), weaker than expectations amid softer outcomes in core goods and services. We estimate March core PCE rose 0.27% m/m (3.1% y/y). Key takeaways from the March CPI data • March CPI is the first inflation report since the Iran conflict began and carries early imprints of it. As expected, headline CPI inflation surged to 0.9% m/m, led primarily by higher gasoline prices. Indeed, energy inflation contributed about 70bp to headline CPI compared with 4bp in February. Elsewhere, food inflation moderated from February, led by deflation in food-at-home (grocery) and moderation in food services inflation (Figure 1). • Core CPI inflation slowed 2bp, to 0.20%m/m (2.6% y/y), weaker than forecasts (Barclays: 0.26%; consensus: 0.30% m/m). Core goods inflation moved largely sideways amid another month of used car deflation—the fourth in a row. Elsewhere, apparel prices rose a solid 1% m/m SA, on the heels of the 1.3% increase in the prior month, which indicates further tariff passthrough amid spring price setting. There were firmer inflation prints across recreation, education and “other” goods. The job losses from cost pres- sure in those industries should exceed the small employment gains implied by the oil and gas multipliers. The net impact on growth depends on the relative size of the spillovers, but we note that the GDP multipliers for wholesale and retail trade are among the highest of any industry. Canadian consumers will also feel the squeeze from higher energy costs. Canada lacks sufficient pipeline capacity to move western crude to eastern refineries, and as a result imports supply roughly 40% of total refinery demand nation- ally. This reliance is far higher in the population-dense east- ern provinces of Ontario and Quebec, which depend on imported crude sourced from the US, the Middle East, and other international suppliers. Many eastern refineries are also optimized to process lighter foreign grades rather than the heavier crude produced in Alberta. THEME OF THE WEEK: EM HOLDINGS ACROSS SHOCKS Historically, global shocks trigger EMFX depreciation as investors cut risky exposures and rotate into haven assets. What differentiates the current sell-off from episodes such as the 2013 Taper Tantrum, the 2020 COVID shock, or the 2022 Russia -Ukraine con flict is the starting point: EMFX entered this episode heavily overweight, which explains a large share of the initial underperformance. However, positioning has already adjusted sharply, with EMFX correcting from around the 90th percentile to near the 10th percentile within the first three weeks of the war. Since then, foreign investor holdings have largely stabilized at these much lighter levels. With geopolitical risks likely past their peak, this cleaner positioning leaves EMFX well-placed to outperform as risk premia fade and investors selectively rebuild exposure. Also, in contrast to the labor market comfort that observers seemed to infer from the press conference, the minutes were more specific that the participants remain concerned over the labor market: " The vast majority of participants judged that risks to the employment side of the mandate were skewed to the downside. The qualifier "vast" added some emphasis to the point. A protracted conflict in the Middle East appeared to add to the downside risks. We suspect subsequent rebounds will falter in the 99.5-100 area in the weeks ahead. Longer term, the index has been consolidating in this broad range for nearly a year and on the heels of the 1H25 impulsive slide. The repeated failed attempts to break above 100 makes the price action look like bearish consolidation, which leaves the dollar vulnerable to another leg lower in the months ahead. Furthermore, the S&P 500 Index/Gold ratio continues to bearishly consolidate below its 1Q26 breakdown area (1.5-1.55 for the nominal ratio). The ratio has seen a bearish progression of range break- downs and consolidations unfold since 2021, which in turn leaves that ratio vulnerable to another leg lower. In our view, both the dollar and that ratio’s setup keep the multi-year hard asset outperformance (debasement) trend intact. Unlike the 1970s and 2000s hard asset out- performance regimes that saw material impulsive dollar declines, the dollar has remained mostly range-bound since 2018 (when gold started to rally) and 2021 (when the S&P 500 started to underperform the gold rally). Given the dollar's chart setup noted above, we would not rule out a catch-down dollar trade in the months ahead. records.text: US Economics Weekly10 April 2026 ab 13 FOMC minutes: two-sided risks The FOMC meeting minutes contained a lot of information we already knew, such as the risks shifting (charts below), most participants assumed a rate cut or cuts were still appropriate in 2026, and the System Open Account Manager signalled the pace of asset purchases might gradually slow at some point after April 15. The new news was the discussion of the risks stemming from the energy price shock. Although "many" thought there might be a reason to raise rates in the future, more, or to be specific "most" thought they might need to cut rates more than previously assumed. If most FOMC participants are raising the odds they have to cut more, that would not appear to be influencing the market reaction. In the desire to make the risk description more two-sided, not many made the case in light of the energy price increase already underway by the time of the meeting. "Some participants judged that there was a strong case for a two-sided description of the Committee's future interest rate decisions in the postmeeting statement, reflecting the possibility that upward adjustments to the target range for the federal funds rate could be appropriate if inflation were to remain at above-target levels." records.text: At the higher end of the rating spectrum, CLOs still trade wider than IG bonds in absolute spread terms, but the differential sits at the tighter end of the historical relationship (Exhibit 13). We would use widening in senior CLO spreads as opportunities to add relative exposure. While the underlying leveraged loans in the CLO structures skew towards a less defensive borrower base (relative to IG-rated borrowers), historical data shows the risk of impairment for senior tranches remains low, owing to structural protections which include overcollateralization and interest coverage tests that can redirect cash flows away from junior liabilities. In fact, according to S&P’s most recent CLO Default study (published in July 2025), there have not been any defaults of investment grade CLO tranches (rated BBB- or higher) since 2010. Additionally, no USD or EUR broadly syndicated loan CLO tranche originally rated AAA has ever defaulted. This should help senior tranches remain resilient, absent a broad, systemic impairment of market beta—not our base case. Finally, we also assess CLO relative value with other segments of structured credit. records.text: The historical linkage between gas and oil prices and changes in natural gas markets make it difficult to statistically estimate the economic impacts of natural gas price changes separate from broader energy (specifically oil) prices. Estimates based on regimes where oil-indexing was more common will overstate the oil-gas relationship today, while historical estimates may understate the economic impacts given the LNG market growth over the last 10 years. In this Global Economics Analyst, we therefore take an exposure-based approach to assess the incremental impacts of recent gas price changes. We first quantify the exposures of inflation and activity to natural gas for global economies. We then estimate the impacts of price changes on inflation and GDP based on our own and historical estimates of passthrough rates. Finally, we update our global rules of thumb to quantify the incremental economic impacts of natural gas price changes under our natural gas analysts’ forecasts. Our estimates suggest that the outsized increase in global LNG prices will lead to a somewhat larger-than-normal impact on global growth and inflation from the recent energy price increase, particularly in Europe. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 3 AI is not yet a macro labor story, but it is no longer invisible This week we published two notes on AI. The first revisits the past five innovation waves to identify common patterns and lessons. The key takeaway is that while these waves boosted productivity and at times caused short-lived labor market disruptions, they did not lead to sustained technological unemployment—employment ultimately proved resilient. Our base case aligns with this historical experience: we expect GenAI to be a net labor-augmenting technology—disruptive in the near term, but ultimately supportive of higher productivity and real wages. The second note turns to the present, aiming to identify the most likely path of AI’s impact on the labor market by extracting micro-level signals from macroeconomic data. We do this through a dashboard that tracks a range of labor market indicators in real time, allowing us to assess how AI-related dynamics are beginning to show up beneath the surface (see Exhibit 2 ). Our analysis suggests that, so far, the impact of AI on the labor market is better described as narrow, early-stage, and largely visible in micro data rather than in aggregate outcomes. We find that the macro signal remains faint: unemployment trends across occupations with different levels of AI exposure look broadly similar, and even after adjusting for cyclical factors, the implied drag from AI is small—on the order of at most ~10 basis points on the overall unemploy

records.text: a while. After this week’s ceasefire, shipping via the Strait of Hormuz has remained very subdued relative to pre-war levels. Indeed, our commodity experts estimate it may take some time to re-establish port operator, insurance and operational logistics confidence before traffic can resume in a dura- ble way. Beyond this, it could take at least four months before oil production/flow is restored. For gas, European gas prices are likely to be even more persistent as the lost Qatari and UAE volumes cannot be realistically replaced in the near term and Europe will suffer competition from the disruptions in Asia ahead of winter storage refills. Given the limited visibility on the conflict's evolution and the recent rally in yields, we see limited value in fading current ECB and BoE tightening expectations priced while the contours of a reachable/lasting peace deal are not in sight and energy prices are expected to be sticky for a while even after a durable reopening of the Strait. We there- fore refrain from tactical outright duration exposure in European yields or intra-EMU spreads. Instead, we remain wary of the possibility of a renewed conflict escalation and hold bearish risk hedges in Europe. At the sub-sector level within HG, downgrades in 1Q26 were focused mainly in Healthcare/ Pharma ($29bn), Basic Industries ($26bn), and Automotive ($20bn). Upgrades were con- centrated in Energy ($28bn), Yankee Banks ($19bn), and Technology ($15bn). At the issuer level, the three largest issuers making up 36% of the upgrades were Kinder Morgan ($17.5bn), Commonwealth Bank of Australia ($13.5bn), and Arthur J Gallagher ($9.6bn), while the three largest issuers making up 46% of the downgrades were Abbott Laboratories ($21bn), Dow Chemicals ($13bn), and American Honda Finance ($13bn). Our main takeaway is that the direction of travel for ratings shifted in Q1 in a less favorable direction, though it’s hard to conclude just yet whether this could be the beginning of a larger downgrade wave unless macro fundamentals deteriorate further. Furthermore, the index-level quality buffer built over 2021-25 (25% of IG debt net upgraded) and which is continuing in 2026 via higher-quality issuance instead of rat- ings upgrades, should provide meaningful shock absorption. records.text: Japan Rates Weekly 10 April 2026 Citi Research 3 Bond market rebound only muted despite ceasefire Financial markets in general reacted in a risk-on manner to the ceasefire agreement. The rebound in the equity market was strong, with the Nikkei 225 regaining around 70% of its losses since late February and the S&P 500 regaining about 90% at one point. The rebound in the forex rate, however, has been weaker, with the USDJPY still around ¥159/$ and the DXY regaining roughly half its losses. Crude oil prices have fallen significantly but nevertheless remain at high levels, and we think normalization will take some time. Interest rates remain high in this environment, and the outlook for the policy rate has changed markedly since late February. Market pricing is for the Fed to leave its policy rate unchanged throughout 2026, and the ECB to hike twice (although these differ from the view of our Economist Team). With the inflation outlook ratcheting upward and an increased burden on fiscal policy, long-term interest rates look unlikely to fall far. Nevertheless, there is little sign of a major change in the range of long-term interest rates relative to short-term rates. In other words, a permanent shift in the level is not priced in, but there is risk if policy rates are hiked. The pricing of an April rate hike diminished in the yen rates market this week. records.text: About State Street PriceStats PriceStats is a source of high frequency inflation information drawn from prices of over five million items sold by online retailers. The items include food, beverages, electronics, apparel, furniture, household products, prescription drugs and over-the-counter medicines. The prices are collated for all the countries we monitor to produce individual Country Inflation Series. Country Inflation Series detect changes in inflation trends with real-time data. We publish the indices with a lag of three business days; they are direct reflections of the prices of real products on sale at online retailers in each country. Country Inflation Series are not seasonally adjusted and are not designed to match official data. The interactive Country Inflation Series charts overlay against the relevant official measures of inflation, in all cases non-seasonally adjusted. We rank each of the ~200 issuers in our sample with a 35% weight for gross leverage, a 25% weight for profit margin, 25% weight for interest coverage, and a 15% weight for payout ratio. The weighting tilts toward the the metrics that we believe matter most for spread resilience through the cycle, i.e., balance sheet conservatism, earning power, interest coverage and finally shareholder return discipline to a lesser extent. The current screen skews constructively toward Mining and Tech. Microsoft tops the list on the back of best-in-class EBITDA margins, minimal gross leverage given it remains the only hyperscaler that has not issued any debt recently and an improving interest coverage ratio. This is followed by Newmont, Barrick and BHP, a group of Metals & Mining issuers that are benefiting from the post-2020 deleveraging cycle and high margins. On the other end, our weaker cohort is mostly cyclical companies with idiosyncratic issues.

records.text: M Update 2 PCE Inflation: Third consecutive strong print, but core deceleration is coming Core PCE inflation rose 0.37% m/m in February, close to our expectation (consensus 0.4%, MSe 0.38%). As expected, January PCE was revised upwards (+3bp) and February downwards (-3bp). Our small forecast error is explained by weaker-than- expected non-profits institutions inflation (a component imputed by the BEA). The February reading is consistent with core PCE 3-month annualized inflation at 4.43% (3.65% in January), and the 6-month annualized pace at 3.41% (3.12% in Jan). The 12-month comes at 2.97% in January (vs 3.95% in Jan). Our prediction of sequential acceleration in core PCE during 1Q26 materialized, but we think it is mostly driven by temporary forces such as tariff pass-through and residual seasonality. We expect deceleration in core PCE inflation staring in 2Q26, as goods inflation normalize, seasonality brings down core services ex-housing inflation, and shelter continues softening. This deceleration will open the door for monetary easing in 2H26. As expected, core goods PCE came in very strong (0.84%m/m). Reflecting continued tariff pass-through and perhaps some short-term noise in jewelry and computer software (both less exposed to the tariff impulse). After this print we think that the total effect of tariffs on core PCE prices is about 650bp by February. records.text: Global Economic Weekly | 10 April 2026 9 We still don’t rule out an April hike, especially if energy prices moved closer to the ECB’s adverse scenario again (i.e. oil at USD 119 and gas at EUR 87 on average), and/or if markets are pricing a lot for the ECB by then. But the ceasefire deal has arguably reduced that risk somewhat. And market pricing, in particular, is something the ECB could impact quickly – they just have to say word before the meeting. Beyond timing, risks are also tilted to one more (rather than less) hike this year. But equally, we think the economy cannot stomach these levels of policy rates for long. Cuts are likely to follow. We pencil in quarterly cuts from Jun-27. We would expect a terminal rate at or below 1.5% in 2028, with risks of getting there earlier, especially if gas prices do not rise as much or as durably as our commodity team expects. Risk scenarios: from non-linearities to alternative energy price paths Let’s be clear on the intrinsic risks to our base case: we don’t assume any non-linear deterioration in the outlook. Yet, the risk thereof is real. The energy shock is (currently) smaller than in 2022. But the backdrop is different: The real economy is not in a recovery phase. The labour market is no longer as tight. Profit margins have compressed meaningfully. Consumer sentiment is low, savings intentions high. Trade tensions have already been weighing on the outlook. Note that agricultural pric- es have moved less than energy and fertilizer, and it may take some time for price pressures to pass through, given that much of the fertilizer supply for this year's crops had already been purchased before prices started to rise. We recently dis- cussed food inflation in more detail here. Consumption shifts down While the softer core CPI number last month was welcome news, consumers still consume food and energy, and the expected 0.7% rise in overall PCE prices in March will be a headwind to real consumer spending last month. The afore- mentioned strength in Chase's card spending data suggests that the first response of consumers to higher energy prices will be to lower their savings rate. However, with the Febru- ary aggregate savings rate already low at 4.0%, future efforts to repair and rebuild personal finances may weigh on the vibrancy of spending growth beyond March. Even before the conflict started, the pace of consumer spend- ing growth was already looking tepid. In contrast, the US, Canada, and Australia are self-sufficient and prices are determined locally, so impacts should be much smaller. Third, natural gas prices are mostly determined at a local level and price formation varies across economies. For instance, in Europe gas prices are benchmarked to TTF prices which are in turn determined by global LNG market supply and demand. In most ASEAN economies, prices are benchmarked to the Japan Korea Marker (JKM) which is also determined by the global LNG market, but governments are more active in regulating prices. Fourth, while in most DM economies the passthrough of wholesale price increases to consumers and businesses is determined by market forces—with the merit order principle leaving natural gas as the marginal energy source that is most relevant in setting price—in many EM economies domestic prices are either controlled by the government (e.g., China) or regulated via price caps and subsidies (e.g., much of Asia and LatAm), which should limit the immediate economic impacts. records.text: On their own, the outsized natural gas price response suggests rising energy prices will have a larger impact on inflation and activity than the historical patterns and statistical estimates which inform our oil-based rules of thumb would suggest. We see additional (structural) reasons why the economic impacts of higher natural gas prices are larger today. First, the natural gas share of overall primary energy has drifted up over time—its global share has increased to 23.6% today from 20.1% in 1990, driven by an increase to 31.7% from 20.4% in high-income countries—suggesting estimates on historical data might understate exposures. Second, LNG markets have expanded over the last decade, leaving domestic prices in several economies (particularly Europe and Asia) more exposed to global supply shocks. Third (and related to the expansion of the global LNG market), natural gas pricing has moved away from crude-indexed contracts (again, particularly in Europe and Asia and particularly after the natural gas shortages in 2022) and become more sensitive to spot LNG price changes (Exhibit 2). The US and Iran’s two-week ceasefire announcement has n sustained notable, if uneven, relief to the US rates market. Our commodity strategists view the news as largely consistent with their base case for a recovery in Persian Gulf exports over the coming month, but note the situation remains fluid with risks to their price forecast still skewed to the upside. Compared to the post-February extremes, points across the nominal UST curve have retraced only about 20-30% of the peak move versus pre-war levels through Thursday compared to oil having unwound 40-45% and a nearly complete S&P500 rebound. Despite still elevated uncertainty, the reversal has been more notable in implied vol and carry-sensitive pockets (i.e. spreads, Exhibit 1), with the mix of modestly lower yields and meaningfully lower vol reflecting a reduction in right tail risks (Exhibit 2). We expect that broader rate/vol directionality will likely persist in the near term. Renewed escalation in the conflict would likely upend recent consolidation, while a lasting ceasefire and signs that flows through the Strait of Hormuz are beginning to normalize are key to a further build in conviction that the asymmetry is towards cuts and a lower terminal rate. In short, it would indicate a recession. Takeaways: Growth and the ECB response to inflation There is a focus at the moment on the extent to which the Iran shock will increase inflation and pressure the ECB into hiking policy rates. The ceasefire announcement is potentially good news but there are uncertainties and oil prices remain elevated. Spot oil prices are about halfway between the ECB's baseline and 'adverse' scenarios. Forward oil prices are above the 'adverse' scenario. Relative to the ECB's baseline, there is still upside risk for inflation. There is also downside risk to growth. Growth was arguably more resilient than expected in the last energy shock in 2022. Will it be resilient again in 2026? There were some exceptional circumstances like the post-pandemic economic momentum and labour hoarding that don't apply in 2026. The fiscal easing isn't as significant in 2026 either. The market should keep its mind open to the prospect of weaker growth. In this note we highlight that economic growth looks to have been softer than expected in early 2026 even before the Middle East conflict began (we recently showed that recession risks are rising). So far the market's attention has predominantly focused on the risk of persistent inflation stemming from the energy shock rather than on the potential for growth to be hit harder than assumed. This week's ceasefire announcement is positive news. But uncertainties persist, oil prices remain elevated and in this note we focus on the downside risks to growth. In the first half of this note we look at growth conditions in the euro area in early 2026 prior to the start of the conflict in the Middle East. There is a growing risk that economic growth was softer at the start of this year than the consensus and ECB projections. Overall, however, we think France may be much better positioned than Germany – or even Italy – to cope with energy shocks. First, the 2022 inflation shock was much less pronounced here than elsewhere (courtesy of swift and sizeable policy intervention), so the scars should be less deep. Second, French energy supply is much more secure, thanks to a large share of nuclear and renewable energy. This creates a significant comparative advantage, not only in the short term but also for medium‑term price prospects compared with peers such as Italy and Germany. Still, lower inflation than elsewhere is both an advantage and a challenge. The nominal growth spurt that can help to at least deflate deficits will be smaller here as well. Meanwhile, monetary policy – already too tight going into the energy shock – will get even tighter. Luckily, the 2025 deficit surprised at 5.1% of GDP, 30bp below plans. Morgan Of course, we’ve written about how conventional discount speed modeling is difficult; models project speeds to accelerate on most collateral, though the empirical evidence around seasoning and higher turnover is weak. But with conventionals, at least one only has to worry about turnover—cash-outs and buyouts are minimal. Ginnie borrowers are more prone to cash-out, since it’s harder for them to get 2nd liens (due to their weaker credit) and they may be more prone to tapping equity (since they had limited cash on hand for an initial down payment). Ginnie borrowers are also more prone to default, and predicting when that will lead to a buyout is more complicated than for conventionals. There are just more degrees of freedom to contend with in modeling Ginnie discount speeds, arguably leaving more room for error. That being said, when looking at trailing 12m CPRs, we generally feel more confident in model valuations in 2.5s, where there’s less of a discrepancy between trailing speeds and projected speeds (in OASis and YB). And in 2s, Ginnies—particularly the 2022 vintage— have paid closer to the life model speeds than their conventional counterparts. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 3 Economics: World In Motion Bruna Skarica Where do we stand? The events in the Middle East are fast-changing and commodity markets have been volatile. In this note, we take stock of how the market-implied conditioning assumptions have evolved since the February and the March meetings (freezing the market pricing mid-day on April 9th, after the news of a 2-week cease-fire in the Middle East had been announced), with the aim of kick-starting the April meeting analyses. We also wanted to summarise what we know about how the BoE might think about and model the recent energy shock - and highlight where we might differ - drawing from a number of past MPRs, staff working papers and MPC speeches. Most market participants we talk to tend to, in the post-Bernanke world, downplay the importance of the central forecast and the MPR more broadly. However, staff analyses have proved instrumental at the February meeting, while the central forecast and the associated policy rules still appear to be the most easily digestible summary of the meeting. What's next? There are a couple of "known knowns" worth reiterating: • In the March minutes, and using energy futures as of March 16, the staff assessed headline inflation would rise to "close to 3.5%Y in March, almost 0.5pp higher than expected in the February MPR"; • CPI inflation was expected to be ~3%Y in 2Q26, and at 3.5%Y in 3Q26, with the direct contribution of energy prices to headline inflation at 75bp in 3Q

records.text: different levels of AI exposure look broadly similar, and even after adjusting for cyclical factors, the implied drag from AI is small—on the order of at most ~10 basis points on the overall unemployment rate. This muted aggregate picture should not be surprising given that AI adoption is still in its early phases. Where the signal does begin to emerge is in the micro data, particularly among younger workers. Early-career employees—who tend to be more concentrated in routine, automatable tasks—appear to be the leading edge of adjustment. For this group, unemployment has risen more sharply in highly AI-exposed occupations since 2023, alongside a modest increase in layoff flows and a noticeable rise in unemployment persistence. In other words, not only are more young workers in exposed roles losing jobs, but they are also taking longer to find new ones. Importantly, this pattern is not being offset by exits from the labor force for retraining, suggesting that the adjustment is happening within the labor market rather than outside of it. At the same time, the broader labor market remains far from a displacement story. Industry-level data show no evidence that more AI-exposed sectors are shedding jobs; if anything, employment growth in these industries has held up or even outperformed. Even after adjusting for long-term trends and cyclical dynamics, the macro data fail to reveal a clear disruption signal. This divergence between micro hints and macro stability reinforces the ide

Still, the announcement brought relief to markets that remain willing to adopt the de-escalation narrative. Escalation seems less likely for now, but even if the ceasefire persists, we are unlikely to move back to the pre-war scenario. Some disruption in energy markets will remain, still driving growth lower and inflation higher. But even in the bear case, a repeat of the 1970’s is unlikely with an economy that has gradually become less sensitive to oil, especially in the US. The war dividend so far: mild stagflation We recently revised our global economic forecasts in line with our new commodities forecasts to reflect the economic impact of the war so far (see report: The toll war: lower growth, higher inflation). On global growth, we revised our 2026 forecast downward by 40bp to 3.1% while keeping 2027 at 3.4%. On global inflation, we marked up our 2026 forecast up by 90bp to 3.3% and 2027 by 10bp to 2.5%. This staflationary shock will have a faster impact on inflation than on growth and we expect monetary policy rates to tighten on average about 30bp vs our previous projections (see Exhibit 1 and Exhibit 2). Of course, the uncertainty in the outlook for how sustained the ceasefire will be could cause vol to stay elevated, which is a concern for our basis outlook.
