records.text: 3 AI boom creates water challenge: Rapid growth of AI-driven digital infrastructure is creating new – and often underappreciated – pressures on global water resources. Global water consumption across the AI supply chain is estimated to rise to around 1,200 billion liters by 2030 from about 560 billion liters in 2023 (International Energy Agency, 2025). Around two-thirds of water consumption by the AI ecosystem is currently associated with primary energy supply and electricity generation and around a quarter with data center cooling, while the rest is linked to semiconductor and microchip manufacturing, which requires ultra-pure water. Geographic constraints: Unlike electricity, which can be expanded through additional generation and transmission infrastructure, water availability is fundamentally constrained by geography, hydrology, and climate. These structural constraints make scaling water supply more difficult than expanding power capacity. Regulation likely to strengthen: The water stress issue is attracting global policy attention. UN research warns that the world is in a state of “water bankruptcy,” where long-term water use has exceeded renewable inflows and safe depletion limits, and parts of water and natural capital have been damaged beyond realistic prospects of full recovery (see Madani, 2026). records.text: the US has backed off large-scale strikes against Iran following the cease-fire announcement, the deal remains fragile. Iran quickly re-closed the Strait following Israeli attacks on Lebanon and, while PM Netanyahu stated Israel would enter into direct negotiations with Lebanon on Thursday, he made it clear that strikes would continue. While Vice President Vance is set to hold direct talks with Iran this weekend, headlines suggest both sides are far apart on the details of the deal. Indeed, Iran has set out specific conditions for a more lasting ceasefire and is likely willing to endure a longer conflict to realize these ambitions (see Geopolitical Perspectives: Iran’ s strategy: Positioning to “outlast” rather than “outgun”, Joyce Chang, 4/6/26). During this period, Iran has limited incentive to fully reopen the Strait without a comprehensive cease-fire agreement as it retains its core leverage (see Oil Flash Note: Hormuz oil flows: 12% -> 15%, Natasha Kaneva, 4/7/26). Uncertainty surrounding the cease-fire is likely to keep breakeven volatility elevated and sensitivity to headlines high over the next 2 weeks, leaving risk appetite depressed. As we have shown previously, breakevens exhibit an inverse relationship to risk sentiment, which we proxy using the VIX in our model (see TIPS Strategy, US Fixed Income Markets Weekly, 3/20/26). Longer-run inflation expectations appear (almost) anchored The NY Fed survey of consumer expectations for March showed the median 1y-ahead measure of inflation expectations increased 0.4pp, to 3.4%, amid a surge in gas price expectations, while the 3y-ahead measure ticked up 0.1pp, to 3.1%, and the 5y-ahead measure was unchanged, at 3.0%. This will likely provide some comfort to the FOMC that, at least for now, longer-run inflation expectations appear anchored. However, the median of the point predictions in the NY Fed survey (arguably noisier measures, but more comparable to other surveys such as the University of Michigan's) did show more meaningful increases, with the 5y-ahead measure increasing 0.5pp, to 3.6%, the highest value since early 2022. Furthermore, the preliminary April reading of the University of Michigan's survey suggested that inflation expectations continued to rise in early April. The year-ahead expectations jumped 1pp to 4.8% this month, recording the largest one-month increase in a year, and the long-run expectations (over the next 5-10 years) ticked up 0.2pp, to 3.4%, though most of that likely reflects the increase in expected inflation over the coming year. 10 April 2026 13 Barclays | Global Economics Weekly: Truce and dare

Also, the pass-through from wholesale energy prices to retail electricity ones is more direct and faster than elsewhere. But, more than compensating that, the increase in energy generation through renewables makes Spain less sensitive to large moves in gas prices than the rest of the region and, certainly, than in 2022. This also creates a significant comparative advantage in the short term. Still, the consumer will feel the squeeze, and corporate capex too, in a context of heightened uncertainty. Those two are the main drivers of our forecast revision. In the meantime, with announced fiscal measures, we expect the budget deficit to move pretty much sideways slightly above 2% (ending in 2.4% in 2027). This takes us back to the point we made in our Year Ahead report for Spain . Despite near-term headwinds not threatening the Spanish growth outperformance, the bigger threat in our view is the medium-term outlook for public debt public debt as pension payments soar - without reform of the system or higher productivity growth. Without reforms, public debt is set to rise significantly over time. The challenge is clear, but political appetite for reform remains low.

In the US, not all planting has been done yet, and more fertilizer will be required during the growing process. Consequently, decisions by farmers in coming months will influence the volume of this year’s harvest, and thus prices. As an example, consider corn, which as noted above is the most intense user of nitro- gen fertilizer. According to the March 31 USDA Prospective Plantings report, US farmers planned to cut their corn acreage this year by 3%, which could involve switching to alternate crops like soy, for which prospective plantings are up 4%. The June 30 USDA Acreage report will show actual plant- ings, and by August the crop production data will start to show actual harvest amounts, reflecting both acreage and yields. Better Together Debt-to-Equity Relative Value across HY sectors Key Points: We discuss the cheapest and most expensive bonds using DEVal (debt-to-equity valuation gap) within HY sectors. 2) we include fundamental analysis and views; 3) DEVal back-testing shows 6% outperformance. Investment Overview With factor and single-name investing becoming ever more important in evaluating portfolio performance, we partnered with the Barclays QPS team to evaluate a new factor component, DEVal, which measures the relative value between bonds and equities using structural models. We overlay the signals across our US high yield coverage, noting the top bonds that screen as cheap and expensive, along with our fundamental thoughts, both where we agree and where the DEVal signal contradicts our fundamental rating. What is DEVal? DEVal measures the relative value between bonds and equities of the same issuer through the use of a structural model. When the firm is overall fairly valued, a more-positive DEVal means that the bond is cheaper compared to other bonds, and could outperform subsequently when the mispricing corrects. In backtesting, we found that US HY bonds with higher DEVals outperformed bonds with lower DEVals by over 6% per year with an information ratio of 1.43. Implications of eroding independence The academic evidence on the consequences of eroding CBI is unambiguous, and the historical record in Latin America provides a particularly stark illustration. The most immediate consequence of a compromised CBI is the de-anchoring of inflation expectations. For Colombia specifically, inflation expectations at 6.3% for end-2026 and 4.8% for 2027 already suggest imperfect credibility. Grajales-Olarte et al. (2025)’s methodology to estimate BanRep’s credibility shows the credibility stock reaching record low levels (Figure 3). Any perception that BanRep has become susceptible to govern- ment pressure would push expectations further from target, requiring an even more aggressive tightening to restore anchoring—the opposite of the outcome the government desires. CBI directly affects sovereign borrowing costs in developing countries. This mechanism operates through creditor confi- dence: investors accept lower yields when they believe that the central bank will not monetize fiscal deficits or subordi- nate price stability to political objectives. Just-released auction investor category data show that foreign investors stepped back, while investment funds at the long-end remained resilient. As rate vol subsided, April auctions have fared better so far. This is a reprint of US Treasuries: Treasury auctions: Ides of March, published on 8 April 2026. In a rare development for the Treasury market in the post-COVID era, auctions from 2y through 10y all tailed at the March auctions, underscoring the lack of investor demand amid heightened geopolitical uncertainty and elevated volatility. As the Middle East conflict intensified and oil prices surged above $100/bbl last month, investors pared back expectations for rate cuts this year. Rates sold off, the curve flattened, and appetite at Treasury auctions weakened. The auction tails have been benign and less volatile across tenors in the context of historical auction performance ( Figure 2). The last time auctions tailed across the curve was in June 2022, and the magnitude of those tails was much larger. That period was one of the most volatile in recent history, driven by sharp repricing of the Fed policy path as the market reacted to persistently high inflation prints. records.text: Global Economic Weekly | 10 April 2026 11 Italy: Growth downgrade meets rising fiscal pressures Among the main Euro area countries, Italy remains among the most exposed to energy shocks because of its energy mix (especially for gas). We revised down Italian GDP growth forecasts to 0.2% in 2026 and 0.6% in 2027, from 0.7% and 0.9% respectively. In terms of the quarterly profile, we expect growth close to zero in 2Q26 and two quarters of mildly negative growth in 2H26, with the trough in 3Q26. Sequential growth should then accelerate over the course of 2027, peaking in 2Q27 (0.4% qoq), with an average growth rate of 0.3% qoq in 2H27. Consumption is expected to be the main driver of the slowdown, while investment should remain supported by the implementation of the National Recovery and Resilience Plan (see report: Euro Area Viewpoint: Italy in 2026: stability, risks and the ultimate test), despite uncertainty-related headwinds weighing on private capital expenditure. We now expect HICP inflation to average 3.1% in 2026, around 170bp higher than in our previous forecast, before easing to 1.9% in 2027. The inflation uplift is expected to be slightly larger than the euro‑area average, reflecting a faster pass‑through to consumer energy prices, given the structure of Italy’s energy market. Beyond the oil effect, the April–June harvest should raise agricultural exports, producing larger-than-usual USD inflows that will be converted into ARS (Figure 2). records.text: Euro Area Outlook The fog of ceasefire The US-Iran ceasefire will not easily erase the scars on euro area growth and inflation left by the Middle East conflict. We continue to expect two rate hikes this year, although a de- escalation of the conflict could argue for a more patient ECB in the near term. • Incoming high-frequency indicators are consistent with sub-trend growth in the first quarter, suggesting that underlying economic momentum in the euro area was weakening even before the outbreak of the conflict in the Middle East. • If sustained, a US-Iran ceasefire could help to reduce the tail risks of broader energy supply disruptions and commodity prices that rise by even more than currently embedded in our growth and inflation forecasts. However, the path towards a normalisation of the energy outlook remains fragile and highly uncertain. • With oil and gas prices set to remain significantly higher than in the pre-war environment for an extended period, we continue to think the ECB will need to tighten monetary policy to limit the propagation and persistence of the inflation shock through indirect and second- round effects. We continue to expect the ECB to raise key policy rates by 25bp at both the April and June meetings, but acknowledge that the ceasefire could grant the Governing Council more flexibility around the timing of policy tightening. The IPCA rose 0.88% m/m in March, from 0.70% in February, coming in well above consensus expectations of 0.77% (Barclays: 0.78%), causing annual inflation to accelerate to 4.14% y/y, from 3.81%. While the end of the seasonal increase in tuition would usually cause the monthly headline to decelerate in March, higher food and transport prices ended pushing it higher, and further than hinted by the earlier upside surprise in the IPCA-15 preview. Transport costs rose 1.64% m/m, from 0.74% a month earlier, driven by higher fuel prices (4.5%, from -0.5%), even in the absence of any official increases by Petrobras to gasoline thus far, and an ongoing increase in airfares on top of an unseasonal jump in February. Food-at- home prices explained 7bp of our 10bp forecast error; they grew 1.94% m/m, from 0.23% a month earlier, the largest monthly gain since April 2022, influenced by perishables, milk, grains and beef. Core measures came in closer to expectations, up 0.43% m/m (Barclays: 0.39%; Broadcast consensus: 0.38%), from 0.62% in February, with the annual measure reaching 4.38% y/y, from 4.46%. records.text: relief in 2H • GDP contraction in 1Q likely despite solid Feb IP • Fiscal update from Hacienda evidences challenges There were not many surprises to our macroeconomic scenar- io after the releases this week. If anything, downside risks to growth, and modestly to inflation, are still in place. We con- tinue to expect a GDP contraction in 1Q26. Sentiment sur- veys and January demand-side data back our view, even if February IP was mildly positive. This framework is in stark contrast to the optimistic view of the Ministry of Finance (Hacienda), which released its updated macroeconomic framework late last week. While we agree that the fiscal dete- rioration will not be large in the context of offsetting forces in energy prices, we see important hurdles that won’t stabilize debt soon (Figure 1). Changes to the Fiscal Responsibility Law and the new Infrastructure Law approved this week are growth-positive but only until 2027. Growth optimism from Hacienda contrasts significantly with Banxico’s view and this week’s minutes were quite emphatic on the downside risks. This view on economic activity has validated the dovish bias, but with inflation struggling to resume its downward trend after the non-core shocks in March, it is not surprising that there is only space for one more cut to 6.5% in the current context. records.text: Danny Suwanapruti +65-6889-1987 | danny.suwanapruti@gs.com Goldman Sachs (Singapore) Pte Santanu Sengupta +91(22)6616-9042 | santanu.sengupta@gs.com Goldman Sachs India SPL Global Markets Daily: Asian FX Outlook Post Ceasefire and Implications of India’s FX Regulations 10 April 2026 | 5:57PM SGT Asian curves bear-flattened significantly last month as the market repriced n inflation expectations. After the announcement of a ceasefire in the Middle East on 8th April, front-end Asian rates fell sharply (by around 5-30bp across the region). Even after the correction, we think that most Asian curves are still pricing in too many hikes (~2-3 hikes in Korea, ~3 hikes in India, ~1.5 hikes in Thailand) versus our forecasts. We assessed that the Asian economies most exposed to higher oil prices are n likely to be the Philippines, Thailand and India. Their respective currencies were the regional underperformers in March. KRW also underperformed, which we attribute to the broader ‘risk off’ sentiment and drawdown in Korean equities. The reaction in Asian FX markets on the day of the ceasefire announcement was broadly just a reversal of the prior underperformers. We remain most constructive on the CNY and the MYR. Risks are also ris- ing that some economies, particularly in Asia, could face abrupt supply disruptions if fuel and other inputs become scarce. As in earlier episodes, uncertainty about the path to (or durability of) resolution, and the potential for more persis- tent supply chain dislocations, is adding to the economic and political risk premium. There are, however, important balance of payments differenc- es this time. While current accounts are likely to weaken, many EMs are entering the shock with narrower fiscal defi- cits and smaller output gaps, which have improved their cur- rent accounts relative to their starting points in 2022. In fact, several of the most exposed economies still have current account cushions that can absorb higher import bills before becoming destabilizing. Among fuel importers, India, the Philippines, Poland, and South Africa stand out as markets where deterioration looks most likely. Korea is an exception, where the current account surplus is expected to improve as technology tailwinds outweigh the oil shock. The financial account backdrop may also make the adjust- ment less punitive than in 2020 or 2022. Outflows to date have been concentrated in a handful of Asian economies with deep equity markets, while other markets have been affected more by crowded positioning and proximity to the conflict. For the first time in years, a change of gov- ernment in Hungary appears genuinely plausible. Looking at the evolution of polls over time, Tisza has consoli- dated its position as favorite to win the most seats, and in recent weeks has managed to increase popularity, despite the challenging political environment. As we have noted before, Hungary's polling landscape is best understood as two parallel ecosystems. Different pollsters consistently produce very dif- ferent results, and these differences are not random: some pollsters invariably show Fidesz winning, while others invari- ably show it losing. In the average of all published polls, Tis- za leads Fidesz by 6-7 points (Figure 1), but if we include only the most reputable pollsters, that gap widens to 12 points or more. The Dollar continues to move in unison with n headline sentiment, but we think the focus will soon move towards the economic aftermath, which in our view should be selectively supportive for the Dollar. Under our commodity strategists’ baseline assumption that energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz will gradually normalize over the next month, our economists still expect a significant deterioration in current account balances across much of Asia. In this way, we see important differences between this and prior policy evolutions; traffic through the Strait has been curtailed for more than a month, and that will have an impact on economic activity. As a result, we think the 2022 analogy will likely provide a better template for FX markets than 2025 in terms of how long the conflict can impact parts of the FX market. There are a number of important differences in terms of the magnitude and focus of the shock—including the starting point for policy and inflation, and the countries that are likely to face the most significant challenges—but our focus is more on the length of time that it took for FX markets to fully account for the fallout compared to the relatively shorter effect on broader risk sentiment and volatility. Delegating monetary policy to an independent, conservative central banker—as formalized by Rogoff (1985)—solves this commitment problem by remov- ing the inflationary bias from the policy process. As inflation stabilized in most countries during the 1990s, central bank independence became the key institutional prescription for combating inflation (Goodfriend, 2007). The last five decades have been characterized by significant changes in the institutional design of central banks around the world, generally moving toward granting monetary authori- ties a greater degree of independence from the executive branch. Romelli (2022) constructs an Extended Central Bank Independence Index (CBIE) and documents 370 reforms in central bank design between 1923 and 2023, of which 279 represent improvements to independence. CLOs: Remaining defensive, but we see opportunities for senior risk on the horizon Developments in the broadly syndicated leveraged loan market—and, by extension, the CLO universe—remain a focus for many market participants. On a year-to-date basis, CLO spreads have moved wider alongside other segments of the credit market. records.text: M Idea 6 In any case, while the scale of the pass-through of the energy shock to wage growth will certainly be part of the MPC debate in April, as we see it, the key discussion will be around how big of a hit to growth and employment is the BoE ready to accept for how much of a faster return to target? As external member Taylor outlined in this speech, if the BoE had kept interest rates 1pp higher throughout 2025, the estimated output gap at the start of 2026 would have been ~60bp wider, for the benefit of just one quarter of an earlier return to target vs. February MPR forecasts. How are we thinking about the scenarios? Central banks that have published scenarios in March already - the ECB, Riksbank - focused on the scale of the energy shock (the ECB modelled oil prices at US$145 per barrel and gas prices at €106 per MWh in their severe scenario, with the unwind of the shock slow vs. their baseline forecast). By the time we get to the BoE's April meeting, there should be a bit more certainty around where commodity market futures will settle, and so our starting assumption is that the BoE will model alternative scenarios based on the degree of second-round effects from a base case direct shock stemming from higher oil and gas prices. It is important to stress that the choice of scenarios does matter a lot for the tone of the meeting - the ECB scenarios were not symmetric in the near-term, but rather depicted varying degrees of inflation overshoot, based on commodity prices. Since we’ve already discussed agricultural prices above, we want to isolate the portion of energy costs in the 88% of food spending that goes to non-farm sources like retail overhead. The USDA Food Dollar tells us that 3% of total costs are energy-related (less than half as much as the household CPI share), and for simplicity we assume the same for just the non-farm portion, since it is difficult to strip out farm energy used solely for domestic food. Of that energy expense, petroleum-linked costs like diesel transportation are most relevant. However, past studies don’t find much pass-through from energy prices to food prices, at least outside of agricultural goods. Baumeister and Kilian (2014) remark that there is no evidence of oil price shocks leading to more than a negligible increase in retail food pric- es. Likewise, Diab and Karak (2023) note that while higher gasoline prices raise food costs, they do not find an effect on non-farm food costs. With 97% of final food costs coming from non-energy sources, labor costs are more important, especially in food away from home, and wage inflation is much lower now than during the commodity price surge in 2022. The stagflation shock is widespread but uneven In the US, we revised growth down by 50bp to 2.3% this year, with the direct impact from the war accounting for about 3/4 of the revision. For inflation, we have an 70bp revision on headline and we now expect core PCE 30bp higher at 3.1% by end-2026. In the Euro area, we marked down growth by 60bp and raised inflation forecasts by 160bp to 3.3%, with core at 2.3%. In China, inflation would likely remain low at 1%, and we think growth would still reach 4.5%, a mild 20bp downward revision. Monetary policy divergence remains alive We still expect the Fed to cut rates by 50bp this year, but we pushed back cuts from June/July to September/October (with risks of no cuts). For the ECB, we expect 50bp of hikes, but also a cutting cycle next year. Similarly, we also expect the BoE to deliver 50bp hikes to insure against second round effects. BoJ appears to prioritize growth over inflation, and we keep forecasts unchanged. In EM, rate hikes in Asia appear contained relative to the 80-100bp higher rates expected, on average, in LatAm and EEMEA. records.text: In Mexico, the full March CPI report confirmed the trend already observed in the first half of the month. While there was a notable upside surprise early in March—driven by strong increases in agricultural prices, particularly tomatoes—these pressures eased in the second half, with no renewed spike. As a result, headline inflation rose to 0.86% m/m, lifting annual inflation to 4.59% y/y, from 4.02% in February. Importantly, despite elevated oil prices, direct energy-related pressures remained contained, consistent with our view that the government’s gasoline excise tax (IEPS) mechanism continues to smooth price spikes. In terms of contributions, airfares (also affected by Easter seasonality), electricity, and gasoline added 5.5bp, 3.5bp, and 3bp, respectively. Meanwhile, the impact of shocks at the beginning of the year—including excise tax hikes on flavored beverages and tobacco, as well as the minimum wage increase—continues to track projections. Import tariffs from non-FTA countries again proved negligible, likely largely reflecting front-loaded export activity to Mexico in Q4 2025. All in, core inflation was more in line with expectations at 0.38% m/m, with annual core inflation broadly stable at 4.45% y/y. Despite high uncertainty and upside risks from potential shocks via air travel, LPG, natural gas, and fertilizers, which could eventually feed into food and restaurant prices, we expect these effects to be more moderate and transitory than in 2022. Although Senator Tillis (R-NC) has reaffirmed his unwillingness to confirm Warsh until the Department of Justice probe into Chair Powell ends, we expect that Warsh will be sworn in by the September meeting at the latest. Once chair, Warsh will be able to shape the policy options at each meeting to be more dovish. Assuming a resolution of the Iran war in the near-term, his dovish arguments should be helped by better looking sequential inflation data as tariff effects should be fading. records.text: No fundamental stress, but signs of thicker tails and less convincing technicals Since the end of last year, a more challenging macro backdrop, focus on private n credit, and concerns around AI-led disintermediation have weighed on CLO debt. Liability spreads have widened, and mezzanine tranches have underperformed the decline in loan prices as investors demand more compensation for subordination and tail risk. Fundamentals do not yet reflect this more challenging backdrop. The share of n CCC loans is below typical limits and has trended lower. Additionally, loan downgrades into CCC territory have declined and upgrade rates out of the CCC bucket have remained stable. The market, however, is pricing for deterioration, reflected in a rising share of collateral trading at distressed levels. On technicals, a lower share of resets could imply less manager conviction over n the durability of the cycle and reduced economic appeal of extending reinvestment on older collateral at current spreads. Remaining defensive and preferring structure We continue to recommend defensive positioning across managers and collateral n pools. Reset and refi deals screen as less clean, with higher distressed exposure and, in some cases, reinvestment funded by selling weaker loans at discounts. Mathematically the setting of the funds rate, R(t), is following function of inflation and unemployment: R(t) = r(lr) + π(t) + 0.5(π(t) − π(lr)) + 2(u(lr) − u(t)) We show graphs of that rule in many of our publications, including our recent scenario analysis analysing the impact of energy supply disruptions (link here). We also show the implications above, compared to our updated forecast for the funds rate. The rule can be a useful guide to where the path of policy might be headed. For example, last year we expected more rate cuts than the FOMC's SEP , because our economic projections differed from the FOMC. In retrospect, the three 25 bp rate cuts were pretty close to what the policy rule implied. The rule also does not need to be static. In the August 22, 2025 quote from Chair Powell's Jackson Hole speech, and again in the December 10 quote above, Chair Powell describes the forward-looking nature of the approach, considering the time it might take to return inflation and employment to mandate-consistent levels. The FOMC may not line up monetary policy with the rule at every point in time, but may be forward-looking, depending on their expectations for the evolution of the labor market and inflation. records.text: ed. Even after adjusting for long-term trends and cyclical dynamics, the macro data fail to reveal a clear disruption signal. This divergence between micro hints and macro stability reinforces the idea that AI’s impact is still nascent and unevenly distributed. What is becoming clearer, however, is that AI is already reshaping the nature of work. Measures of task change show that even as labor market churn slowed in 2025, workers —especially in medium- and high-exposure occupations—continued to report shifts in their job activities. This pattern is consistent with early evidence of task reconfiguration within roles, suggesting that AI is beginning to alter how work is done before materially changing how many workers are employed.

Morgan Looking further ahead Looking further ahead, it is possible that some agricultural prices for this year’s US harvest could go higher than implied by futures, either because of direct pass-through from higher fertilizer prices, or because of reduced crop supply. In the US, not all planting has been done yet, and more fertilizer will be required during the growing process. Consequently, decisions by farmers in coming months will influence the volume of this year’s harvest, and thus prices. As an example, consider corn, which as noted above is the most intense user of nitro- gen fertilizer. According to the March 31 USDA Prospective Plantings report, US farmers planned to cut their corn acreage this year by 3%, which could involve switching to alternate crops like soy, for which prospective plantings are up 4%. The June 30 USDA Acreage report will show actual plant- ings, and by August the crop production data will start to show actual harvest amounts, reflecting both acreage and yields. Larger effects could be possible into next year if prices for fertilizer remain high. records.text: Index (CAI, travel balance adjusted) delivered a downside surprise, compounded by a downward revision to the January reading. The February reading was weak at -0.4%m/m sa. In addition, the January index—which had previously pointed to strong consumption growth—was revised down by 0.7%-pts, from a 0.4% increase to a 0.3% decline. As a result, real consumption growth over the first two months of the year came in at -2.2%q/q saar, indicating a high likelihood that 1Q26 con- sumption will contract (Figure 1). We are revising our 1Q pri- vate consumption forecast from 1.5%q/q saar to -0.5%, and accordingly lowering our real GDP growth forecast to 1%. Since the onset of the Iran conflict, real money investors have been consistently strong buyers of the USD. And while positions have recovered from near five‑year lows, allocations remain largely neutral, with investors not yet overweight the currency. Digging deeper into the data reveals that domestic US investors have been the most active dollar buyers. This is reflected clearly in our USD Domestic Hedge Ratio indicator (i.e. the FX hedge ratio that US investors have adopted on their overseas portfolios). This has risen from 11.5% on February 27 th to 24% now , the magnitude being the most dramatic increase over an approximate month timeframe in the history of the series back to 1998. Last year it was US investors that led the dollar selling charge, reducing their hedge ratio from over 25% to the aforementioned low of 11.5%, the reverse is true now. While there are signs the USD strength i s reaching its limits , especially once positioning reaches overweight levels, there is a cap on downside risk until the geopolitical environment is meaningfully less turbulent. records.text: 2 Europe Economic Weekly | 10 April 2026 Weekly view Hikes here, cuts there We changed our global macro forecasts on 1 April. The narrative is unsurprising: less global growth (-40bp to 3.1%), more inflation (+90bp to 3.3%) and broadly speaking more hawkish central banks. But not everywhere. Our US colleagues still think the Fed is more likely to cut than not – the energy price increase just triggers a delay from Jun/Jul to Sep/Oct. The bar to hike seems high. The contrast to big central banks in Europe is stark: • The ECB is very worried about bigger and faster second-round effects than the Fed, and very (too?) eager to prevent them from unfolding in the first place, even if the growth damage from the initial energy price shock ends up being larger. We expect them to hike in Jun/Jul (25bp each), even if we also think that 2027 cuts to below current deposit rate levels are unavoidable anyway. • The BoE may be less inclined to hike today than the ECB. But they actually have a different underlying inflation starting point with already elevated inflation/wage expectations. So we think they may eventually deliver the exact same policy rate path as the ECB, with perhaps more risks of only one rather than two hikes. The smaller central banks are more diverse. Norges Bank has a clearer inflation challenge, hence we pencil in a hike in June. records.text: M Update 4 Next Week: All Eyes on Washington Euro area | A week for policy makers: Next week brings the release of final March inflation across several EA countries. Final prints will likely confirm the flash estimate, which showed EA headline rising to 2.5%Y on the back of higher energy inflation - see here. On the real side, EA industrial production is likely to decline by -0.3%M in February, we think, in line with recent surveys suggesting the momentum remains fragile. On the policy front, we have the ECB accounts of the March meeting, alongside a packed schedule of public appearances at the IMF Spring Meetings (see here). In March, the ECB kept rates on hold. Its projections and alternative scenarios showed large risks to inflation on the back of both higher energy prices and indirect/second round effects. Risks to growth were seen as more contained. In the accounts, we look for details on the Council discussion around the risks to the inflation outlook, and specifically how much it endorsed the views from the scenarios - namely second round effects, and the suggested asymmetry in inflation vs growth risks. Global policy discussions at the IMF and World Bank Spring Meetings come at a delicate juncture, with markets reassessing the macro implications of persistent geopolitical risks, and expectations for central banks. records.text: Moody’s reviews Belgium (Aa3, negative) and S&P reviews the Netherlands (AAA, stable). Bund ASW: The stall after the fall About a year ago, we wrote German ASWs: Hibernating bears. Our core thesis was that the tightening trend in ASWs (cheaper cash vs swaps) should re-assert itself over time and that the tariff turmoil-driven widening would not persist. We had discussed specific technicalities and dynamics around Schatz, Bobl, Bund and Buxl ASW and concluded that, all else equal, we saw most potential for Bobl and Bund-ESTR to tighten. Specifically, for Bund-ASWs, our tightening thesis rested on the following pillars: (i) repo rates should gradually cheapen away from the DFR towards the MRO as excess liquidity becomes less ample under the ECB's new operational framework (ii) we were already living through a global bond glut and the announcement of the German fiscal stimulus (increasing free-float), will exacerbate this challenge, especially with price-sensitive investors having to absorb the supply (ii) the swap leg activity is unlikely to impart a richening impulse on ASWs until the rate cycle pivots to rate hikes. These technical factors were an overlay on our structural arguments around more European integration and less fear of core-periphery frictions that could diminish the role of Bunds as a safe-haven. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 5 Financial Conditions: The market is doing the Fed's work so far Following the conflict in the Middle East and the uncertainty it brings for the next steps for monetary policy, we include the evolution of our FRB/US-based model of financial conditions, which aims to capture how changes in asset prices weigh on future economic activity. The index includes five daily variables: the 10-year Treasury yield, S&P 500 returns, the corporate BBB credit spread, the valuation of the U.S. dollar, and the price of oil. These are aggregated based on their estimated growth elasticities relative to the federal funds rate, using the Federal Reserve’s FRB/US model. As a result, the index can be interpreted as the equivalent change in the federal funds rate, expressed in basis points, required to generate a similar effect on economic activity. Since hostilities in the Middle East began on February 28, the tightening in financial conditions is equivalent to about a 48bp rise in the federal funds rate. Since the ceasefire announcement on April 7, financial conditions have eased by 24bps. The tightening in financial conditions over this period reversed all the easing earlier this year, most of which occurred between the December and January FOMC meetings and was primarily driven by a weakening U.S. dollar. In other words, a more persistent energy shock could potentially hit growth harder than the ECB thinks. This could have ramifications for the monetary policy response. Our baseline view is that for risk management reasons the ECB will hike by 50bp to 2.50%. 2.50% is the upper end of the range of neutral. Hikes to this level signal the ECB's commitment to price stability while not overly burdening growth. The uncertainties are high and there are risks on both sides. A durable ceasefire and rapid re-opening of the Strait of Hormuz might mean the ECB does not need to hike at all - although with household inflation expectations already showing a clear rise in March and further rises in HICP inflation largely baked in, some hikes still feel more likely than none at this point. At the same time, the longer the normalisation of Middle East energy supply is delayed, the greater the risk that 50bp of hikes might not be sufficient. However, this does not mean the relationship between energy prices and the scale of hikes will be linear. If growth estimates are too optimistic, there might be a limit to how far the ECB can hike. We may, however, see no cuts this year We see good reasons to retain our out-of-consensus call for cuts this year including the fact that markets are pricing in cuts again, albeit 7bp, following news of the ceasefire (Exhibit 10). That said, we acknowledge that our call is on shaky footing and the risk is towards no cuts this year. The Fed, while still having a dovish bias, isn’t as dovish as it was a year ago with policy rates closer to estimates of neutral and following the recent string of hot inflation prints. Governor Waller, who we view as the dovish thought leader, was more balanced in recent remarks. Kevin Warsh in April 2008 also expressed concerns over rising commodity prices, arguing a the time that “We must not wait until [inflation] expectations have broken out because by then it will be too late.” Therefore, if inflation continues to surprise to the upside, the war persists for longer than we expect, inflation expectations begin to climb, and/or wage inflation inflects higher, the Fed may feel it prudent to guide the markets to more two-sided risks around its next policy move. For now, however, the modal outcome is for cuts this year. More recently, we have emphasized that US policy uncertainty helped weaken the Dollar over the last year, and recent events could potentially add more momentum in this direction. That said, cyclical forces are much more important for FX returns over an investment horizon, and we see a number of reasons to be cautious in applying these bearish long-run considerations to the near-term outlook. First and foremost, as we discuss in more detail above, the energy shock will likely have more adverse economic effects on other regions than the relatively self-reliant US. We see this as a key difference to last year, when US policy uncertainty had a bigger net effect on prospective US returns. In some cases, this may make it more difficult to assess whether prospective US returns continue to warrant a weaker Dollar over the near term. Second, while there is always a lot of inertia in reserve currency choice, that is especially true in the GCC, where most of their exports are invoiced in Dollars, the currencies are pegged against the Dollar, and—by extension—almost all of their reserves are held in Dollars. These experiences point to the interaction of multiple factors determining the macroeconomic impact of shocks. Our focus is on assessing three: the nature and magnitude of the shock; the underlying resilience of the expansion; and the monetary policy response. We believe this assessment justifies a con- structive baseline view: the global expansion will absorb the latest shock with a drag slowing growth to trend and a sub- stantial but transitory inflation spike. But the assessment highlights tail risks and vulnerabilities. The non-linearities associated with a sustained closure of the Strait of Hormuz is the greatest tail risk. The biggest vulnerability is the possibili- ty of a short-circuiting of business sentiment normalization in its early stages before it rebalances demand and lifts job growth. This could force the government to return to austerity to protect its credit rating, risking continued economic stagnation. CPI outturns promote EM patience While headline inflation is moving up, the March increases in EM have been more modest than expected. Higher energy prices were tempered by smaller food price gains and more benign core readings. These outturns reinforce our view that the recent hawkish tilt in pricing central bank hikes is over- done. In Asia, India and Korea central banks expectedly signaled a wait-and-watch approach to an adverse supply shock this week. This is the general attitude around the region where we have no rates projected outside the Philippines. The 1.6%-pt headline inflation surge last month reflected low energy buf- fers and limited fiscal space. Still, our base case is for a hike to be delayed until August. Coal as a stabiliser, but on a gradually receding path The Middle East conflict has triggered a short-term, cyclical rise in coal demand across Asia, as disruptions to LNG and oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz have prompted temporary fuel switching. Higher LNG prices have led some Asian economies, including Korea, to lift caps on coal-fired output, and pushed Thailand and the Philippines to boost coal generation to stabilize power supply.15 These regional adjustments reinforce coal’s role as the default backup fuel during periods of geopolitical stress (Figure 19). In China, coal still accounts for over 50% of total consumption, with supplies largely domestically sourced, providing a buffer against external shocks (Figure 20). While China’s long-term energy trajectory is shifting toward green and low-carbon sources, coal consumption is likely to remain elevated in the near term given its critical role in power system stability and as a backup to renewable energy. 2025 saw the highest level of new coal power capacity additions in a decade, and a strong buildup and pipeline continue in 2026. Several factors underpin coal demand. First, rising electricity consumption, especially from AI, data centers, cloud computing, 5G and industrial internet, continues to rely heavily on coal. While higher commodity prices were the primary drag on their z-scores, investor sentiment also deteriorated sharply, with real money aggressively selling FX and equities against a modest overweight. The constructive takeaway is macro fundamentals have provided an important buffer: Asian exports surprise d to the upside thanks to resilient AI-related demand, strong imports coverage, and steady current-account surpluses. • The EM ex-Asia backdrop looks materially more challenging, with BRL, MXN, ZAR, PLN , HUF and CZK all slipping into negative territory for the first time since mid -2025. The key distinction versus Asia is investor behavior and macro fundamentals have both deteriorated. Media sentiment analysis also points to a pronounced deterioration in sentiment, with institutional investors remaining heavy sellers of FX. The notable exception is CLP, which continues to attract inflows, supported by its broad commodity expo sure. We were therefore well -timed in locking in LatAm profits and reassessing aggregate risk exposure amid war-related uncertainty. That said, we believe investors should not abandon EM altogether; rather, selectivity will be key as we await greater clarity on the geopolitical and macro outlook. CHART OF THE MONTH: THE REAL MONE

records.text: test NIQ-RSM Hospitality Tracker suggested that dismal weather and cautious spending stunted managed hospitality groups’ growth in February with like-for-like sales down 0.2% y-o-y (from -0.1% in Jan-26). On our models, however, this still spells some improvement on a monthly basis. While we do not expect output to recoup its lost activity from January, we still see a 1% m-o-m rise in February. Elsewhere, we expect the info/comms industry to also continue its expansion (0.2% m-o-m). Real-estate activity, we think, will likely have also bounced back with new buyer enquiries picking up and sales expectations rising – as per the latest RICS data. The latest ONS BIC survey also pointed to a rise in turnover across February – just before the Iran conflict began. We expect output here to have increased by 0.2% m-o-m. Professional services activity, we estimate, would have only risen by 0.1% m-o-m. Administrative and support services output will likely have also risen – especially after the 2.2% m-o-m drop in January. The latest KPMG/REC survey pointed to a meaningful improvement in permanent job placements. We pencil in a 1% m-o-m rise. Lastly, we see a marginal rise in public administration output. The latest public finances data showed a jump in current spending with investment also up in February (0.5% of GDP - 0.1pp above levels seen last year). In countries where internet retailing is a small share of transactions, retailers tend to tie their online prices to offline prices in order to minimise costs associated with making pricing decisions. In countries where online transactions have a significant market share, online and offline prices are closely related and online prices may lead offline as the demographic of computer-literate, middle-class, cash-rich and time-poor consumers to which online retailers sell are less price-sensitive than the average consumer. records.text: To size the headwind to industrial production from higher gas prices, we first survey academic literature. Studies on the impact of natural gas price changes specifically (as opposed to broader energy prices) mostly focus on two episodes. First, a recent body of research uses the 2022 gas crisis in Europe to estimate that a 10% increase in natural gas prices lowers industrial production by around 0.7%. Second, studies use the decline in natural gas prices during the US shale boom and find smaller impacts, estimating that a 10% decline in gas prices boosted US industrial production by around 0.3%. Given the limited academic evidence (and lack of estimates for most economies in our coverage), we rely on estimates of broader energy price effects on industrial production to size the impact of higher gas prices on industrial output. We first leverage shocks from Känzig (2021) to estimate a panel regression that identifies elasticity of industrial production to broader energy prices. We then combine this estimated elasticity with the country-specific natural gas share of energy consumption and industrial production share of GDP to estimate the hit to output from a 10% increase in natural gas prices. Third, rising oil prices could trigger energy substitution and spillover effects, lifting prices of coal and gas and amplifying PPI pressure across energy-intensive industries. While rising PPI prices, led by raw materials such as energy and chemicals, should support profitability in upstream sectors, we are concerned about margin compression in midstream and downstream industries (eg, autos, clothing) given still weak domestic demand and softer core CPI inflation. Indeed, the PPI breakdown indicates that consumer goods related PPI stayed firmly in contraction in March, underscoring the limited pricing power of downstream producers and the difficulty of passing higher input costs on to consumers. Moreover, the March NBS manufacturing PMI survey suggests that although input prices have risen sharply across manufacturing sectors, pass-through to output prices has so far remained relatively muted. Notably, the gap between output prices and input prices reached a four-year wide in March, indicating that profitability in downstream sectors has come under increasing pressure. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 7 1Q GDP tracking 2.2% Our 1Q GDP tracking inched up to 2.2% from 2.0%. A strong durables report for February after a very weak January report pushed up our estimate for equipment investment growth to 8.0% from 3.0%, adding 0.3 pct pt to 1Q GDP growth. Offsetting some of that greater strength, revisions to December and January consumer spending estimates in the income and spending report pulled down our consumption tracking by enough to subtract 0.1 pct pt from GDP. A couple of factors temporarily boost 1Q GDP: Government expenditures rise 4%, as output moved back to trend after the 4Q shutdown. The government does not make up for lost output, but output does return to its (slowing) trend. The 1Q rebound in federal spending will not be repeated. A plunge in reported software prices adds to 1Q real investment in intellectual property. The PPI data reported in the coming week will update our estimate. Software prices are volatile enough in recent quarters that we would not extrapolate the decline into later quarters. Together, those temporary factors contribute about ½ of a point to our 1Q GDP estimate. However, we estimate a slightly larger drag on GDP from the upward bias to 1Q consumer prices.
